0002-lido-locator.summary: Lido's validators are found from its LidoLocator contract, which Lido's own documentation lists; every other Lido contract is read from it on chain.
0002-lido-locator.decision: This contract is Lido's LidoLocator, the directory from which all of Lido's other contracts are read.

grounds.text: Lido's documentation lists this address as its Lido Locator
The contracts it lists agree: the staking router and stETH both withdraw to the vault it names

0002-lido-locator.would_change: Lido documentation naming a different locator, or a move to a new one.
0002-lido-locator.explanation:
Lido's validators are identified from its own contracts, starting from a single address: the LidoLocator at 0xc1d0…2eb, which [Lido's documentation lists among its deployed contracts](https://docs.lido.fi/deployed-contracts/). The locator is a directory; every other Lido contract used here (the staking router, the node operator registries, the withdrawal vault, stETH) is read from it on chain rather than taken from any list.

The addresses read from it are mutually consistent. The withdrawal credentials returned by the staking router and by stETH both point to the withdrawal vault the locator names, and stETH's Aragon kernel grants its permission manager role to Lido's Agent contract. A validator is counted as Lido's when its public key appears in one of Lido's node operator registries reached in this way; its operator is the node operator whose keys it is.

The decision would change if Lido's documentation named a different locator, or if Lido moved to a new one, which would be recorded as a new anchor.

0003-everstake-pool.summary: This contract is Everstake's pooled-staking Pool (the one Trezor stakes through): Everstake's published audit links it to Everstake's deployer, and Trezor's own code and guide use it.
0003-everstake-pool.decision: This contract is the Pool of Everstake's pooled ETH staking; the validators it deposits are Everstake's.

grounds.text: Trezor's code and staking guide name this contract as the Everstake pool that Trezor stakes through
Everstake's blog names a batch deposit contract as Everstake's own
The account that deployed this Pool also deployed that batch deposit contract
An independent audit describes Everstake's Pool, depositing with its rewards treasury as withdrawal address

0003-everstake-pool.would_change: An Everstake publication listing different contracts, or evidence the deployer works for another organisation.
0003-everstake-pool.explanation:
The contract 0xd523…be34 is the Pool of Everstake's pooled ETH staking, the pool through which Trezor's wallet stakes. Validators it deposits are attributed to Everstake as allocator. All 20,677 deposits sent through it use a single withdrawal address, 0x6be4…1e67; about 16,100 validators were active in October 2026 with some 0.51M ETH.

Trezor's use of the pool. Trezor's firmware repository gives this address as the mainnet pool for its Ethereum staking ([issue 3517](https://github.com/trezor/trezor-firmware/issues/3517)), and [Trezor's staking guide](https://trezor.io/guides/sending-receiving-staking-funds/staking-assets-in-trezor-suite/staking-ethereum-eth-in-trezor-suite) says that staking is provided by Everstake through the Everstake staking pool. [ChainSecurity's audit](https://reports.chainsecurity.com/Everstake/ChainSecurity_Everstake_ETHB2CStaking_Audit.pdf) of Everstake's staking contracts describes a pool that deposits with its rewards treasury as withdrawal address, which is how this contract behaves.

The link from Everstake itself. [Everstake's blog](https://everstake.com/resources/blog/everstakes-eth2-batch-deposit-contract-security-audited-by-ackee) announces the audit of its own batch deposit contract and links [the auditor's report](https://github.com/Ackee-Blockchain/public-audit-reports/blob/master/2025/ackee-blockchain-everstake-eth2-batch-deposit-report.pdf), which gives that contract's mainnet address. On chain, the account that created that batch deposit contract also created this Pool and its withdrawal address. The account that deployed the Pool therefore also deploys a contract Everstake publicly calls its own. The Pool and its withdrawal address also share one proxy administrator.

5,465 accounts have sent deposits to the pool; as pool participants, their identities say nothing about who controls the validators. The 95 validators deposited through Everstake's batch deposit contracts are not attributed by this decision. A deployment key could in principle deploy contracts for others, so the link from Everstake remains an inference. The decision would change with an Everstake publication listing different contracts, or evidence that the deployer or the Pool is operated for another organisation.

0005-p2p-deployer.summary: Contracts created by this account are P2P.org's, per P2P.org's own code repositories and docs, so validators deposited through them are run and allocated by P2P.org.
0005-p2p-deployer.decision: This account is P2P.org's contract deployer; validators deposited through contracts it created are run and allocated by P2P.org.

grounds.text: P2P.org's own code repositories name this account as its deployer and contract owner
P2P.org's documentation lists contracts that this account created
It created the four contracts that relayed about 23,000 deposits from 2023 on

0005-p2p-deployer.would_change: A P2P.org statement that the account deploys for others, or evidence its key changed hands.
0005-p2p-deployer.explanation:
The account 0x588e…033a deploys P2P.org's contracts. Validators deposited through contracts it created are attributed to P2P.org as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. In October 2026 about 8,800 such validators were active, with some 0.37M ETH.

Identification. P2P.org's own code names the account: a mainnet test in its [fee distributor repository](https://github.com/p2p-org/eth-staking-fee-distributor-contracts/blob/dcea97b5294999ec9c28c50155669804bb6a2d01/test/foundry/Deoracleized.t.sol) gives it as P2P.org's deployer, and one in its [SSV proxy repository](https://github.com/p2p-org/p2p-ssv-proxy/blob/84e06c3c05e624cc7bbfb39ee40c3ca671f9411b/test/MainnetIntegration.t.sol) uses it as contract owner. [P2P.org's documentation](https://docs.p2p.org/docs/unlimited-unified-api) lists mainnet contracts that this account created. On chain it created the four contracts that relayed about 23,000 deposits from 2023 onwards: two depositor contracts, an SSV proxy factory and the "Unlimited" depositor, whose deposits only P2P.org's operator can make.

Why P2P.org is the allocator. The client keeps the withdrawal address and can exit, but P2P.org holds the validator keys and decides how the stake behaves at the consensus layer, which is the control this dataset measures. P2P.org is therefore treated as an allocator with one operator, itself. The same rule is applied to every provider's depositor contracts. Of the 15,825 such validators that have exited, 462 were exited or consolidated by requests from the client's withdrawal address; the rest by voluntary exits signed with the validator key, which P2P.org (or its SSV operators) holds.

The deployer also created two Safe wallets, through the Safe factory, which sent 926 deposits. They are left out, since they are not depositor contracts. The decision would change with a P2P.org statement that the account deploys for others, or evidence that its key changed hands.

0006-binance-eth2-depositor.summary: This account makes the deposits for Binance's staking: the withdrawal address its deposits credit sends its withdrawn stake to the staking address of Binance's wBETH token; validators withdrawing to that address are Binance's.
0006-binance-eth2-depositor.decision: This account makes Binance's staking deposits; validators withdrawing to an address it deposited to are Binance's.

grounds.text: Every execution credential in its 99,749 deposits points to one withdrawal address, 0x8e60…8224
All 32,000 validators with older credentials switched to that one address together in April 2023
That address has sent all its withdrawn stake, 1.74M ETH, to the staking address set in Binance's wBETH token contract
This account, and the account that funded it, have also paid that staking address directly

0006-binance-eth2-depositor.would_change: A Binance statement or proof-of-reserves list contradicting it, or evidence the address holds stake for a client.
0006-binance-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xbdd7…32a8 makes the beacon deposits for Binance's ETH staking. Validators withdrawing to an address its deposits used are attributed to Binance's staking as allocator. In practice there is one such address, 0x8e60…8224: 123,016 validators have withdrawn to it, of which 76,900 were active in October 2026 with about 3.49M ETH. Binance decides who runs this stake; whether Binance runs the validators itself is not established, so no operator is recorded.

The deposit pattern. Between October 2021 and January 2026 the account sent 99,749 deposits. Every one with execution-layer credentials (90,576) names 0x8e60…8224; the other 9,173 used BLS credentials. All 32,319 validators in the group with BLS credentials changed to 0x8e60…8224 in April 2023, immediately after withdrawals were enabled, which shows a single holder of all their keys. Of the group's 26 deposit senders, 22, covering 121,893 validators including 0xbdd7…32a8, received their first ETH from 0xf17a…4a18, an account whose 524 transactions consist of deposits, the funding of these senders, and transfers to Binance's own wallets.

The link to Binance runs through wBETH, Binance's wrapped staked ETH, whose Ethereum contract [BNB Chain's announcement of the token](https://www.bnbchain.org/en/blog/new-wrapped-beth-is-now-available-on-bnb-chain) names. wBETH's verified source sends staked ETH to the address returned by ethReceiver(), which on chain is 0x26ad…6b86, set at the contract's initialisation and unchanged since. The withdrawal address 0x8e60…8224 has made 46 transactions in all: a 0.0001 ETH test transfer and 45 transfers to 0x26ad…6b86 totalling 1,739,061 ETH, the withdrawn stake. The deposit account and its funder have also paid 0x26ad…6b86 directly. wBETH's supply on Ethereum, about 3.52M ETH at its exchange rate, is close to the stake of these validators, though wBETH also exists on BNB Chain and need not correspond one to one.

Binance's proof-of-reserves list of 1 October 2026 does not name this account or 0x8e60…8224, but one of its listed wallets, and an account funded only by listed wallets, made deposits naming 0x8e60…8224 in 2026, which decision 0323 records. Explorer labels and community label sets naming the accounts as Binance's are recorded as leads, not relied on. The decision would change with a Binance statement or proof-of-reserves list contradicting it, or evidence that 0x8e60…8224 holds stake for a client rather than for Binance's staking product.

0007-kraken-eth2-depositor.summary: This account makes the deposits for Kraken's staking: its main withdrawal address paid the first gas of Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account; validators withdrawing to the addresses it deposited to are Kraken's.
0007-kraken-eth2-depositor.decision: This account makes Kraken's staking deposits; validators withdrawing to the addresses it deposited to are Kraken's.

grounds.text: Its deposits credit six withdrawal addresses; all 39,000 of its validators with a BLS credential moved to one, 0x210b…2a1b, in April 2023
0x210b…2a1b gave the first gas, within 40 minutes, to Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account and two other depositors
About 590k ETH of this stake exited just after withdrawals opened, when Kraken was reported to unstake

0007-kraken-eth2-depositor.would_change: A Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence the addresses hold stake for clients rather than Kraken's staking.
0007-kraken-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xa40d…8703 makes the beacon deposits for Kraken's ETH staking. Validators withdrawing at any time to an address its deposits used are attributed to Kraken's staking as allocator, and those addresses are taken to be held by Kraken. 105,102 validators have withdrawn to them; about 7,000 were active in October 2026 with some 1.04M ETH, most of it in compounding validators.

The deposit pattern. Between December 2020 and April 2025 the account sent 89,954 deposits. 39,111 used a single BLS withdrawal credential, and all of those changed to the address 0x210b…2a1b in April 2023, immediately after withdrawals were enabled: one holder of that key. The rest name six execution addresses, 0x210b…2a1b holding the most.

The link to Kraken. Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account is identified in decision 0010. On 21 March 2025, within 40 minutes (blocks 22,095,102 to 22,095,288), 0x210b…2a1b gave the first gas to that account and to two other deposit accounts (decisions 0008 and 0009). One account paying first gas to all three in the same window is taken to hold them all. In April and May 2023, about 591k ETH of this stake exited, which matches [reports that Kraken withdrew about 556k ETH of staked Ether](https://forkast.news/kraken-to-withdraw-us1-17-bln-of-staked-ether-in-line-with-sec-ruling-settlement/) after its settlement with the SEC.

Following the stake as it moves. In 2026 Kraken moved its validators by consolidation requests (EIP-7251), which only a source validator's withdrawal address can send: in March into compounding validators at the same addresses, and in June into validators at eight new addresses, now holding about 850k ETH. Addresses reached in this way are followed as Kraken's, so the stake remains attributed after it moves.

Kraken's own infrastructure. In [August 2025](https://www.payward.com/press-release/kraken-first-major-exchange-dvt-ethereum-staking-ssv-network) Kraken said its ETH staking runs entirely on SSV Network's distributed validators. Every validator attributed here, and to Kraken's other deposit accounts, is registered on SSV on single-owner clusters run by accounts whose first ETH came from the gas funder of Staked, the staking provider Kraken owns. This corroborates the attribution; it names no addresses.

Limits. Kraken publishes proof of reserves but no staking addresses. The identification is as strong as decision 0010, which rests on Kraken's announced restaking and on its EigenLayer operator's self-published metadata, and which is itself weak because anyone can delegate to an operator. Six other accounts deposit through the same contract into other addresses; they may be Kraken's institutional clients and are not included here. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that these addresses hold stake for clients rather than for Kraken's staking product.

0008-kraken-240-depositor.summary: This account (0xed20…8ab0), funded by the same account as Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account and depositing like Kraken's other accounts, makes deposits for Kraken's staking.
0008-kraken-240-depositor.decision: This account (0xed20…8ab0) makes deposits for Kraken's staking; validators withdrawing to its addresses are Kraken's.

grounds.text: Its first gas came from 0x210b…2a1b, within 40 minutes of the same top-up to Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account
Its principal came from 0x210b…2a1b, a withdrawal address of Kraken's main depositor (decision 0007)
It deposits through the same contract as Kraken's main depositor and moved its stake in the same weeks

0008-kraken-240-depositor.would_change: A Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence it deposits keys chosen by a client.
0008-kraken-240-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xed20…8ab0 makes deposits for Kraken's staking, and validators withdrawing to its addresses are attributed to Kraken's staking as allocator. It deposited 8,173 validators between April 2025 and February 2026, through the same batch deposit contract as Kraken's main deposit account (decision 0007); in October 2026 about 880 of its validators, mostly compounding, were active with some 0.23M ETH.

The link to Kraken. On 21 March 2025 the address 0x210b…2a1b, one of Kraken's withdrawal addresses under decision 0007, gave this account its first 0.1 ETH of gas. Within the same 40 minutes it gave the first gas to Kraken's EigenLayer restaking account (decision 0010) and to another deposit account (decision 0009). One account paying first gas to all three in the same window is taken to hold them all. The same address then sent this account 33 ETH just before its first deposit, and 32,906 ETH before its first large batch.

The pattern. Like Kraken's other accounts in 2025, it deposited most validators with its own address as withdrawal address. It moved its stake by consolidation in the same weeks of March and June 2026 as Kraken did, partly into an address that carries the same contract code as one of Kraken's own consolidation targets.

Limits. The batch contract it used has no caller check, so using it does not by itself show that Kraken sent a deposit; the link rests on the funding. The identification is also only as strong as decision 0010, which rests on Kraken's announced restaking and on its EigenLayer operator's self-published metadata. Whether Kraken holds this stake for itself or for a client, Kraken chose who runs the validators, which makes it the allocator. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposits keys a client chose.

0010-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-4462.summary: This account, funded by Kraken's tagged wallets, deposits into an EigenLayer pod it owns, matching Kraken's announced restaking of customers' ETH; its validators are Kraken's.
0010-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-4462.decision: This account makes deposits for Kraken's staking, restaked through an EigenLayer pod it owns; its validators are Kraken's.

grounds.text: Its deposits all go to an EigenLayer pod it owns, created through EigenLayer's pod manager
Kraken announced in October 2024 that it would restake customers' ETH through EigenLayer
It delegates to an EigenLayer operator whose own published metadata names it Kraken

0010-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-4462.would_change: A Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence it deposits keys chosen by a client.
0010-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-4462.explanation:
The account 0x4462…e86c made deposits for Kraken's staking, restaked through an EigenLayer pod it owns; its validators are attributed to Kraken's staking as allocator. It deposited 3,802 validators between May and September 2025, holding as much as 122k ETH; by October 2026 they had been consolidated into other validators.

Restaking. Every deposit went to an EigenLayer pod created through EigenLayer's pod manager and owned by this account, so the withdrawals are the account's. Kraken [announced in October 2024](https://decrypt.co/286494/kraken-launches-restaking-on-ethereum-based-protocol-eigenlayer) that it would restake customers' staked ETH through EigenLayer, so pods owned by Kraken's accounts are expected. Restaking delegates the pod's stake to an EigenLayer operator for additional services; it does not change who runs the validators. The account delegates to an operator whose [own published metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Layr-Labs/eigendata/7dd2961e836d888698ce66f25ae1e6b8a135b500/operators/Kraken2/metadata.json) names it "Kraken [2]".

The link to Kraken. Its first gas came on 21 March 2025 from 0x210b…2a1b, a withdrawal address of Kraken's main deposit account (decision 0007), within the same 40 minutes as the first gas of two other deposit accounts (decisions 0008 and 0009). Another of Kraken's withdrawal addresses then sent it 23 ETH just before its first deposit and 107,000 ETH before its large batches of June 2025. It deposited through the same batch contract as Kraken's main account, later paid the first gas of a further Kraken deposit account (decision 0012), and its pod consolidated its validators in June 2026, the same weeks as Kraken's other accounts.

Limits. This decision is the reference point for several others, and it is itself weak. The restaking announcement is reported by a third party, and anyone can delegate to an EigenLayer operator, so the operator's name shows only that the account chose a Kraken-named operator. The funding from Kraken's withdrawal addresses is the stronger link. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposits keys a client chose.

0013-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-45e3.summary: This account, funded by Kraken's tagged wallets, deposits into an EigenLayer pod it owns, matching Kraken's announced restaking of customers' ETH; its validators are Kraken's.
0013-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-45e3.decision: This account makes deposits for Kraken's staking, restaked through an EigenLayer pod it owns; its validators are Kraken's.

0013-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-45e3.would_change: A Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence it deposits keys chosen by a client.
0013-kraken-eigenpod-depositor-45e3.explanation:
The account 0x45e3…667e makes deposits for Kraken's staking, restaked through an EigenLayer pod it owns; its validators are attributed to Kraken's staking as allocator. It deposited 240 validators between December 2025 and May 2026, all to its pod; in October 2026, after consolidation, 108 compounding validators were active with some 79k ETH.

Restaking. Every deposit goes to an EigenLayer pod created through EigenLayer's pod manager and owned by this account, so the withdrawals are the account's. Kraken [announced in October 2024](https://decrypt.co/286494/kraken-launches-restaking-on-ethereum-based-protocol-eigenlayer) that it would restake customers' staked ETH through EigenLayer. Restaking delegates the pod's stake to an EigenLayer operator for additional services without changing who runs the validators. The account delegates to an operator whose [own published metadata](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Layr-Labs/eigendata/7dd2961e836d888698ce66f25ae1e6b8a135b500/operators/Kraken/metadata.json) names it "Kraken", though anyone can delegate to it.

The link to Kraken. Its first gas came in November 2025 from 0xed9b…, a withdrawal address of Kraken's main deposit account (decision 0007), within the same 40 minutes as the first gas of two other Kraken restaking accounts (decisions 0011 and 0012). Its principal, about 79,000 ETH, came from the same address. It deposited through the same batch contract as Kraken's main account, and its pod consolidated its validators in June 2026, the same weeks as Kraken's other accounts.

The batch contract has no caller check, so using it does not by itself show that Kraken sent a deposit; the link rests on the funding. Whether Kraken holds this stake for itself or for a client, Kraken chose who runs the validators. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposits keys a client chose.

0016-coinbase-staking-2021.summary: These 96 addresses held Coinbase's 2021 retail staking: their deposits were funded by Coinbase's tagged hot wallets in fixed batches, and their withdrawals went back to Coinbase.
0016-coinbase-staking-2021.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 96 addresses were Coinbase's retail staking, from 2021.

grounds.text: All 96 addresses sent every payment out to 0x69e2…325e (rewards) or 0xc7bf…a019 (exited stake)
All 38,000 validators moved to these 96 addresses within two days of withdrawals opening, ~400 each
They pass on 84% and 95% of what they get to 0xa9d1…3e43, which receives all minted cbETH, or to the deposits' funders
Coinbase's own code names the cbETH contract whose minted tokens all go to 0xa9d1…3e43

0016-coinbase-staking-2021.would_change: A Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence the addresses belong to someone who only funded deposits from Coinbase.
0016-coinbase-staking-2021.explanation:
These 96 withdrawal addresses held Coinbase's retail staking from 2021. The validators, 38,494 in all with about 1.23M ETH, made up as much as 15.5% of all stake in mid-2021; all had exited by 2025. Coinbase is the allocator; the stake was its customers'. Coinbase ran validators both itself and through providers, and which ran these is not established, so no operator is recorded.

Deposits. Each validator was deposited directly to the deposit contract from a different single-use account, between April 2021 (when Coinbase launched ETH staking) and April 2023. In a sample of 400 deposits, each sender received exactly 32 ETH plus gas in a single transfer seven to nine blocks before depositing, and 392 of the 400 transfers came from the same small set of Coinbase hot wallets. 38,303 validators used one of 193 BLS withdrawal credentials.

The move to execution addresses. On 13 and 14 April 2023, within two days of withdrawals being enabled, all 38,303 validators with BLS credentials changed to execution credentials, into exactly 96 addresses holding 400 or 401 validators each. Making that change requires each BLS key, so a single holder of all 193 keys acted at once, in fixed-size buckets.

Where the ETH went. Every one of the 96 addresses' outgoing transactions was checked in full. All of their 1,378,914 ETH went to two accounts: rewards to 0x69e2…325e and exited stake to 0xc7bf…a019. Those two pass on most of what they receive to 0xa9d1…3e43, which receives all newly minted cbETH (the token [Coinbase's own published code](https://github.com/coinbase/agentkit/blob/f2f3e8c11a91d56a17979a229a172ba6e61a85c2/typescript/agentkit/src/action-providers/erc20/constants.ts) names as its staked ETH), or to the wallets that funded the deposits. The same operation's other deposit group is attributed in decision 0017.

There is no deposit account to anchor on, since every validator came from a fresh account, so the attribution is made for the addresses as a whole. Explorer labels on the funding wallets and the receiving accounts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence that the addresses belong to someone who merely funded deposits from Coinbase.

0017-coinbase-staking-2021-b.would_change: A Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence the addresses belong to someone who only funded deposits from Coinbase.
0017-coinbase-staking-2021-b.explanation:
These 93 withdrawal addresses held more of Coinbase's retail staking from 2021, by the same arrangement as decision 0016. The validators, 37,291 in all with about 1.19M ETH, made up as much as 6.8% of all stake in early 2023; all had exited by April 2025. They form a separate group from 0016's only because their deposit senders and BLS keys do not overlap. Coinbase is the allocator; the stake was its customers'. No operator is recorded.

Deposits. Between March 2021 and April 2023 the validators were deposited steadily, 36,358 of them directly from single-use accounts and 933 through Coinbase's batch deposit contract. In a sample of 200 deposits, each sender received exactly 32 ETH plus gas in a single transfer a few blocks before depositing (median ten blocks), and 198 of the transfers came from the same Coinbase hot wallets that funded 0016's deposits. 37,190 validators used one of 197 BLS withdrawal credentials.

The move to execution addresses. On 14 and 15 April 2023, two days after withdrawals were enabled, all 37,190 validators with BLS credentials changed to execution credentials, into exactly 93 addresses holding 400 or 401 validators each: one holder of all the keys acting at once, in fixed-size buckets, as in 0016.

Where the ETH went. Every address's outgoing transactions were checked in full. 92 of the 93 sent everything to the same two accounts as 0016's: rewards to 0x69e2…325e and exited stake to 0xc7bf…a019. The remaining address also sent 32 ETH, one validator's stake, to an account about which nothing is known. Those two accounts pass most of what they receive to 0xa9d1…3e43, which receives all newly minted cbETH (named as Coinbase's staked ETH token in [Coinbase's own published code](https://github.com/coinbase/agentkit/blob/f2f3e8c11a91d56a17979a229a172ba6e61a85c2/typescript/agentkit/src/action-providers/erc20/constants.ts)), or to the wallets that funded the deposits.

Explorer labels on the counterparties are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence that the addresses belong to someone who merely funded deposits from Coinbase.

0020-coinbase-staking-2023.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 412 addresses are Coinbase's retail staking, from 2023.

grounds.text: Each address holds exactly 400 validators, each deposited from a single-use account, as in 2021
All 411 addresses that have swept rewards sent them to 0x69e2…325e; 387 sent their exited stake to 0xc7bf…a019
They pass on 84% and 95% of what they get to 0xa9d1…3e43, which receives all minted cbETH, or to the deposits' funders
Coinbase's own code names the cbETH contract whose minted tokens all go to 0xa9d1…3e43

0020-coinbase-staking-2023.would_change: A Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence that addresses belong to someone else: notably 24 that return exited stake to the account that funded them.
0020-coinbase-staking-2023.explanation:
These 412 withdrawal addresses hold Coinbase's retail staking from April 2023, continuing the arrangement of its 2021 staking (decisions 0016 and 0017). Between April 2023 and September 2026 they received 164,800 validators; 88,151 were active in October 2026 with about 2.8M ETH. Coinbase is the allocator; the stake belongs to its customers. No operator is recorded.

The pattern. Each address holds exactly 400 validators, every one deposited directly to the deposit contract, with credentials naming the address, from a sender account that made no other deposit. Each sender received its 32 ETH in a single transfer about ten blocks before depositing. For 387 of the 412 addresses the funding came from the same small set of hot wallets that funded the 2021 staking; for one it came from an account those wallets first funded; for 24 it came from 0x7c87…b102, a high-volume wallet.

Where the ETH goes. Every address's outgoing transactions were checked in full. All 411 that have swept rewards sent them to 0x69e2…325e, and 387 sent their exited stake to 0xc7bf…a019. Those two accounts pass 84% and 95% of what they receive to 0xa9d1…3e43 or to the wallets that funded the deposits. 0xa9d1…3e43 receives all newly minted cbETH, the token Coinbase's own published code ([its AgentKit token list](https://github.com/coinbase/agentkit/blob/f2f3e8c11a91d56a17979a229a172ba6e61a85c2/typescript/agentkit/src/action-providers/erc20/constants.ts)) names as its staked ETH. Rewards and principal therefore return to Coinbase.

The 24 addresses funded by 0x7c87…b102 sweep their rewards to the same account as the others, but send their exited stake to 0x6dca…3287, which has returned all it received (127,552 ETH) to 0x7c87…b102. That fits a client staking through Coinbase: Coinbase runs the validators and collects their rewards, while the principal returns to its source. Coinbase remains the allocator.

Explorer labels on the funding wallets are recorded as leads, not relied on. The decision would change with a Coinbase statement contradicting it, or evidence that any of these addresses belongs to someone else, notably the 24 whose exited stake goes elsewhere.

0023-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2020.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 7 addresses are Bitcoin Suisse's staking, from 2020.

grounds.text: Every block their validators have proposed since 2020, 140,776 of them, is signed "bitcoinsuisse.com"
All switched to these 7 addresses in mid-2023, which only the holder of their keys could do
Their withdrawals go to 0x7b45…fcb1, which also receives those of Bitcoin Suisse's later staking (decision 0024)

0023-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2020.would_change: A Bitcoin Suisse statement contradicting it, or evidence clients chose the operators or held the withdrawal keys.
0023-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2020.explanation:
These seven withdrawal addresses hold Bitcoin Suisse's staking from 2020. Their validators, 13,857 deposited between November 2020 and May 2023, were the largest single group at the beacon chain's launch, 13.7% of all stake on 1 December 2020. About 8,900 were active in October 2026 with some 0.29M ETH. Bitcoin Suisse is the allocator; the stake is its clients' and possibly its own.

The graffiti. Every block proposed by a validator that has ever withdrawn to one of these addresses carries graffiti beginning "bitcoinsuisse.com", alone or followed by client codes: 140,776 blocks by 13,826 validators, with no other graffiti at all.

The deposits and keys. Every validator was deposited by one of six accounts that made no other deposits, and no other account has deposited to these addresses. All used BLS credentials, and between May and July 2023 each was changed to one of these seven addresses. Only the holder of a validator's BLS key can make that change.

The link to Bitcoin Suisse's later staking. The addresses send their withdrawals to 0x7b45…fcb1, which also receives those of Bitcoin Suisse's later staking (decision 0024). In one block on 20 October 2023 five of these addresses and two of 0024's swept to it together, so one operator runs both.

Limits. Graffiti is set by whoever runs a validator, and anyone could type a name. A fleet of this size signing Bitcoin Suisse's own domain on every block for six years is taken to be Bitcoin Suisse's, or run for it under its name. That also makes Bitcoin Suisse the likely operator, though no operator is recorded. Explorer labels on the deposit accounts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Bitcoin Suisse statement contradicting it, or evidence that clients chose the operators or held the withdrawal keys.

0024-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2023.summary: These 9 addresses hold Bitcoin Suisse's staking since 2023: every block their validators proposed is signed bitcoinsuisse.com, and they withdraw to the same wallet as its 2020 staking.
0024-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2023.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 9 addresses are Bitcoin Suisse's staking, from 2023.

0024-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2023.would_change: A Bitcoin Suisse statement contradicting it, or evidence a client chose its own operator for some of these validators.
0024-bitcoin-suisse-staking-2023.explanation:
These nine withdrawal addresses hold Bitcoin Suisse's staking since 2023, continuing its staking from 2020 (decision 0023). 17,449 validators were deposited to them between May 2023 and August 2026; about 10,500 were active in October 2026 with some 0.34M ETH. Eight of the addresses hold exactly 2,000 validators each, and the ninth was still filling. Bitcoin Suisse is the allocator.

The graffiti. Every block proposed by a validator that has ever withdrawn to one of these addresses carries graffiti beginning "bitcoinsuisse.com", alone or followed by client codes: 66,061 blocks by 14,993 validators, with no other graffiti at all.

The link to Bitcoin Suisse's 2020 staking. All nine addresses sweep their withdrawals to the same wallet, 0x7b45…fcb1, as the 2020 addresses do. In one block on 20 October 2023, two of these addresses swept to it together with five of the 2020 addresses: one operator runs both. Some sweeps go instead to an account first funded by that wallet, which itself sent 1,644 of these deposits.

The deposits. All went directly to the deposit contract, from 287 sending accounts. Many were funded by accounts already linked to Bitcoin Suisse; others look like clients' own accounts. Whoever funded a deposit, the validator's withdrawals go to Bitcoin Suisse's wallet, so Bitcoin Suisse holds the stake and set up the validators. Thirteen other small groups of validators deposited alongside these, each withdrawing to its sender's own address, are left out, since they may be clients' own.

Limits. Graffiti is set by whoever runs a validator, and anyone could type a name. A fleet of this size signing Bitcoin Suisse's own domain on every block is taken to be Bitcoin Suisse's, or run for it under its name; no operator is recorded. Explorer labels on the accounts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Bitcoin Suisse statement contradicting it, or evidence that a client chose its own operator for some of these validators.

0025-okx-eth2-depositor.summary: This account makes the deposits for OKX's staking: OKX's signed proof-of-reserves file lists it and every validator withdrawing to the addresses it deposited to.
0025-okx-eth2-depositor.decision: This account makes OKX's staking deposits; validators withdrawing to the addresses it deposited to are OKX's.

grounds.text: OKX's signed proof-of-reserves file lists this account, and as OKX's staking every validator withdrawing to its two addresses
Each validator's row is signed "I am an OKX address" with the key of the withdrawal address it names
No other account deposited to either withdrawal address

0025-okx-eth2-depositor.would_change: An OKX statement contradicting it, or evidence it deposits keys chosen by clients.
0025-okx-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0x5a00…3a11 makes the beacon deposits for OKX's ETH staking, and validators withdrawing to the addresses it deposits to are attributed to OKX's staking as allocator. 38,902 validators were first deposited by it between December 2020 and September 2026; about 6,500 were active in October 2026 with some 0.64M ETH, increasingly in compounding validators.

OKX's own proof of reserves. OKX publishes [a wallet file with each proof of reserves](https://static.okx.com/cdn/okx/por/chain/por_csv_2026100300_V4.zip); the snapshot of 3 October 2026 was used. The file lists this account itself among OKX's addresses. It also lists 7,718 validators as native ETH staking, 7,678 of them withdrawing to this account's two withdrawal addresses, 0xe839…506c and 0xd5f8…7634. Each staking row carries the signature of a message reading "I am an OKX address". Recovering the signer of every one of the 8,031 staking rows gives in each case the withdrawal address the row names, so OKX holds those addresses' keys.

The list was checked in both directions. Every validator withdrawing to either address and active at the snapshot is on the list, and every listed validator that appears in the sampled beacon state is one of them. No other account has ever deposited to either address. Withdrawn ETH goes to addresses OKX's file also lists.

What this establishes. A row in the file shows that OKX holds the validator's withdrawal key and counts the validator in its reserves as staked customer ETH, which makes OKX the allocator. The file does not say who operates the validators, so no operator is recorded. The decision would change with an OKX statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposits on clients' instructions to keys they chose.

The contracts' public source code lets anyone deposit, so a few depositors may use other operators

0029-figment-eth2-depositor-1.would_change: A Figment statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys Figment does not run.
0029-figment-eth2-depositor-1.explanation:
The contract 0xf2be…dab1 is a Figment depositor contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Figment as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 73,344 validators were deposited through it between February 2022 and October 2026, from 551 sending accounts to 552 withdrawal addresses; about 17,400 were active in October 2026 with some 580k ETH.

Identification. [Figment's documentation](https://docs.figment.io/docs/our-eth-batch-smart-contract) names two batch deposit contracts as its own. One of them was created by the account 0x1dae…3e3c, which also created this contract and a second one (decision 0030). All four have the same verified source code (FigmentEth2Depositor). A contract created by the account that created Figment's documented contract, with Figment's own code, is taken to be Figment's.

Why Figment is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This follows the general rule applied to providers' depositor contracts (as for P2P.org, decision 0005).

The largest client was Celsius (14,107 validators, all exited by January 2024; see decision 0028). Celsius held its customers' ETH, but under the same rule Figment, the provider it chose, is the allocator, with Celsius holding the withdrawal address.

Limits. The contract's deposit function is open to anyone while it is not paused, so a deposit through it does not by itself prove that Figment runs the validator; a client could in principle deposit keys run elsewhere. Explorer labels naming the contract as Figment's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Figment statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors use the contract with keys Figment does not run.

0033-kiln-batch-deposit-v1.explanation:
The contract 0x9b8c…e394 is Kiln's first batch deposit contract, now retired: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Kiln as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 21,323 validators were deposited through it between November 2021 and March 2024, from 123 sending accounts; they held as much as 535k ETH, and almost all have since exited.

Identification. [Kiln's documentation](https://docs.kiln.fi/v1/kiln-products/more-tools/eth-batch-deposit-contract) names this contract as its V1 batch deposit contract and marks it deprecated, and [Kiln's code repository](https://github.com/kilnfi/deposit-batch-contract) names the same contract. Its successor is decision 0034.

Why Kiln is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005), including where the client is an integrator or a custodian.

Limits. The contract lets anyone deposit, so a few depositors may have used it with keys run by other operators. The decision would change with a Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors used the contract with keys Kiln did not run.

0034-kiln-batch-deposit-v2.summary: Kiln's documentation names this as its batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run by Kiln for its clients.
0034-kiln-batch-deposit-v2.decision: This contract is Kiln's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Kiln.

grounds.text: Kiln's documentation names this contract as its V2 batch deposit contract
It took over from the V1 contract the same page names: V2's first deposit was 2024-03-27, V1's last 2024-03-30

0034-kiln-batch-deposit-v2.would_change: A Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys Kiln does not run.
0034-kiln-batch-deposit-v2.explanation:
The contract 0x5768…867e is Kiln's batch deposit contract (version 2): validators first deposited through it are attributed to Kiln as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 20,785 validators were deposited through it between March 2024 and October 2026, from 326 sending accounts; about 4,400 were active in October 2026 with some 0.41M ETH, much of it in compounding validators.

Identification. [Kiln's documentation](https://docs.kiln.fi/v1/kiln-products/more-tools/eth-batch-deposit-contract) names this contract as its V2 batch deposit contract, alongside a deprecated V1 contract (decision 0033). V2 took over from V1: its first deposit was on 27 March 2024 and V1's last on 30 March 2024. The account that created it also created other contracts Kiln operates, including the one behind MetaMask's validator staking.

Why Kiln is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). It holds where the client is itself an integrator or a custodian.

Limits. The contract is open to anyone, so a deposit through it does not by itself prove that Kiln runs the validator. Explorer labels on the contract and its creator are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors use the contract with keys Kiln does not run.

0035-kiln-ledger-live-dedicated.summary: Kiln's documentation names this as the contract behind Ledger Live's dedicated staking; validators deposited through it were run by Kiln.
0035-kiln-ledger-live-dedicated.decision: This contract is Kiln's dedicated-staking contract used from Ledger Live; validators deposited through it were run and allocated by Kiln.

grounds.text: Kiln's documentation names this contract as the one behind dedicated staking from Ledger Live
Each of its 25,900 validators had its own withdrawal address, one per staker
All had exited by November 2025, after the Ledger Live staking app was retired

0035-kiln-ledger-live-dedicated.would_change: A Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys Kiln does not run.
0035-kiln-ledger-live-dedicated.explanation:
The contract 0x1e68…0270 is Kiln's dedicated-staking contract, through which users of the Ledger Live wallet staked ETH. Validators first deposited through it are attributed to Kiln as allocator and operator, while each staker kept their own withdrawal address. 25,909 validators were deposited through it between November 2022 and September 2025, from 6,333 sending accounts, each validator with its own withdrawal address; they held as much as 460k ETH. All had exited by November 2025, after the Ledger Live staking application was retired.

Identification. [Kiln's documentation](https://docs.kiln.fi/v1/integrations/wallets/stake-from-ledger-live/using-kiln-dapp/dedicated-validators) names this contract as the one behind dedicated staking from Ledger Live.

Why Kiln is the allocator. A staker depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the staker keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005), and it holds where the staker reaches the provider through a wallet integration such as Ledger Live.

The decision would change with a Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors used the contract with keys Kiln did not run.

0037-kiln-factory-8659.summary: This contract was created by Kiln's tagged deployer, so validators deposited through it are taken to be run by Kiln; no source names the contract itself.
0037-kiln-factory-8659.decision: This contract is Kiln's; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Kiln.

grounds.text: The same account created the batch deposit contract Kiln's documentation names as its own
No published source names this contract itself

0037-kiln-factory-8659.would_change: A Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys Kiln does not run.
0037-kiln-factory-8659.explanation:
The contract 0x8659…aa83, a factory that creates per-client staking contracts, is taken to be Kiln's: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Kiln as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 1,214 validators were deposited through it between November 2025 and October 2026, from 1,210 sending accounts, each with its own withdrawal address; about 1,060 were active in October 2026 with some 0.11M ETH, many of them compounding.

Identification. No published source names this contract. It was created by the same deployment account that created Kiln's documented version 2 batch deposit contract (decision 0034) and the contract behind MetaMask's validator staking. That is the only link, which makes this the weakest of the Kiln attributions.

Why Kiln is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). However, the MetaMask contract created by the same deployment account turned out to be administered by Consensys rather than Kiln (decision 0135), so a contract's creator does not by itself settle who runs it.

An explorer label on the deployment account is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with a Kiln statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors use the contract with keys Kiln does not run.

0038-stakefish-eth2-depositor.summary: This contract, whose code is stakefish's published batch deposit contract and whose validators almost all sign stakefish's graffiti, is stakefish's; validators deposited through it are run by stakefish.
0038-stakefish-eth2-depositor.decision: This contract is stakefish's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by stakefish.

grounds.text: Its verified code is the batch deposit contract in stakefish's own repository, as it stood five days before deployment
Of 21,061 validators deposited through it that have proposed a block, 20,773 sign stakefish's graffiti
Anyone paying its fee can deposit through it, and 279 of those validators sign other graffiti

0038-stakefish-eth2-depositor.would_change: A stakefish statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys stakefish does not run.
0038-stakefish-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The contract 0x0194…d801 is stakefish's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to stakefish as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 25,334 validators were deposited through it between November 2020 and October 2026, from 1,278 sending accounts; about 4,100 were active in October 2026 with some 0.30M ETH.

The code. The contract's verified source is identical, once comments and blank lines are removed, to [the batch deposit contract in stakefish's own repository](https://github.com/stakefish/eth2-batch-deposit/blob/21d92341d6/contracts/BatchDeposits.sol) as it stood on 18 November 2020, five days before the contract was created. stakefish [announced the completion of its audit](https://blog.stake.fish/getting-closer-to-launch-the-stakefish-batch-deposit-contract-audit-is-complete/) before launch. The contract charges a service fee for each validator, paid to the provider.

The graffiti. Of the 21,061 validators deposited through it that have proposed a block, 20,773 have signed graffiti naming stakefish ("Stake Earn Relax 🐠 stakefish" or similar). 279 signed only other graffiti and nine only blank.

Limits. Anyone can deploy a copy of published code, and anyone paying the fee can deposit through the contract, so neither the code nor the route alone shows that stakefish runs a validator. With almost every validator signing stakefish's name, the contract is taken to be stakefish's. The 279 validators signing other graffiti are probably clients of other operators using the contract; they remain with stakefish here. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a stakefish statement contradicting it, or evidence that more depositors use the contract with keys stakefish does not run.

0039-kiln-vpool-00a0.summary: This contract is one of Kiln's vPools, created by the same factory as Kiln's tagged vPool implementation; validators it deposits are run by Kiln.
0039-kiln-vpool-00a0.decision: This contract is one of Kiln's vPools; the validators it deposits are run and allocated by Kiln.

grounds.text: Its factory recorded "Kiln" as its operator's name when created, and the pool calls itself "Kiln vPool Shares"
Every block proposed by its validators, 32,205 of them, is signed "Kiln.fi"
A vPool deposits validators itself, from keys registered with its own factory

0039-kiln-vpool-00a0.would_change: Evidence the vPool's keys come from an operator other than Kiln.
0039-kiln-vpool-00a0.explanation:
The contract 0x00a0…3bb9 is one of Kiln's vPools, a pooled-staking contract that takes ETH from an integrator's users and deposits validators itself from keys registered with its own factory. Validators it deposits are attributed to Kiln as allocator and operator. It deposited 16,853 validators between August 2023 and October 2026, all withdrawing to a single withdrawal recipient contract; about 9,700 were active in October 2026 with some 0.31M ETH.

Identification. No published source names this address; the identification rests on what the contract records about itself and on its validators' graffiti. The pool's name() returns "Kiln vPool Shares", and when its factory was created it recorded "Kiln" as its operator's name. Its code, and that of the factory system it belongs to, is Kiln's vPool suite, with Kiln named as author in the verified source. Every one of the 32,205 blocks its validators have proposed is signed "Kiln.fi".

Why the code alone is not enough. Another vPool built from the same Kiln code and the same factory system names itself "Coinbase Cloud vPool Shares" and records Coinbase Cloud as its operator, and none of its blocks name Kiln (decision 0040). Running Kiln's code therefore does not by itself make a vPool Kiln's; here the pool's own records and its graffiti both name Kiln.

Why Kiln is the allocator. Users and integrators that stake through Kiln's vPool have chosen Kiln, which supplies the keys and runs the validators; this is the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). The decision would change with evidence that the vPool's keys come from an operator other than Kiln.

evidence.ref: SetMetadata("Kiln", "", "") emitted by vFactory 0xc63d…ba86 at its creation, block 17,791,853

0041-blockdaemon-batch-deposit.summary: This contract is a deployment of Blockdaemon's open-source batch deposit contract, which Blockdaemon's docs direct clients to; validators deposited through it are run by Blockdaemon.
0041-blockdaemon-batch-deposit.decision: This contract is Blockdaemon's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Blockdaemon.

grounds.text: Its code is Blockdaemon's open-source batch deposit contract, down to its distinctive deadline check
Blockdaemon's docs have clients send deposits to its batch contract before an agreed deadline
No published source names this deployment, so someone else could have deployed the same code

0041-blockdaemon-batch-deposit.would_change: A Blockdaemon statement that it is not its contract, or evidence someone else deploys it.
0041-blockdaemon-batch-deposit.explanation:
The contract 0x3f12…242f is a deployment of Blockdaemon's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Blockdaemon as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 53,652 validators were deposited through it between November 2022 and October 2026, from 105 sending accounts; about 32,700 were active in October 2026 with some 1.09M ETH.

Identification. The contract's verified source is [Blockdaemon's open-source batch deposit contract](https://gitlab.com/Blockdaemon/open-source/eth2-batch-deposit-contract/-/blob/main/contracts/eth2-batch-deposit.sol), differing only in minor keywords and a constructor check. It includes a distinctive feature: each batch carries a deadline, and the contract rejects a transaction submitted after it. That matches [Blockdaemon's staking API](https://docs.blockdaemon.com/reference/postethereumstakeintent), which reserves validators for a client for a fixed period and returns an unsigned transaction addressed to its batch deposit contract.

Limits. No published source names this particular deployment, and the code is open source, so another party could have deployed it. It was created through a Safe by an account with no known name, and its deposit function has no caller check. The identification rests on the code match and on how the contract is used.

Why Blockdaemon is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address (the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts, as for P2P.org in decision 0005). Among the clients is Celsius, whose 6,294 validators deposited through this contract in 2023 are therefore Blockdaemon's rather than Celsius's own (decision 0028).

The decision would change with a Blockdaemon statement that the contract is not its own, or evidence that another party deploys and uses it.

0042-etherfi-node-beacon.summary: This contract is the template behind ether.fi's node contracts (ether.fi's code); validators withdrawing to an ether.fi node, or to an EigenLayer pod one owns, are ether.fi's.
0042-etherfi-node-beacon.decision: This contract is the template of ether.fi's node contracts; validators withdrawing to an ether.fi node, or to an EigenLayer pod one owns, are allocated by ether.fi.

grounds.text: ether.fi's StakingManager, named in its deployment records, reports this contract as its node beacon
ether.fi's deployment records name the account that created and controls it
ether.fi's code says each node contract owns one EigenLayer pod
23,330 node contracts were created from it; 103,000 validators withdraw to them or their pods

0042-etherfi-node-beacon.would_change: An ether.fi statement contradicting it, or evidence some nodes serve stakers who chose their own operator.
0042-etherfi-node-beacon.explanation:
ether.fi's validators are found through the contract 0x3c55…c03f, the template (beacon) from which ether.fi creates a node contract for each validator or group of validators. Validators withdrawing to an ether.fi node contract, or to an EigenLayer pod that a node owns, are attributed to ether.fi's staking as allocator. They numbered about 103,000 in all, 24,540 of them active in October 2026 with about 1.7M ETH.

Identification. The beacon was created by, and is owned by, 0x25e8…912d. [ether.fi's deployment records](https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts/blob/master/deployment/EtherFiNodesManager/2026-06-26-22-16-11.json) name that account as its StakingManager, and [ether.fi's code](https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts) states that each node contract owns one EigenLayer pod. 23,330 node contracts have been created from the beacon. 488 of them receive withdrawals directly (one validator each, from May 2023); the other 23,308 each own an EigenLayer pod that their validators withdraw to (from November 2023). The pods' owners are read from EigenLayer's pod contracts.

Why ether.fi is the allocator. Node operators obtain validators through ether.fi's auction and whitelist, and the stake comes from its liquidity pool (eETH) or, in its early period, from stakers who chose ether.fi. Most deposits were sent through two Safe multisigs; they are not needed to identify the stake, since the withdrawal side identifies ether.fi directly. No operator is recorded, because the auction records that would name one are not read. No validator here has a conflicting allocator claim.

An explorer label naming the beacon as ether.fi's is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with an ether.fi statement contradicting it, or evidence that some nodes were created for stakers who chose their own operator.

0043-renzo-proxy-admin.summary: This contract administers Renzo's contracts, including the RestakeManager its docs list (read on chain); validators withdrawing to EigenLayer pods those contracts own are Renzo's.
0043-renzo-proxy-admin.decision: This contract administers Renzo's contracts; validators withdrawing to EigenLayer pods those contracts own are allocated by Renzo.

grounds.text: Renzo's documentation lists its RestakeManager, and this contract is that contract's administrator
It administers five contracts that own EigenLayer pods and point to the RestakeManager

0043-renzo-proxy-admin.would_change: A Renzo statement contradicting it, or a pod owner under it that is not Renzo's.
0043-renzo-proxy-admin.explanation:
The contract 0x9162…1982 administers Renzo's contracts. Validators withdrawing to an EigenLayer pod owned by one of the contracts it administers are attributed to Renzo's restaking (ezETH) as allocator. 42,890 validators have withdrawn to such pods, first activated in December 2023; by October 2026 only about 550 remained active, Renzo having withdrawn almost all of its native restaking.

Identification. [Renzo's documentation](https://docs.renzoprotocol.com/docs/contracts) lists its RestakeManager contract. The RestakeManager's EIP-1967 administrator slot holds 0x9162…1982. That administrator controls five contracts which own EigenLayer pods; all five share one implementation and each stores the RestakeManager's address. Four were created by Renzo's deployment account and the fifth by another account. All the validators withdrawing to their pods were deposited through a proxy contract that Renzo's deployment account created.

Why Renzo is the allocator. Renzo chooses the node operators that run its validators and the EigenLayer operators its delegators delegate to. No operator is recorded. No validator here has a conflicting allocator claim.

No source names the administrator itself, so the link rests on chain data from the documented RestakeManager. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Renzo statement contradicting it, or a pod owner under this administrator that is not Renzo's.

A further 81 validators withdrawing to the same address were deposited in 2022 and 2023, before River's own deposits began, through the Safe multisig 0xde55…6b62; since they withdraw to Liquid Collective's address, they are Liquid Collective's too. No validator here has a conflicting allocator claim.

Why Liquid Collective is the allocator. River deposits with keys supplied by the node operators Liquid Collective registers, so the protocol chooses the operators. No operator is recorded, because River's operator registry is not read.

Explorer labels on the contracts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Liquid Collective statement contradicting it.

0047-staked-eth2-depositor-4.would_change: A Staked or Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence the account deposited keys Staked did not run.
0047-staked-eth2-depositor-4.explanation:
The account 0x8626…1b32 deposited validators that Staked runs: validators whose first deposit it sent are attributed to Staked as allocator and operator, while the client keeps its own withdrawal address. It sent the first deposits of 332 validators between 12 June 2021 and 12 June 2024. All have since exited.

The route. [Staked's repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract) names 0x39dc…da29 as its batch deposit contract, and [Staked's FAQ](https://staked.us/faq/eth2/) says it takes up to 185 validators a transaction. Staked ran validators for clients, who deposited from their own wallets and kept their withdrawal keys. The same contract is also the route Consensys documents for its staking clients, whose accounts never batch more than 100 validators and pay fee recipients of their own (decisions 0142 to 0149 and 0229 to 0236); this account's validators pay Staked's instead.

The fee recipient. After the Merge, 332 of its 332 validators that proposed blocks paid their rewards to Staked's fee recipient 0xe94f…6ca0c, in 3,234 of 3,252 blocks. That address is Staked's execution-reward pool (decision 0153): [Staked says it collects its validators' execution-layer rewards](https://staked.us/faq/ethereum-withdrawals/) and pays them on to stakers after its commission, and this address has made over 9,000 payments to stakers. Its first incoming transfer came from a wallet linked by funding to the account that created Staked's batch contract, and that wallet has received 800 ETH of commission from it.

Staked has been part of Kraken since December 2021; it is kept as its own provider. Explorer labels naming the account as one of Staked's depositors are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Staked or Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposited keys Staked did not run.

It sent the first deposits of 185 validators on 22 November 2020. 183 were active in October 2026.

The route. [Staked's repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract) names 0x39dc…da29 as its batch deposit contract, and [Staked's FAQ](https://staked.us/faq/eth2/) says it takes up to 185 validators a transaction. Staked ran validators for clients, who deposited from their own wallets and kept their withdrawal keys. The same contract is also the route Consensys documents for its staking clients, whose accounts never batch more than 100 validators and pay fee recipients of their own (decisions 0142 to 0149 and 0229 to 0236); this account's validators pay Staked's instead.

The fee recipient. After the Merge, 183 of its 183 validators that proposed blocks paid their rewards to Staked's fee recipient 0xe94f…6ca0c, in 2,295 of 2,317 blocks. That address is Staked's execution-reward pool (decision 0153): [Staked says it collects its validators' execution-layer rewards](https://staked.us/faq/ethereum-withdrawals/) and pays them on to stakers after its commission, and this address has made over 9,000 payments to stakers. Its first incoming transfer came from a wallet linked by funding to the account that created Staked's batch contract, and that wallet has received 800 ETH of commission from it.

Staked has been part of Kraken since December 2021; it is kept as its own provider. Explorer labels naming the account as one of Staked's depositors are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Staked or Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposited keys Staked did not run.

[Staked's repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract) names 0x39dc…da29 as its batch deposit contract, and [Staked's FAQ](https://staked.us/faq/eth2/) says it takes up to 185 validators a transaction. Staked ran validators for clients, who deposited from their own wallets and kept their withdrawal keys. The same contract is also the route Consensys documents for its staking clients, whose accounts never batch more than 100 validators and pay fee recipients of their own (decisions 0142 to 0149 and 0229 to 0236); this account's validators pay Staked's instead.

The fee recipient. After the Merge, 885 of its 885 validators that proposed blocks paid their rewards to Staked's fee recipient 0xe94f…6ca0c, in 11,000 of 11,105 blocks. That address is Staked's execution-reward pool (decision 0153): [Staked says it collects its validators' execution-layer rewards](https://staked.us/faq/ethereum-withdrawals/) and pays them on to stakers after its commission, and this address has made over 9,000 payments to stakers. Its first incoming transfer came from a wallet linked by funding to the account that created Staked's batch contract, and that wallet has received 800 ETH of commission from it.

Staked has been part of Kraken since December 2021; it is kept as its own provider. Explorer labels naming the account as one of Staked's depositors are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Staked or Kraken statement contradicting it, or evidence that the account deposited keys Staked did not run.

0069-upbit-eth2-depositor.summary: Upbit says it runs its own validators and began staking ETH in 2022; this account and the twelve before it were funded by the same wallets that run Upbit's Polygon validator, so its deposits are Upbit's.
0069-upbit-eth2-depositor.decision: This account makes Upbit's staking deposits; validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are Upbit's.

grounds.text: Upbit's operator Dunamu says Upbit runs its own validators and began staking ETH in 2022
Every gas payment to Upbit's Polygon validator came from wallets that fund this account's deposits
This account and twelve before it deposited all these validators in turn from January 2022
96% of the 1.22M ETH they deposited came from one closed network of wallets; most of the rest is restaked rewards

0069-upbit-eth2-depositor.would_change: An Upbit statement contradicting it, or evidence that the funding wallets or the withdrawal address belong to someone other than Upbit.
0069-upbit-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0x4489…7f97 makes the beacon deposits for Upbit's ETH staking, and validators withdrawing to its withdrawal address, 0x7e2a…2d05, are attributed to Upbit as allocator. 37,657 validators have withdrawn to that address; about 20,100 were active in October 2026 with some 0.64M ETH. Upbit runs its own validators, but no operator claim is made.

What Upbit says. Dunamu, Upbit's operator, states in its [half-year report for 2026](https://dart.fss.or.kr/dsaf001/main.do?rcpNo=20260814003803) that Upbit Staking runs its own validators and nodes, keeps staked assets in cold wallets, and began staking with Ethereum in 2022. It publishes no Ethereum addresses. In June 2026 Dunamu announced that Upbit was [the largest of Polygon's 102 validators](https://news.mtn.co.kr/news-detail/2026062410251155977), with about 413 million POL. On Polygon's staking contract at that date exactly 102 validators were active and the largest held 413.25 million POL, so that validator is Upbit's; its owner and signer accounts are on Ethereum.

The deposits. Every validator withdrawing to 0x7e2a…2d05 was first deposited by one of 13 accounts used in sequence: twelve from January 2022 to April 2023 (with BLS credentials, later changed to 0x7e2a…2d05), then 0x4489…7f97 from April 2023. Each account began where the previous one stopped, and each received a 0-ETH transaction from the same account just before it started depositing: one operator setting up each new depositor.

The link to Upbit. The 13 accounts received 1,215,587 ETH. 96% came from a closed network of wallets which deal almost only with one another, an operator's internal wallet system rather than a public venue; most of the rest is restaked rewards. Every gas payment ever made to the signer of Upbit's Polygon validator (21 payments) came from wallets in that same network, and its owner account was funded by another. Withdrawn stake returns to the network.

Limits. The link from Dunamu's statements to these addresses runs through the Polygon validator and the shared wallets; Dunamu names no Ethereum address. Since the funding network is closed and covers every deposit since 2022, a customer staking independently would have to share Upbit's internal wallets. Explorer labels and community label sets naming the accounts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with an Upbit statement contradicting it, or evidence that the funding wallets or the withdrawal address belong to someone other than Upbit.
