0070-mantle-meth-staking.summary: mETH Protocol's documentation names this as its Staking contract; validators withdrawing to the addresses it deposits to are Mantle's (mETH).
0070-mantle-meth-staking.decision: This contract is the Staking contract of Mantle's mETH Protocol; validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are allocated by Mantle.

grounds.text: mETH Protocol's documentation names this as its Staking contract
Its deposits all use the withdrawal contract mETH's documentation names, and no other deposits do

0070-mantle-meth-staking.would_change: mETH's docs or contracts showing the contract deposits on others' behalf.
0070-mantle-meth-staking.explanation:
The contract 0xe3cb…e8f is the Staking contract of Mantle's mETH Protocol, and validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are attributed to Mantle as allocator. It deposited 30,681 validators between October 2023 and August 2026; mETH held 1.7% of all stake at its peak in 2024, and about 6,100 validators with 0.19M ETH in October 2026.

Identification. [mETH Protocol's documentation](https://docs.mantle.xyz/meth/components/smart-contracts/staking-meth.md) names this contract as its Staking contract, and the address its validators withdraw to, 0xd4e1…493f, as its consensus-layer receiver. Every deposit the contract sent uses that withdrawal address, and no validator deposited in any other way withdraws to it. All of the contract's transactions came from a single account.

Why Mantle is the allocator. [mETH's documentation on node operators](https://docs.mantle.xyz/meth/dev/node-operators.md) explains that the protocol uses several node operators, whose validators its own service requests and funds. The protocol therefore chooses the operators. No operator is recorded.

Explorer labels on the contracts are recorded as leads. The decision would change if mETH's documentation or contracts showed the Staking contract depositing on others' behalf.

0071-rocket-pool-storage.summary: Rocket Pool's own software names this as RocketStorage, where it registers its contracts; validators withdrawing to pools created by those contracts are Rocket Pool's.
0071-rocket-pool-storage.decision: This contract is RocketStorage, Rocket Pool's contract registry; validators withdrawing to pools created by the contracts it registers are allocated by Rocket Pool.

grounds.text: Rocket Pool's own node software names this address as RocketStorage
The contracts it registers as pool creators created every Rocket Pool minipool and megapool

0071-rocket-pool-storage.would_change: Treating Rocket Pool's permissionless node operators as allocators of their own validators, or a pool creator found not to be Rocket Pool's.
0071-rocket-pool-storage.explanation:
The contract 0x1d8f…fa46 is RocketStorage, the registry in which Rocket Pool records the addresses of its contracts. The pools created by the contracts it registers as pool creators (minipools, and since the Saturn upgrade megapools) are Rocket Pool's, and validators withdrawing to them are attributed to Rocket Pool as allocator. 44,533 validators have withdrawn to 42,362 minipools and 113 megapools; Rocket Pool held 3.1% of all stake at its peak in 2023, and about 13,200 validators with 0.42M ETH in October 2026.

Identification. [Rocket Pool's own node software](https://github.com/rocket-pool/smartnode/blob/af2a4284652fcc430dd72181e4f6e2a7e5bce056/shared/services/config/smartnode-config.go) gives this address as its mainnet storage contract. Reading the registry on chain, block by block, gives the pool-creating contract in force at each time: the minipool manager from November 2021, the minipool factories after the Redstone and Atlas upgrades, and the megapool factory after Saturn. Every Rocket Pool minipool and megapool was created by one of them. The node deposit contracts registered at each time made 41,603 first deposits, all withdrawing to pools of these creators. The pool-creator rule also finds 162 solo validators that joined Rocket Pool between April 2023 and June 2024 by changing their BLS credentials to an Atlas minipool; they are counted as Rocket Pool's only from the change.

Why Rocket Pool is the allocator. Node operators join without permission and bond part of each validator's stake; the protocol assigns rETH holders' ETH to them by its own rules. Treating the protocol rather than each node operator as the allocator is a framing choice, discussed among the method's failure modes. No operator is recorded.

Explorer labels on Rocket Pool's contracts are recorded as leads. The decision would change if permissionless node operators were treated as the allocators of their own validators, or if a pool creator were found not to be Rocket Pool's.

0072-htx-eth2-depositor-1.summary: This account's ETH came from a reserve wallet whose ownership HTX (formerly Huobi) proved by signature, and from the hot wallets that fill it; its validators moved to an address HTX's reserves started.
0072-htx-eth2-depositor-1.decision: This account made HTX's (formerly Huobi) staking deposits; validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are HTX's.

grounds.text: HTX's proof of reserves signs for a wallet that sent this account 15,000 of its 40,000 ETH
Another 15,000 ETH came from hot wallets that keep that reserve wallet filled
Its validators moved to an address whose first transaction came from another signed HTX reserve wallet

0072-htx-eth2-depositor-1.explanation:
The account 0x194b…9d5b2 made HTX's (formerly Huobi) first staking deposits, and validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are attributed to HTX as allocator. It deposited 1,243 validators in December 2020; together with HTX's second deposit account (decision 0073), its validators held 2.8% of all stake at their peak in early 2021. All have since exited. HTX's customers owned the stake.

HTX's reserve wallets. HTX's proof-of-reserves snapshots of [December 2022](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/9c076d8b56423de666100a481566e0a30a8db0fc/snapshot/huobi_por_20221201_part.csv) and [May 2023](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/a3b042159258e58f6b10198788367a3ebf6d0dfa/snapshot/huobi_por_20230501.csv) list reserve addresses, each with a signature from the address's own key over a fixed message, which proves that HTX controls it.

The funding. The account received 40,000 ETH in ten transfers in December 2020. 15,000 ETH came from 0xcac7…c3fc, one of the signed reserve wallets, and another 15,000 from two high-volume hot wallets that keep that reserve wallet supplied (390,000 ETH between them).

The withdrawal address. All the validators were deposited with BLS credentials and later changed to 0x08de…375d. That address's first transaction was 0.1 ETH from 0xa5d7…951e, another signed reserve wallet, in April 2023; it has since sent its withdrawals on, and part of them back to HTX's other deposit account to be restaked.

Explorer labels on the accounts are recorded as leads. No operator is recorded. The decision would change with an HTX statement contradicting it.

evidence.note: Signed HTX reserve wallet 0xa5d7 makes the first transaction to the withdrawal address 0x08de

0073-htx-eth2-depositor-2.summary: Much of this account's ETH came from reserve wallets whose ownership HTX (formerly Huobi) proved by signature; its validators withdraw to an address HTX's reserves started.
0073-htx-eth2-depositor-2.decision: This account made HTX's (formerly Huobi) staking deposits; validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are HTX's.

grounds.text: Two wallets HTX's proof of reserves signs for sent this account 38,503 ETH
Its validators withdraw to an address whose first transaction came from another signed HTX reserve wallet
That address sends withdrawals back to this account to be restaked

0073-htx-eth2-depositor-2.explanation:
The account 0xb73f…2b7c made HTX's (formerly Huobi) staking deposits from December 2020 to November 2023, and validators withdrawing to the address they used are attributed to HTX as allocator. It sent the first deposits of 2,744 validators; together with HTX's first deposit account (decision 0072), its validators held 2.8% of all stake at their peak in early 2021. All have since exited. HTX's customers owned the stake.

HTX's reserve wallets. HTX's proof-of-reserves snapshots of [December 2022](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/9c076d8b56423de666100a481566e0a30a8db0fc/snapshot/huobi_por_20221201_part.csv) and [May 2023](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/a3b042159258e58f6b10198788367a3ebf6d0dfa/snapshot/huobi_por_20230501.csv) list reserve addresses, each with a signature from the address's own key over a fixed message, which proves that HTX controls it.

The funding. The account received 87,980 ETH in 131 transfers between December 2020 and October 2023. 38,503 ETH came from two of the signed reserve wallets, and 5,796 ETH came back from its own withdrawal address to be restaked.

The withdrawal address. Its 1,633 validators with BLS credentials were later changed to 0x08de…375d, and its 1,111 later validators were deposited with that address directly. The address's first transaction was 0.1 ETH from another signed reserve wallet in April 2023, and it sends withdrawals on and back to this account.

Explorer labels on the accounts are recorded as leads. No operator is recorded. The decision would change with an HTX statement contradicting it.

evidence.note: Signed HTX reserve wallet 0xa5d7 makes the first transaction to the withdrawal address 0x08de

0074-wex-eth2-depositor.summary: This account was funded from wallets that WEX's former ETH funded in 2017, as reported when WEX collapsed; its validators are attributed to whoever holds WEX's former funds.
0074-wex-eth2-depositor.decision: This account made the deposits for the staking of WEX's former funds; validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are attributed to WEX's former funds, holder unknown.

grounds.text: 2018 reports trace BTC-e's ETH to a WEX wallet in July 2017, and 480,000 ETH on to another WEX wallet
The chain matches them exactly: 485,705 ETH on 29 July 2017, then 480,000 ETH to one exchange hot wallet
80% of this account's ETH came from wallets those WEX wallets funded in 2017, dormant until 2020

0074-wex-eth2-depositor.would_change: Evidence of who held WEX's ETH in 2020, or that these wallets passed to someone unconnected with WEX.
0074-wex-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xbb84…86db made deposits for the staking of the former funds of WEX, the exchange that succeeded BTC-e and closed in 2018. Validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are attributed to "WEX (former funds; holder unknown)" as allocator: whoever controlled WEX's former wallets in 2020. 650 validators withdraw there, all active in October 2026; they made up 2.4% of all stake at the beacon chain's launch.

The 2017 wallets. [ForkLog reported in October 2018](https://forklog.com/news/bitkoin-birzha-binance-zamorozila-svyazannye-s-wex-scheta) that 485,705 ETH left an address that had belonged to BTC-e on 29 July 2017, and that 480,000 ETH more went in 32 transactions, from September 2017 to January 2018, to another WEX wallet. The chain matches exactly: on 29 July 2017 one exchange hot wallet sent 485,705.46 ETH to another address, its last outgoing transaction; that address then sent 480,000 ETH in 33 transfers between September 2017 and January 2018 to a further exchange hot wallet.

The deposits. In November 2020 the account received 15,514 ETH from 95 wallets, many in a single block, and deposited 500 validators with BLS credentials, later changed to 0xf4d1…63c5; that address itself deposited 150 more in 2023. 80% of the account's ETH came from wallets funded out of the 2017 WEX wallets' outflows, most of them funded in September 2017 and then dormant until 2020. Its first funder received its only ETH from WEX's hot wallet in September 2017.

Limits. The identification rests on news reports from 2018, which give amounts and dates but no addresses; the chain matches them exactly. WEX had closed two years before the deposits, so who held the funds in 2020 is unknown. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. No operator is recorded. The decision would change with evidence of who held WEX's ETH in 2020, or that these wallets passed to someone unconnected with WEX.

evidence.note: First funding, from 0xfaf2, which got its only ETH from 0xb3aa in 2017
485,705 ETH leave BTC-e's former address for 0x8eb3 (29 July 2017)
0x8eb3 starts sending 480,000 ETH to the hot wallet 0xb3aa

0077-everstake-eth2-depositor.summary: This account made Everstake's first staking deposits: its validators moved to a multisig whose owners deposited 12,000 more, and nearly all of them sign Everstake's graffiti.
0077-everstake-eth2-depositor.decision: This account made deposits for Everstake; validators withdrawing to the address its validators moved to are allocated by Everstake.

grounds.text: All its 200 validators later moved to one multisig wallet, which only their key holder could do
Owners of that wallet deposited 12,000 more validators to it in 2024
Of the 12,499 validators withdrawing there that have proposed, 12,486 sign "Everstake / Pro" graffiti

0077-everstake-eth2-depositor.would_change: Evidence that address belongs to an Everstake client rather than Everstake.
0077-everstake-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xf79c…00b9 made Everstake's first staking deposits, and validators withdrawing to the address its validators moved to, the multisig wallet 0x2bf9…4087, are attributed to Everstake as allocator. 12,567 validators have withdrawn to that wallet; about 9,400 were active in October 2026 with some 0.30M ETH.

The chain of control. The account deposited 200 validators in November 2020, all with BLS credentials. By June 2023 all 200 had been changed to 0x2bf9…4087, a 2-of-4 Safe multisig created that month; only the holder of their keys could make the change. Two of the Safe's owners then deposited 12,345 more validators to it in 2024, through a batch contract, and a third owner created the Safe.

The graffiti. Of the 12,499 validators withdrawing to the Safe that have proposed a block, 12,486 have signed graffiti beginning "Everstake / Pro"; twelve only left blocks blank and one signed only a client version string. A fleet of this size signing Everstake's name on nearly every block is taken to be Everstake's.

Limits. Graffiti is chosen by whoever runs a validator, and anyone could type a name; the identification rests on that, and on the chain of control from the first deposits. It also suggests Everstake runs the validators, though no operator is recorded. Whether the ETH is Everstake's own or its clients' is not established. Explorer labels and community label sets naming the accounts are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the Safe belongs to a client of Everstake rather than to Everstake.

evidence.note: First deposit through 0x9ac8 to the Safe

0078-stakewise-pool-escrow.summary: StakeWise's own list of its contracts names this as its V2 Pool Escrow; validators withdrawing to it were StakeWise's pool's.
0078-stakewise-pool-escrow.decision: This contract is the Pool Escrow of StakeWise V2; validators withdrawing to it were StakeWise's pool's.

grounds.text: StakeWise's own list of its mainnet contracts names this as its V2 Pool Escrow
Its validators were deposited through StakeWise's Pool and Oracles contracts, from the same list

0078-stakewise-pool-escrow.would_change: StakeWise's contract list naming a different escrow.
0078-stakewise-pool-escrow.explanation:
The contract 0x2296…f079 is the Pool Escrow of StakeWise's version 2 staking pool, and validators withdrawing to it are attributed to StakeWise as allocator. 2,751 validators withdrew to it; they made up 0.53% of all stake at their peak in 2021, and all have since exited.

Identification. [StakeWise's own list of its mainnet contracts](https://github.com/stakewise/contracts/blob/29022d7c4628420efe5fed0560e5269db07d9892/networks/mainnet.md) names this contract as its V2 Pool Escrow, together with the pool's Pool and Oracles contracts. The validators were deposited through the Pool contract from February 2021 (912 first deposits, most of them sent by one of its operators of the time) and through the Oracles contract from January 2022 (1,839), all with the Pool Escrow as withdrawal address.

StakeWise chose the operators of its pool, so it is the allocator; no operator is recorded. StakeWise's version 3 vaults are covered by decision 0105. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change if StakeWise's contract list named a different escrow.

0079-stakewise-solos.summary: This contract, whose source is in StakeWise's repository, ran StakeWise's Solos service; validators deposited through it were run by StakeWise.
0079-stakewise-solos.decision: This contract is StakeWise's Solos contract; validators deposited through it were run and allocated by StakeWise for users who kept their own withdrawal key.

grounds.text: It was created by the account that created 15 of the 60 contracts StakeWise lists as its mainnet contracts
Its source code, in StakeWise's repository, describes validators StakeWise registers for users

0079-stakewise-solos.would_change: Evidence the contract was used with keys StakeWise did not run.
0079-stakewise-solos.explanation:
The contract 0xeadc…6ceca ran StakeWise's Solos service, in which StakeWise ran standalone validators for users who kept their own withdrawal key. Validators first deposited through it are attributed to StakeWise as allocator. 381 validators were deposited through it, making up 0.14% of all stake at their peak; all have since exited.

Identification. The contract's verified source is Solos, whose [source in StakeWise's repository](https://github.com/stakewise/contracts/blob/526a3c12f5cc45b4008e3c1a16a1b8f1494d85b5/contracts/collectors/Solos.sol) describes it: users can create standalone validators with their own withdrawal key through this contract, for a monthly price, with StakeWise's operators registering the validators. On chain, it was created by the account that created 15 of the 60 contracts StakeWise lists as its mainnet contracts.

Why StakeWise is the allocator. Users chose StakeWise's service, and StakeWise's operators registered and ran the validators, while the users kept the withdrawal key; this is the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). No operator is recorded. An explorer label is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with evidence that the contract was used with keys StakeWise did not run.

0080-cream-eth2-depositor.summary: CREAM's docs list every transaction it deposited to the beacon chain with; this account sent most of them, and all the validators moved to one address. They were CREAM's crETH2 staking.
0080-cream-eth2-depositor.decision: This account made the deposits for CREAM Finance's crETH2 staking; validators withdrawing to the address they moved to were CREAM's.

grounds.text: CREAM's docs list the 17 transactions that deposited its 787 crETH2 validators; this account sent 13 of them
786 of those validators moved to one withdrawal address, which no other validator uses
CREAM ran the validators for crETH2 holders as a custodial service, with an 8% fee

0080-cream-eth2-depositor.would_change: Evidence the account deposited for others, or a CREAM statement contradicting it.
0080-cream-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xb2c4…2fdb made the deposits for the crETH2 staking of CREAM Finance, a lending protocol: validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are attributed to CREAM as allocator. 786 validators withdrew there; they made up 2.1% of all stake at the beacon chain's launch, and all exited in April and May 2023.

What CREAM published. CREAM's documentation [lists every deposit transaction of its migration to Ethereum 2.0](https://github.com/CreamFi/cream-docs/blob/049f43ad1103626776d9e1bc4a28097704df4e7e/eth2/migration-schedule.md), seventeen transactions covering validators 0 to 786, and [names its crETH2 contract](https://github.com/CreamFi/cream-docs/blob/049f43ad1103626776d9e1bc4a28097704df4e7e/eth2/ethereum-2.0-contract-address.md). CREAM ran the validators for crETH2 holders as a custodial service, for 8% of the rewards.

On chain. The seventeen listed transactions deposited 787 validators between November 2020 and June 2021, all with BLS credentials; this account sent thirteen of them. 786 of the validators were later changed to 0x1cd9…62ed, and they are every validator that address has ever had.

CREAM chose and ran the validators for its token holders, so it is the allocator. No operator is recorded. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the account deposited for others, or a CREAM statement contradicting it.

0081-ankr-eth2-staking.summary: This contract, which Ankr's docs name its mainnet GlobalPool, made the deposits for Ankr's liquid staking; validators withdrawing to the withdrawal pool its docs name are Ankr's.
0081-ankr-eth2-staking.decision: This contract made the deposits for Ankr's liquid staking; validators withdrawing to its withdrawal pool are Ankr's.

grounds.text: Ankr's developer docs name this contract its mainnet GlobalPool, the contract users stake ETH through
The same docs name the address its validators withdraw to as the withdrawal address for Ankr validators

0081-ankr-eth2-staking.would_change: Evidence the contract deposited for others, or that the tag is wrong.
0081-ankr-eth2-staking.explanation:
The contract 0x84db…6670 is Ankr's liquid staking pool, which made the deposits for Ankr's ETH liquid staking: validators withdrawing to the withdrawal pool it names are attributed to Ankr as allocator. 1,840 validators were deposited through it between November 2020 and November 2025; they made up 1.4% of all stake at their peak in early 2021, and 261 were active in October 2026.

Identification. [Ankr's developer documentation](https://www.ankr.com/docs/staking-for-developers/smart-contract-api/eth-api/) names this contract as its mainnet GlobalPool, the contract users stake ETH through, and its [page on liquid staking mechanics](https://www.ankr.com/docs/staking-for-developers/dev-details/eth-liquid-staking-mechanics/) names 0x6742…9348 as the withdrawal address for Ankr's validators. Every validator deposited through the pool either names that withdrawal address or was later changed to it from BLS credentials.

Ankr chooses the operators of its pool's validators, so it is the allocator. No operator is recorded. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the contract deposited for others.

0083-bitpie-depositor.summary: Bitpie names this account as its ETH 2.0 staking address, with 900 validators; validators whose first deposit it sent, and the address they withdraw to, are Bitpie's staking.
0083-bitpie-depositor.decision: This account made the deposits for Bitpie's (a wallet app) staking; validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are Bitpie's.

grounds.text: Bitpie publishes this account as its ETH 2.0 staking address: 900 validators, 28,800 ETH
It sent the first deposits of exactly 900 validators, all later moved to one withdrawal address
Bitpie pools its users' ETH into these validators and keeps 10% of the rewards

0083-bitpie-depositor.would_change: A Bitpie statement contradicting it, or evidence that the withdrawal address is not Bitpie's.
0083-bitpie-depositor.explanation:
The account 0xa858…32ed made the deposits for the staking service of Bitpie, a wallet app: validators withdrawing to the address they moved to are attributed to Bitpie as allocator. It deposited exactly 900 validators, 28,800 ETH, between November and December 2020; they made up 2.4% of all stake at their peak in December 2020, and 148 were active in October 2026. The stake is Bitpie's users'.

What Bitpie published. [Bitpie's announcement of November 2022](https://bitpie.zendesk.com/hc/zh-cn/articles/7550883279247) discloses this account as its ETH 2.0 staking address, with 900 validators and 28,800 ETH. [Its guide of March 2021](https://bitpie.zendesk.com/hc/zh-cn/articles/360003812175) explains the service: users stake from 0.1 ETH through Bitpie's custodial cloud wallet, Bitpie sets up a validator for every 32 ETH, issues tokens one for one, and keeps 10% of the rewards.

On chain. The account sent the first deposits of exactly 900 validators, all with BLS credentials, later changed to 0x9f4b…481a. Every block these validators have proposed since September 2022 carries graffiti that encodes this account's own address, in the format used for the beacon chain's commemorative tokens, so whoever ran them put Bitpie's address in their graffiti. The account and its withdrawal address were both first funded by the same wallet, and the withdrawal address pays out to many addresses, as Bitpie's wallet paying its users would.

No operator is recorded. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Bitpie statement contradicting it, or evidence that the withdrawal address is not Bitpie's.

0084-stakehound-eth2-depositor.summary: This account made the deposits for StakeHound's liquid staking, including the validators whose withdrawal key was lost, as reported in the press.
0084-stakehound-eth2-depositor.decision: This account made the deposits for StakeHound's liquid staking; the validators it deposited are StakeHound's.

grounds.text: Every validator it deposited that has proposed a block, 1,863 of 2,045, signed "StakeHound ⚡️Allnodes"
1,172 of its validators still have no withdrawal address, holding about 37,500 ETH
That matches the 38,178 ETH StakeHound said in 2021 was locked when a withdrawal key was lost

0084-stakehound-eth2-depositor.would_change: Evidence the account deposited for others, or that the tag is wrong.
0084-stakehound-eth2-depositor.explanation:
The account 0x607e…31b7 made the deposits for the liquid staking of StakeHound, and the validators it deposited are attributed to StakeHound as allocator. It deposited 2,045 validators between December 2020 and May 2023, making up 1.2% of all stake at their peak in 2021. 872 withdraw to 0xf272…9394 and exited in 2023; 1,172, holding 37,504 ETH, are still active.

The graffiti. Every one of the 1,863 validators it deposited that has proposed a block signed "StakeHound ⚡️Allnodes" on its blocks, apart from some blocks carrying client version strings only. The validators name StakeHound, and Allnodes, its node provider, throughout.

The lost key. The 1,172 validators still active have kept their original BLS withdrawal credentials and have no execution withdrawal address. Their 37,504 ETH of principal is consistent with the 38,178 ETH that StakeHound said in 2021 had been locked after the shares of its withdrawal key were lost, [as reported at the time](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/stakehound-accuses-fireblocks-of-losing-74m-of-eth); StakeHound sued its custody provider, which disputed responsibility, and ended its staking service in July 2021. Who runs those validators now is not known.

Limits. Graffiti is chosen by whoever runs a validator, and anyone could type a name; validators signing StakeHound's name on every block are taken to be StakeHound's. No operator is recorded. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the account deposited for others.

0087-bitmine-staking.summary: Validators withdrawing to 111 addresses that proved common control together with BitMine's other wallets, whose combined holdings match BitMine's reported ETH, are BitMine's treasury staking.
0087-bitmine-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 111 addresses are BitMine's own treasury staking.

grounds.text: On 31 August 2026 all 111 sent 0.001 ETH to one of two new accounts within 73 minutes: one holder controls them
With the 98 other senders they held 5.70M ETH, 4.97M staked; BitMine reported 5.90M held and 5.07M staked
Their deposits, with those of decision 0115, rose in the same weeks as BitMine's weekly reported staked ETH
No staking provider behind these validators has been identified, so BitMine is taken as the allocator

0087-bitmine-staking.would_change: A provider identified for these validators, or evidence that an address is held by someone other than BitMine.
0087-bitmine-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 111 addresses are BitMine Immersion Technologies' own treasury staking. In October 2026 they numbered about 1,800, with some 3.1M ETH, most of them compounding (0x02) validators of around 1,900 ETH each, deposited to the address that sent them.

Common control. On 31 August 2026, between 13:26 and 14:39 UTC, 209 accounts each sent 0.001 ETH to one of two newly created accounts that have never sent a transaction. Sending from an account requires its key (for a BitGo custody wallet, its signers), so the senders are controlled by one holder or by parties acting together. All 111 addresses are among them: 93 sent directly, and 18 wallets held at BitGo sent through the same account that made their deposits. The other senders include 74 of the 81 addresses of decision 0115 and 24 further BitMine wallets.

Identification with BitMine. No document names these addresses; the identification rests on BitMine's published holdings. [Its weekly release of 31 August 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-5-90-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-15-6-billion-302864579.html) gives 5,901,112 ETH held and 5,067,309 ETH staked as of 30 August. On 31 August the 209 senders held 732,732 ETH in their balances and 4,965,499 ETH in active validators; with the seven addresses of decision 0115 that did not take part, the staked total is 5,034,487 ETH, 0.6% below BitMine's figure, and the total held is 3% below it. Earlier releases ([4 January 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-4-144-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-14-2-billion-302652341.html), [22 March 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-4-661-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-11-0-billion-302721764.html)) match the deposits of these addresses and those of 0115 week by week.

Who runs the validators. The validators fall into several fleets, told apart by the client versions recorded in their blocks. About 0.94M ETH of this stake is on a fleet running a Nethermind build seen on no other validators, the fleet described under decision 0115. About 1.42M ETH runs as SSV clusters on twelve private operators owned by one account. That account was funded from the same source as the SSV operators of Staked's own validators, so these validators are recorded as run by Staked (since 30 October 2026; tag ssv-operator-owner-staked). Since September 2026 some of these validators have also proposed outside SSV, with Lighthouse's default graffiti. About 0.47M ETH runs Nimbus with its default graffiti, and about 0.16M ETH runs the same Nethermind and Lighthouse releases as Lido's operator MAVAN, though those releases are widely used. BitMine owns MAVAN, the staking platform it launched in [March 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-launch-of-mavan-made-in-america-validator-network-the-companys-proprietary-staking-solution-302724419.html); its subsidiary MAVAN Holdings bought the staking provider Pier Two that month ([quarterly report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001829311/000162828026048157/bmnr-20260531.htm)). None of the other fleets is shown to be MAVAN's, and BitMine said in January 2026 that it was working with three staking providers. Until a provider is identified for a fleet, BitMine is recorded as the allocator of all of them.

Limits. The match with BitMine's figures is close but not exact, compares effective balances with reported totals, and leaves out pending deposits. A custodian running one control check across several clients' wallets would also produce the 31 August transfers, though 16 of the senders are unstaked wallets whose only transaction is that transfer. Explorer labels naming the addresses as BitMine's are recorded as leads. The decision would change if a provider is identified for these validators, or if any address is shown to be held by someone other than BitMine.

0xc3a9…cc16 (validators on the NM9205LH build) sends 0.001 ETH to 0x35ce…, block 25,875,561
BitGo wallet 0x11d0…b112 sends 0.001 ETH to 0x35ce… through a call from 0x0c3b…e40e, block 25,875,846
A decision 0115 address sends 0.001 ETH to the second account, 0x1bae…69c1, block 25,875,747

0090-bitfinex-staking.summary: Validators withdrawing to the address Bitfinex lists as its ETH hot wallet are Bitfinex's staking.
0090-bitfinex-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are Bitfinex's staking.

grounds.text: Bitfinex's own published list of its wallets names this address its ETH/ERC20 hot wallet
An exchange's own wallet holds its stake, so the exchange is the allocator

0090-bitfinex-staking.would_change: Bitfinex's own disclosures not listing the address, or evidence it holds the address for a client.
0090-bitfinex-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x7713…35ec are Bitfinex's staking, with the exchange as allocator. 2,087 validators have withdrawn to it since April 2023, deposited by many accounts; about 1,630 were active in October 2026 with some 52k ETH. The stake is Bitfinex's customers'.

Identification. [Bitfinex's published list of its wallets](https://github.com/bitfinexcom/pub/blob/83d06bdb5f5a2ce05d5ba2db5a426dd44c9f5128/wallets.txt), released with its proof of reserves in November 2022, names this address as its ETH and ERC-20 hot wallet, and as its hot wallet on several other networks. A hot wallet is the exchange's own, so stake withdrawing to it is the exchange's staking. The list dates from late 2022, and nothing on chain suggests the address has changed hands since.

The validators' graffiti names their node operators (for example SSV clusters and Luganodes), not the allocator; they remain operators only. Explorer labels and a community-compiled reserve list are recorded as leads. The decision would change if Bitfinex's own disclosures stopped listing the address, or with evidence that Bitfinex holds the address for a client.

0093-kucoin-staking.summary: KuCoin's own wallet list names two of the accounts that deposited these validators, and the stake KuCoin said it had then matches them to one validator.
0093-kucoin-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to, or deposited by, these addresses are KuCoin's staking.

grounds.text: KuCoin's November 2022 wallet list names two of the four depositing accounts as its own wallets
The other two were first funded by wallets on that list
KuCoin said it then staked 29,696 ETH; these accounts had deposited 29,664 ETH (927 validators)

0093-kucoin-staking.would_change: Evidence that KuCoin holds these validators for a client, or a KuCoin statement contradicting the list.
0093-kucoin-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x9f4c…2a2a, and those deposited by four accounts linked to KuCoin's wallets, are KuCoin's staking, with the exchange as allocator. 927 validators withdraw to that address; 625 were active in October 2026 with 20,000 ETH. The stake is KuCoin's customers'.

KuCoin's own list. [KuCoin's post "Transparency and Trust"](https://www.kucoin.com/blog/9152-34) of 11 November 2022 lists its hot and cold wallets at a snapshot of that day and says KuCoin was then staking 29,696 ETH, without listing the validators. It names two of the four accounts that deposited these validators. The other two were first funded by wallets on the list.

The match. The four accounts deposited all 927 validators between November 2020 and October 2022, before the snapshot: 29,664 ETH, one validator short of the figure KuCoin gave. No other listed address sent deposits or is a withdrawal address.

No operator is recorded. A community-compiled reserve list and explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that KuCoin holds these validators for a client, or a KuCoin statement contradicting its list.

0096-coinex-staking.summary: Validators withdrawing to, or deposited by, wallets that CoinEx's proof of reserves lists and signs for were CoinEx's staking; its reserve files also list the validators themselves.
0096-coinex-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to, or deposited by, CoinEx's signed reserve wallets were CoinEx's staking.

grounds.text: CoinEx's proof of reserves lists these wallets, each with a signature proving CoinEx controls it
Its reserve files also list its staked validators by public key, with these withdrawal addresses

0096-coinex-staking.would_change: CoinEx's own disclosures dropping the addresses, or evidence it holds them for a client.
0096-coinex-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xafed…4399 or 0x5480…fcb2, or deposited by 0x38f6…6336, were the staking of CoinEx, the exchange, with CoinEx as allocator. 1,027 validators withdrew to the first address from April 2024, and 482 were deposited by the third account in June and July 2025, almost all to the second; all have since exited. The stake was CoinEx's customers'.

CoinEx's proof of reserves. For each of its proof-of-reserves snapshots CoinEx publishes a file of its wallet addresses, each with a signature of the message "I am a CoinEx address" (for example the snapshots of [13 November 2024](https://file.coinexstatic.com/CoinEx_Address_2024-11-13.xlsx) and [4 June 2025](https://file.coinexstatic.com/CoinEx_Address_2025-06-04.xlsx)). The signature for 0x38f6…6336 recovers that address. 0xafed…4399 is a multisig wallet with fifteen owners; its listed signer is one of them and the signature recovers it. 0x5480…fcb2 is signed for by another owner of the same multisig.

The validators themselves. The same files list CoinEx's staked validators by public key, with these withdrawal addresses: 529 at the first address in January 2025, falling to 311 by October 2025, then 311 and later 24 at the second from May 2026. CoinEx notes that its wallet assets include on-chain funds managed under staking.

No operator is recorded. A community-compiled reserve list is recorded as a lead. The decision would change if CoinEx's own disclosures dropped the addresses, or with evidence that CoinEx holds them for a client.

0099-bitrue-staking.summary: Validators deposited by and withdrawing to an address funded only by Bitrue's hot wallet, which took over from the wallet that funded Bitrue's published insurance wallet, are Bitrue's staking.
0099-bitrue-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to, or deposited by, this address are Bitrue's staking.

grounds.text: The wallet that funded Bitrue's published insurance wallet handed over to a new hot wallet during Bitrue's announced address change
That new hot wallet supplied all the ETH this address deposited
Its withdrawals go to a wallet that pays only that hot wallet

0099-bitrue-staking.would_change: A Bitrue statement contradicting it, or evidence that the address or its funding wallet holds ETH for a client.
0099-bitrue-staking.explanation:
Validators deposited by and withdrawing to 0x4fd7…717d are the staking of Bitrue, the exchange, with Bitrue as allocator. The address sent the deposits of 302 validators between June 2023 and August 2026, all with itself as withdrawal address, and no one else has deposited to it; 116 were active in October 2026. The stake is Bitrue's customers'.

What Bitrue published. Bitrue's help centre names its insurance fund's Ethereum wallet ([June 2020](https://support.bitrue.com/hc/en-001/articles/360049715433-Bitrue-s-New-Insurance-Wallet-Is-Live), and again in [its statement on transparency of November 2022](https://support.bitrue.com/hc/en-001/articles/12425985186073-Bitrue-s-Statement-on-Transparency)), and [announced that all its ERC-20 deposit addresses would change](https://support.bitrue.com/hc/en-001/articles/360052551853-All-Our-ERC20-Wallet-Addresses-Will-Change-On-August-5th) during maintenance on 5 August 2020, between 04:00 and 12:00 UTC.

The hot wallets. The insurance wallet was funded in June 2020 by 0x3487…d13e, an exchange hot wallet. On 5 August 2020, inside the announced maintenance window, a new wallet, 0x6cc8…fd21, received its first ETH from 0x3487…d13e; within two hours it was receiving customer funds, while 0x3487…d13e's traffic fell sharply and stopped by January 2021. The two wallets share over 700 counterparties: the same customers. 0x6cc8…fd21 supplied all the ETH that 0x4fd7…717d deposited, and 0x4fd7…717d sends its withdrawals to two wallets that pay only 0x6cc8…fd21.

So the stake is funded by, and returns to, the hot wallet Bitrue switched to on 5 August 2020. No operator is recorded.

Limits. The hot wallet is tied to Bitrue by its funding of Bitrue's published insurance wallet and by the timing of the switch, not by name. A community-maintained tracker listing these wallets as Bitrue's is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with a Bitrue statement contradicting it, or evidence that the address or its funding wallet holds ETH for a client.

0x3487…d13e funds the insurance wallet again (1.994 ETH, 2020-06-18)
First transaction of hot wallet 0x6cc8…fd21, from 0x3487, at 05:36 UTC on 5 August 2020, during Bitrue's announced wallet change
0x3487 moves 310 ETH to 0x6cc8 the same morning
0x6cc8 first funds this address (2023-06-02); it sent all 9,354 ETH the address received
This address sends withdrawals to 0x795b…dd40 (17.9 ETH)
0x795b pays 0x6cc8, its only destination (first of 443 transfers, 60,608 ETH)

0103-stakefish-fee-pool.summary: This contract, the fee recipient of blocks signed only with stakefish's graffiti and with the interface of stakefish's documented fee pool, is stakefish's fee pool.
0103-stakefish-fee-pool.decision: This contract is stakefish's fee pool; otherwise unattributed validators paying their fees to it are run and allocated by stakefish.

grounds.text: Every block naming it as fee recipient, 14,637 of them, is signed with stakefish's graffiti or left blank
Its code has the interface of the fee pool stakefish's documentation describes
Over 80% of the validators paying it are already stakefish's by their withdrawal addresses

0103-stakefish-fee-pool.would_change: A stakefish statement contradicting it, or evidence the pool takes validators stakefish does not run.
0103-stakefish-fee-pool.explanation:
The contract 0xffee…143b is stakefish's fee pool: the validators stakefish runs for its partners' customers pay their transaction fees and MEV to it, and it shares them out among those validators. Validators otherwise unattributed whose blocks paid it are attributed to stakefish as allocator for as long as they did. In October 2026 about 670 validators relied on this decision, with some 78k ETH, many of them compounding.

Identification. [stakefish's documentation](https://docs.stake.fish/docs/ethereum-fee-pool.md) describes its fee pool, a smoothing pool it deploys and runs for the validators it operates ([claiming rewards](https://docs.stake.fish/docs/ethereum-fee-pool-claim-rewards.md)), though without giving its address. This contract, a proxy created in September 2022, has the interface of that pool. Every one of the 14,637 blocks naming it as their own fee recipient is signed with stakefish's graffiti ("Stake Earn Relax 🐠 stakefish") or left blank, and of the 13,509 validators that have paid it, 11,222 are already stakefish's by their withdrawal addresses.

As for stakefish's deposit contract (decision 0038), a fee recipient used only by validators signing stakefish's name is taken to be stakefish's. A fee pool claim yields to every other allocator claim. An explorer label is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with a stakefish statement contradicting it, or evidence that the pool takes validators stakefish does not run.
