0104-coinbase-fee-recipient.summary: This address receives the fees of nearly 127,000 validators already known to be Coinbase's, and passes them to Coinbase's own wallets; otherwise unattributed validators paying it are taken to be run by Coinbase.
0104-coinbase-fee-recipient.decision: This address is Coinbase's fee recipient; otherwise unattributed validators paying their fees to it are run and allocated by Coinbase.

grounds.text: Of 128,000 validators paying it, 99% are already Coinbase's by other evidence
The rest paid it in nearly all their blocks, as the fee recipient they registered
Since mid-2024, 95% of the ETH it sent went to Coinbase's staking deposit funder, cbETH wallet and payout wallets

0104-coinbase-fee-recipient.would_change: Evidence that clients of other providers also use this address as their fee recipient.
0104-coinbase-fee-recipient.explanation:
The address 0x4675…a263 is Coinbase's fee recipient: the validators Coinbase runs pay their transaction fees and MEV to it. Validators otherwise unattributed whose blocks paid it are attributed to Coinbase as allocator for as long as they did. In October 2026 about 1,030 validators relied on this decision, with some 33k ETH.

Who pays it. Of the 127,975 validators whose blocks have paid it, 126,944 are already Coinbase's by other evidence (Coinbase's retail staking, decisions 0016, 0017 and 0020), so it is the fee recipient of Coinbase's own validators rather than a client's. The remaining 1,031 paid it in 99.6% of their blocks, including through other block builders' payments to it as the fee recipient they had registered, so they chose it. Which Coinbase service these belong to, for example Prime or Cloud clients, is not known. The address never pays proposers, so it is not a block builder.

Where its ETH goes. From mid-2024 to October 2026 it made over 82,000 payments, totalling 23,351 ETH. 95.5% went to wallets established as Coinbase's from chain data alone: the wallet that funds Coinbase's retail staking deposits, the wallet that receives all newly minted cbETH, and the payout wallets of Coinbase's staking sweeps. Most of the rest went to one wallet not identified.

A fee recipient claim yields to every other allocator claim. An explorer label on the address is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with evidence that clients of other providers also use this address as their fee recipient.

evidence.note: Pays the retail staking deposit funder 0xb5d8…f511 (1.54 ETH); 43,727 such payments since block 20,000,000, 14,398 ETH
Pays the cbETH wallet 0xa9d1…3e43 (1.09 ETH); 34,686 such payments, 7,374 ETH

0105-stakewise-vaults-registry.summary: StakeWise's own deployment list names this as its V3 VaultsRegistry; validators withdrawing to a vault it registered are StakeWise V3's.
0105-stakewise-vaults-registry.decision: This contract is StakeWise V3's vault registry; validators withdrawing to a vault it registered are allocated by StakeWise V3.

grounds.text: StakeWise's own deployment list names this as its V3 VaultsRegistry
Every StakeWise V3 vault is added to it when created
Each vault's own manager chooses its operators; StakeWise is shown as the protocol

0105-stakewise-vaults-registry.would_change: StakeWise's deployment list naming a different registry, or vaults registered elsewhere.
0105-stakewise-vaults-registry.explanation:
The contract 0x3a00…c20e is StakeWise V3's vault registry: every StakeWise V3 vault is added to it when created, and validators withdrawing to a registered vault are attributed to StakeWise V3 as allocator. By October 2026 the registry listed 254 vaults; about 3,000 of their validators were active, with some 0.29M ETH, many of them compounding.

Identification. [StakeWise's own deployment list](https://github.com/stakewise/v3-core/blob/31f40df84492eb3fd64389904fcc012d278b4b41/deployments/mainnet.json) names this contract as its V3 VaultsRegistry. It was created in October 2023 and has recorded each vault's creation since. The shared MEV escrow named in the same list is the fee recipient of many StakeWise validators, which helped identify them.

Why StakeWise is shown as the allocator. Each vault's administrator chooses that vault's operators, so the choice is made within the protocol, by many parties; as with Rocket Pool, the protocol is shown as the allocator. Distinguishing vaults, for example the Genesis Vault run by StakeWise's DAO from institutions' private vaults, would be a possible refinement.

The decision would change if StakeWise's deployment list named a different registry, or if vaults were found to be registered elsewhere.

0109-kelp-proxy-admin.summary: Kelp DAO's own repository lists this contract as the administrator of its contracts; validators withdrawing to EigenLayer pods its NodeDelegators own are Kelp's (rsETH).
0109-kelp-proxy-admin.decision: This contract administers Kelp DAO's contracts; validators withdrawing to EigenLayer pods those contracts own are allocated by Kelp (rsETH).

grounds.text: Kelp DAO's repository lists this contract as the administrator of its contracts
It administers five contracts that own EigenLayer pods, four listed by Kelp as its NodeDelegators
Those validators' blocks pay Kelp's fee receiver or deposit pool

0109-kelp-proxy-admin.would_change: A Kelp statement contradicting it, or a pod owner under this ProxyAdmin that is not Kelp's.
0109-kelp-proxy-admin.explanation:
The contract 0xb61e…dc78 administers Kelp DAO's contracts. Validators withdrawing to an EigenLayer pod owned by one of the contracts it administers are attributed to Kelp's restaking token rsETH, with Kelp as allocator. 10,096 deposits, about 323k ETH, went to those pods between February 2024 and December 2025; about 4,500 validators were active in October 2026 with some 0.14M ETH.

Identification. [Kelp DAO's repository](https://github.com/Kelp-DAO/LRT-rsETH/blob/3dded885f6f797f5959aff449c3a30c5cbb6ce23/README.md) lists this contract as the administrator of its contracts, owned by Kelp's timelock, together with its proxy factory, deposit pool, fee receiver and NodeDelegator contracts. On chain, five contracts administered by it own EigenLayer pods, all created by Kelp's proxy factory; four of them are NodeDelegators listed in the repository, and the fifth, built on another implementation, holds no stake now. Almost all deposits to the pods were sent through the delegators themselves, and the validators' blocks pay Kelp's fee receiver or deposit pool.

Why Kelp is the allocator. Kelp chooses the node operators for each delegator; its repository's notes name them, several running SSV clusters. No operator is recorded here. Before this decision these validators had been taken to be their operators' own, on the strength of an occasional block signed with an operator's name; the withdrawal side now identifies Kelp directly.

The decision would change with a Kelp statement contradicting it, or a pod owner under this administrator that is not Kelp's.

0110-everstake-batch-deposit.summary: An audit Everstake commissioned and announced names this as Everstake's ETH2 batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run by Everstake for its clients.
0110-everstake-batch-deposit.decision: This contract is Everstake's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Everstake.

grounds.text: Everstake's blog announces an audit naming this as Everstake's ETH2 batch deposit contract
The audit report gives this address
It was created by the account that created Everstake's pooled-staking contract
Its validators sign blocks "Everstake / Pro" and pay the same fee recipient

0110-everstake-batch-deposit.would_change: An Everstake statement contradicting it, or evidence some depositors use it with keys Everstake does not run.
0110-everstake-batch-deposit.explanation:
The contract 0x4ff4…7e6d is Everstake's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Everstake as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 66 validators were deposited through it between September 2025 and January 2026, from ten sending accounts, each withdrawing to itself; 65 were active in October 2026 with about 106k ETH, almost all of it in consolidated compounding validators.

Identification. [Everstake's blog announces the audit](https://everstake.com/resources/blog/everstakes-eth2-batch-deposit-contract-security-audited-by-ackee) of its ETH2 batch deposit contract and links [the auditor's report](https://github.com/Ackee-Blockchain/public-audit-reports/blob/master/2025/ackee-blockchain-everstake-eth2-batch-deposit-report.pdf), which gives this contract's mainnet address. On chain, it was created by the same account that created Everstake's pooled-staking contract (decision 0003). Its validators sign their blocks "Everstake / Pro", and all pay the same fee recipient, a Safe multisig shared with the validators of Everstake's second batch contract.

Why Everstake is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). The contract is open to anyone, so a deposit through it does not by itself prove that Everstake runs the validator; the graffiti corroborates it.

The decision would change with an Everstake statement contradicting it, or evidence that some depositors use the contract with keys Everstake does not run.

0111-everstake-batch-deposit-b60b.summary: Created by the account behind Everstake's audited batch deposit contract and its Pool, under the same contract name; validators deposited through it are run by Everstake.
0111-everstake-batch-deposit-b60b.decision: This contract is a later version of Everstake's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Everstake.

grounds.text: It was created by the account behind Everstake's audited batch deposit contract and its Pool
Its published code carries the same contract name as Everstake's audited one
Its validators sign blocks "Everstake / Pro" and pay the same fee recipient
No published source names this contract itself

0111-everstake-batch-deposit-b60b.would_change: Evidence that the creating account deploys for others, or an Everstake statement contradicting it.
0111-everstake-batch-deposit-b60b.explanation:
The contract 0xb60b…2f31 is taken to be a later version of Everstake's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Everstake as allocator and operator, while the client keeps its own withdrawal address. 27 compounding validators, about 50k ETH, were deposited through it on 15 April 2026 by one account withdrawing to itself; all were active in October 2026.

Identification. No published source names this contract. It was created by the same account that created Everstake's audited batch deposit contract (decision 0110) and Everstake's pooled-staking contract (decision 0003). Its verified source carries the same contract name as the audited contract, with different code, as a later version would. Its validators sign their blocks "Everstake / Pro" and pay the same fee recipient, a Safe multisig, as the audited contract's validators do.

It is kept as its own decision because its support is weaker than the audited contract's. A deployment account could in principle deploy contracts for others. The decision would change with evidence that the creating account deploys contracts for others, or an Everstake statement contradicting it.

0112-frax-frxeth-minter.summary: Frax's own code names this as its frxETH Minter, called by Frax's multisig; validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are Frax's (frxETH).
0112-frax-frxeth-minter.decision: This contract is Frax's frxETH Minter; validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are allocated by Frax (frxETH).

grounds.text: Frax's own code checks that its multisig's queued validators are deposited through this contract
All its deposits withdraw to Frax's multisig, which received no deposits any other way
Etherscan's address page attributes it to Frax Finance

0112-frax-frxeth-minter.would_change: A Frax statement contradicting it, or deposits to the same withdrawal address by another route.
0112-frax-frxeth-minter.explanation:
The contract 0xbafa…1138 is the frxETH Minter of Frax Finance's liquid staking token frxETH. Validators withdrawing to the address it deposits to are attributed to Frax as allocator. 7,483 deposits were sent through it between October 2022 and June 2025, holding as much as 237k ETH; about 1,400 validators were active in October 2026 with some 45k ETH.

Identification. Frax's own code ([a script in its frxETH repository](https://github.com/FraxFinance/frxETH-public/blob/018eaf4daf0eb5ca94dfbb275d3fa59008ea829e/node-scripts/validate-msig-add-validators.ts)) checks the validators that Frax's multisig wallet 0x8306…a81c queues, and requires each queued transaction to call this contract. Every deposit sent through the Minter withdraws to that multisig, and the multisig has received no deposits by any other route. The validators sign the graffiti "¤ Frax Finance ¤". Etherscan's address page attributes the contract to Frax Finance; that is recorded as third-party corroboration.

Why Frax is the allocator. Frax's multisig chooses the validator keys the Minter deposits with. No operator is recorded. No validator here has a conflicting allocator claim.

The decision would change with a Frax statement contradicting it, or deposits to the multisig by another route.

0115-bitmine-staking-mavan.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 81 addresses are BitMine's treasury staking, beyond the 111 addresses of decision 0087.

grounds.text: 74 of the 81 sent 0.001 ETH in the same 73 minutes as BitMine's 111 wallets, to the same two new accounts
Each deposits compounding validators of about 1,800-1,900 ETH to itself, as BitMine's wallets do
75 of the 79 with active validators run a Nethermind build seen only on BitMine's validators, which change versions together
With BitMine's labelled wallets, their deposits match BitMine's weekly reported staked ETH within 0.03M

0115-bitmine-staking-mavan.would_change: BitMine's reported staked ETH diverging from these deposits, or evidence an address belongs to another holder.
0115-bitmine-staking-mavan.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 81 addresses are also BitMine Immersion Technologies' treasury staking, beyond the 111 addresses of decision 0087. In October 2026 they held about 1,150 active validators with some 2.0M ETH; together with 0087 this puts BitMine's staking at about 5.1M ETH, against the 5,067,309 ETH it reported staked.

The addresses. Each deposits compounding (0x02) validators of about 1,800 to 1,900 ETH to itself, as BitMine's other wallets do. Most of their stake went through Coinbase's batch deposit contract, the rest through two batch contracts that BitMine's other wallets also used, or directly. 75 of the 79 addresses with active validators have validators on one fleet, recognisable by a Nethermind build that appears on no other validators: BitMine's validators were the first to run it, on 12 May 2026, and the fleet has changed versions together since, alternating with a Geth and Prysm build also seen only on BitMine's validators, and moving to Reth from 13 October 2026. About 1.19M ETH of these addresses' stake is on that fleet, about 0.56M ETH on validators running Nimbus with its default graffiti, and the rest on smaller setups. BitMine owns the staking platform MAVAN, [launched in March 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-launch-of-mavan-made-in-america-validator-network-the-companys-proprietary-staking-solution-302724419.html) on the staking provider Pier Two, which its subsidiary MAVAN Holdings bought that month ([quarterly report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001829311/000162828026048157/bmnr-20260531.htm)). The fleets are not shown to be MAVAN's: MAVAN's validators in Lido run widely used release builds, not this one.

Common control and the match with BitMine's figures. 74 of the 81 took part in the control transfers of 31 August 2026 described under decision 0087, paying the same two new accounts in the same 73 minutes. BitMine publishes its staked ETH every week. Across all 41 weekly releases from [4 January 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-4-144-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-14-2-billion-302652341.html) to [11 October 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-6-03-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash--marketable-securities-holdings-of-16-2-billion-302905339.html), the ETH deposited by these addresses and by those of 0087 matches the reported figure to within 0.033M ETH, and every increase falls in the same week as the reported one.

The seven addresses that did not take part in the control transfers hold 68,988 ETH. They are linked to one another by their funding but not to the others, and they rest on running on the same fleets, depositing the same way, and on the weekly match, which they are needed for: without them the staked total falls further below BitMine's figure. BitMine has said MAVAN would also serve outside clients, so these seven could belong to another client of the same operators.

Explorer labels on the brokers that funded many of these wallets are recorded as leads. The decision would change if BitMine's reported staked ETH diverged from these deposits, or with evidence that an address belongs to another holder.

0116-binance-wbeth.summary: BNB Chain's announcement names this as wBETH on Ethereum, and the ETH paid in to mint it goes to a Binance wallet.
0116-binance-wbeth.decision: This contract is Binance's wBETH on Ethereum: a token for ETH staked with Binance, valued at the rate it publishes.

grounds.text: BNB Chain's wBETH announcement lists this as wBETH's Ethereum contract
All 1.86M ETH paid in to mint it went on to one address
That same address first funded the account holding its operator role

0116-binance-wbeth.would_change: Binance naming another contract as its Ethereum wBETH, or the ETH paid in going somewhere other than Binance.
0116-binance-wbeth.explanation:
The contract 0xa2e3…2e1 is Binance's wBETH (Wrapped Binance Beacon ETH) on Ethereum: a token for ETH staked with Binance, valued at an exchange rate Binance publishes. The decision is used by the "Forms of ETH" page, which counts wBETH's supply at its exchange rate as Binance's issue; it also links Binance's staking to Binance (decision 0006).

Identification. [BNB Chain's announcement of wBETH](https://www.bnbchain.org/en/blog/new-wrapped-beth-is-now-available-on-bnb-chain) lists this as wBETH's Ethereum contract. Binance's own pages could not be retrieved.

On chain. The contract names a receiving account, 0x26ad…6b86, for the ETH paid in to mint wBETH. All 67 of that account's transactions sent ETH to a single address, 1,857,295 ETH in all, and nowhere else. The account holding the contract's operator role was first funded by that same address. In October 2026 the exchange rate was about 1.11 ETH per wBETH, and the supply on Ethereum was 3.18M wBETH.

ETH waiting in the receiving account is counted under wBETH rather than as plain ETH, since it is already in wBETH's supply. An explorer label naming the destination address as Binance's is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with Binance naming another contract as its Ethereum wBETH, or the ETH paid in going somewhere other than Binance.

0117-coinbase-cbeth.summary: A risk report lists this as cbETH's contract, and the cbETH it mints is passed straight to a Coinbase wallet.
0117-coinbase-cbeth.decision: This contract is Coinbase's cbETH: a token for ETH staked with Coinbase, valued at the rate it publishes.

grounds.text: Coinbase's own developer code (AgentKit) lists this as cbETH's Ethereum mainnet contract
Nearly all of its 2.69M minted cbETH went to one account, which passed it on to a single address
Prisma Risk's cbETH assessment lists the same contract

0117-coinbase-cbeth.would_change: Coinbase naming another contract as cbETH, or the minted cbETH going somewhere other than Coinbase.
0117-coinbase-cbeth.explanation:
The contract 0xbe98…9704 is Coinbase's cbETH (Coinbase Wrapped Staked ETH): a token for ETH staked with Coinbase, valued at an exchange rate Coinbase publishes. The decision is used by the "Forms of ETH" page, which counts cbETH's supply at its exchange rate as Coinbase's issue; the wallet receiving its minted tokens also helps identify Coinbase's staking (decisions 0016, 0017 and 0020).

Identification. [Coinbase's own developer code](https://github.com/coinbase/agentkit/blob/f2f3e8c11a91d56a17979a229a172ba6e61a85c2/typescript/agentkit/src/action-providers/erc20/constants.ts) (its AgentKit token list) gives this as cbETH's Ethereum mainnet contract, and [Prisma Risk's assessment of cbETH](https://hackmd.io/@PrismaRisk/cbETH) lists the same contract.

On chain. Every cbETH ever minted, 2,691,301 tokens, went to four accounts, and one of them received all but test amounts. That account passed its cbETH on to a single address, 0xa9d1…3e43: every transfer up to late 2022 did so, as did every one of a sample spread across all its later transactions. cbETH's supply peaked at 1.47M in May 2024 and has been flat at 393,751 since March 2025.

cbETH's backing is held by Coinbase, outside the execution layer, so nothing is netted out of ETH for it. An explorer label on the receiving address is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with Coinbase naming another contract as cbETH, or the minted cbETH going somewhere other than Coinbase.

0120-revolut-staking.summary: Validators deposited by an account funded only by a wallet that handled Revolut's EURR stablecoin from before its launch, and withdrawing back to that account, are Revolut's staking.
0120-revolut-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are Revolut's staking.

grounds.text: The issuer of the Revolut Euro (EURR) stablecoin names Revolut its sole distributor
The wallet that supplied all the depositing account's ETH held EURR before launch and received EURR from the issuance wallet
That account made every deposit, and the validators' withdrawals all return to it

0120-revolut-staking.would_change: A Revolut statement contradicting it, or evidence that the validators are run for a client or chosen by a staking provider.
0120-revolut-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x2b78…7470 are Revolut's staking, with Revolut as allocator; the stake is its customers'. 8,834 validators were deposited between September 2022 and September 2026; about 3,585 were active in October 2026 with some 0.11M ETH.

The deposits. One account, 0xc44b…11c3, made every deposit to the address, and no one else has deposited to it. The account is used only for staking (its other transactions are delegations and bridging on other networks), and its ETH comes from only two places: 0x9b0c…8d46, a high-volume exchange hot wallet, and the withdrawal address itself, which sends it every withdrawal to be restaked or returned. The withdrawal address is its validators' own fee recipient, and their graffiti shows client versions only.

The link to Revolut through EURR. Revolut publishes no Ethereum addresses, and its annual reports give no staking figures. The link runs through EURR, the euro stablecoin Bridge issues for Revolut: [Bridge's transparency page](https://reserves.bridge.xyz/) lists the Revolut Euro token, and [its white paper under MiCA](https://reserves.bridge.xyz/white-papers/bridge-mica-white-paper-eurr-july-2026.pdf) names Revolut's European digital-asset company as the sole distributor, offering it through the Revolut app and Revolut X. The token launched publicly in late August 2026. The hot wallet 0x9b0c…8d46 received EURR test tokens in March 2026, months before launch, when only the issuer and its distributor would hold them; from August 2026 it received EURR from the wallet that received almost all of the supply minted, and it passes EURR to a wallet that pays many end users.

So the stake is funded by, and returns to, a wallet that handled a stablecoin only Revolut distributes, from before its launch. A wallet of the exchange depositing for itself makes Revolut the allocator.

Limits. No Revolut document names a wallet. The wallet that received most of the EURR minted may be Bridge's or Revolut's; the argument holds either way. Explorer labels and community label sets naming the accounts as Revolut's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Revolut statement contradicting it, or evidence that the validators are run for a client or chosen by a staking provider.

evidence.note: 0x2b78 sends 3,490 ETH to 0xc44b, first return of withdrawals
0x9b0c…8d46 sends 986 ETH to 0xc44b; it supplied all 239,153 ETH 0xc44b received apart from withdrawals
0x9b0c receives 5 EURR from the test mint's recipient on 3 March 2026, before EURR's launch
0x9b0c receives EURR from 0x762b…12cf, which got 99.9% of all EURR minted (first of 16 transfers)
0x9b0c sends EURR to 0xb233…c460, which pays it out to end users

0123-coinspot-staking.summary: Validators withdrawing to an address that pays only the wallets refilling CoinSpot's customer-withdrawal wallet, deposited with ETH from the same wallets, are CoinSpot's staking.
0123-coinspot-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are CoinSpot's staking.

grounds.text: A CoinSpot help-centre screenshot of an ETH withdrawal identifies the wallet CoinSpot pays its customers from
The deposit accounts got their ETH from the wallets that refill it and from a wallet that pays almost only them
The validators' withdrawals go only to those wallets, and the address is its validators' own fee recipient

0123-coinspot-staking.would_change: A CoinSpot statement contradicting it, or evidence that the validators are run for a client or chosen by a staking provider.
0123-coinspot-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xe887…a7f7 are CoinSpot's staking, with the Australian exchange as allocator. 4,303 validators withdraw there, 4,302 of them active in October 2026 with about 138k ETH. Most were deposited in 2022 with BLS credentials and changed to this address later; the change was signed by the same holder of their keys, so they count as CoinSpot's throughout.

CoinSpot's customer-withdrawal wallet. CoinSpot's [help-centre guide to transaction history](https://coinspot.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/5458334081039-Locating-coin-deposit-withdrawals-transaction-history) shows a real ETH withdrawal of 28 October 2024. Exactly one transaction on chain matches it, sent by 0xa9bd…6e29, which has made over 228,000 transfers out since 2021: CoinSpot's wallet for paying customers.

The wallets around it. Two wallets in turn refill that withdrawal wallet, supplying 86% of what it has received, and a third refills both and holds the long-term balance. The validators were deposited from four accounts, funded by those same wallets and by one more that sent almost all of its ETH to them, after receiving much of it from large exchanges' hot wallets, as an exchange moving its own ETH between venues would. All deposits went directly to the deposit contract.

Where the ETH goes. 0xe887…a7f7 has sent all its ETH to the refilling wallets and nowhere else, and it is its validators' own fee recipient. Their graffiti shows client versions only. The stake is therefore funded by, and returns to, the wallets that keep CoinSpot's customer-withdrawal wallet supplied, which makes CoinSpot the allocator. Whether a provider runs the validators is not known.

Limits. CoinSpot names no wallet; the link is its own screenshot of one withdrawal, plus chain data. Explorer labels and community label sets on these wallets are recorded as leads; one of them conflicted, and the flows resolve it. The decision would change with a CoinSpot statement contradicting it, or evidence that the validators are run for a client or chosen by a staking provider.

evidence.note: The ETH send in CoinSpot's help-centre screenshot, from its customer-withdrawal wallet 0xa9bd…6e29
0x1918 funds depositor 0x02ce (64,000 ETH in two transfers)
This address sends withdrawals to 0x33a6, which refills 0xa9bd

0126-bitget-staking.summary: This address deposits validators to itself, funded 32 ETH at a time by one wallet, and most of its validators sign "Bitget": it is Bitget's staking.
0126-bitget-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are Bitget's staking.

grounds.text: It deposits all its validators to itself, and 761 of the 906 that have proposed signed "Bitget" (until slot 12,410,001)
One wallet funded it with 884 transfers of exactly 32 ETH, and it pays withdrawals back to that wallet

0126-bitget-staking.would_change: A Bitget statement contradicting it, or evidence that the wallet stakes for a client or through a provider.
0126-bitget-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x1d5b…00dc are the staking of Bitget, the exchange, with Bitget as allocator. 944 validators were deposited between July 2023 and April 2025; 842 were active in October 2026 with about 27k ETH.

The address. It sent every deposit itself, directly to the deposit contract, with itself as withdrawal address. One wallet funded it with 884 transfers of exactly 32 ETH from January 2024, and since June 2025 it has paid withdrawals back to that wallet. It is its validators' own fee recipient.

The graffiti. Of the 906 validators that have proposed a block, 761 signed "Bitget" at least once, on 1,889 blocks up to slot 12,410,001; later blocks carry no name. The rest signed only client version strings or left their blocks blank. An exchange's wallet depositing to itself, with its validators signing the exchange's name for over a year, makes Bitget the allocator and probably the operator, although no operator is recorded.

Limits. Graffiti is chosen by whoever runs a validator, and anyone could type a name; every validator withdrawing to the address is taken to be Bitget's, including those that never signed it. Bitget's proof-of-reserves data gives totals by coin and chain only, with no wallet addresses, so it can neither confirm nor contradict this. Explorer labels and community label sets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Bitget statement contradicting it, or evidence that the wallet holds ETH for a client or stakes through a provider.

evidence.note: Bitget: Hot Wallet sends 32 ETH to 0x1d5b (first)
0x1d5b sends 193 ETH to Bitget: Hot Wallet

0132-golem-foundation-octant.summary: Validators withdrawing to the Safe that the Golem Foundation's own Octant repository lists as its mainnet "Withdrawal Target" are the Foundation's staking for Octant.
0132-golem-foundation-octant.decision: Validators withdrawing to this Safe are the Golem Foundation's staking for Octant.

grounds.text: The Golem Foundation's Octant repository lists this Safe as Octant's mainnet "Withdrawal Target"
100,416 ETH was deposited to it, matching the 100,000 ETH the Foundation is reported to stake for Octant
The Safe deposits to itself, signed by one of its owners; no staking provider's contract was used

0132-golem-foundation-octant.would_change: A Golem Foundation statement contradicting it, or evidence that a staking provider chose the validators' operator.
0132-golem-foundation-octant.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to the Safe multisig 0xba19…7ed1 are the Golem Foundation's staking for Octant, its public-goods funding programme, with the Foundation as allocator. 3,138 validators were deposited between June 2023 and February 2024; 3,136 were active in October 2026 with about 100k ETH.

Identification. [The Golem Foundation's Octant repository](https://github.com/golemfoundation/octant/blob/f94bd7ab74eb65afaf97a8c5e924f1dafe5f13a3/contracts-v1/README.md) lists this Safe as Octant's mainnet "Withdrawal Target", and the project's backend uses it as the destination of staking proceeds. Octant is funded by the rewards of 100,000 ETH that the Foundation stakes; 100,416 ETH was deposited to the Safe.

On chain. The Safe (three of five signers) was created by one of its owners, who also sent every deposit through the Safe to the deposit contract, with the Safe as withdrawal address. No staking provider's contract was used. The Safe is its validators' own fee recipient, and their graffiti shows client versions only.

Why the Foundation is the allocator. It stakes its own treasury and chose how the stake is run. Whether it runs the nodes itself is not known, so no operator is recorded. Community labels naming the accounts as Octant's and the Foundation's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Golem Foundation statement contradicting it, or evidence that a staking provider chose the validators' operator.

evidence.note: 0x4f80 creates the Safe through the proxy factory

0133-mercado-bitcoin-figment.summary: A client staking through Figment: part of its stake was deposited through Figment's contract, and the rest shares its fee recipients, changed on the same day, so Figment allocates all of it.
0133-mercado-bitcoin-figment.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are allocated by Figment, for one of its clients.

grounds.text: One account deposited all of them: 205 through Figment's documented batch contract, 788 directly
Both groups paid the same fee recipient, and both switched to another within the same five hours
So one operator configures both, and Figment runs the 205 deposited through its contract

0133-mercado-bitcoin-figment.would_change: Evidence that another operator runs the directly deposited validators, or that the client chooses their operators itself.
0133-mercado-bitcoin-figment.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xbcc3…e4a2 that no other provider claim covers are attributed to Figment as allocator, for one of its clients. 788 validators were deposited directly to the deposit contract between July 2023 and March 2025; 559 were active in October 2026 with about 18k ETH. The same client's 205 later validators, deposited through Figment's documented batch contract, are Figment's under decision 0031.

The shared configuration. One account sent every deposit to this address, first 788 directly and then 205 through Figment's contract, as Figment's other clients do. The validators of both groups paid the same fee recipient, which no other validator uses, and then both switched to the withdrawal address itself as fee recipient within the same five hours. A fee recipient is set by whoever runs the validator client, so one operator runs both groups; the group deposited through Figment's contract is Figment's, so the rest is too. Both groups' graffiti shows the same client version string only.

Why Figment is the allocator. When an exchange or other client stakes through a provider, the provider is the allocator, and the client holds the withdrawals. The client's identity rests only on explorer and community labels, which are recorded as leads, so it is not named here; the attribution to Figment does not depend on it.

Limits. The client could run both groups' validator clients itself and set the fee recipient, with Figment only depositing the later 205. The decision would change with evidence that another operator runs the directly deposited validators, or that the client chooses their operators itself.

0134-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet.summary: Validators deposited through Coinbase's batch contracts from Coinbase Prime custody accounts, and running on Coinbase's own validator fleet, are Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake run by Coinbase.
0134-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 706 addresses are Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake, run by Coinbase, except those that Figment runs (decisions 0136, 0137 and 0166).

grounds.text: Since 2025, 82% of their stake came from accounts given gas by the one that paid for Grayscale's deposits, held by Coinbase Custody
Their validators run Coinbase's retail fleet's client builds, in the same mix and at the same times; none names another operator
Most of the rest share those accounts' fee recipients, or sweep to a wallet first funded by one that Coinbase's retail staking pays
Coinbase reports running validators holding 4.5M ETH, 12% of staked ETH, in Q1 2026, excluding stake it routes to partner providers

0134-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet.would_change: A named operator in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying this stake is run by partners.
0134-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 706 addresses are the stake of Coinbase Prime custody clients, run by Coinbase on its own validator fleet; Coinbase is the allocator. The exception is the validators Figment runs, attributed to Figment in decisions 0136, 0137 and 0166. In October 2026 the addresses held about 18,900 active validators with some 0.80M ETH.

Selection. The starting point was active validators first deposited through Coinbase's two batch deposit contracts. Those contracts are open to anyone, so the route alone is no evidence: an earlier attribution resting on it was reverted (decisions 0018 and 0019). Validators signing another operator's name, and those running a fleet shared with BitMine's wallets, were left out.

Custody. In most cases the account that sent the deposits received a small amount of gas from 0xa863…6c0f shortly before depositing. That account paid for 361 of the 363 deposit transactions of Grayscale's ether funds, whose custodian is Coinbase Custody (decision 0136), so an account it pays gas for is one whose keys Coinbase holds. Since January 2025, when its payments begin, 82% of the stake considered here was deposited by accounts it paid. Among earlier depositors, 66 addresses sweep their rewards together, in the same few blocks, to a wallet linked by its funding to Coinbase. Most of the remaining addresses share fee recipients with these. Custody is recorded separately in decision 0167.

Operator. Clients write their version into block graffiti as a short build string. Of the 10,905 blocks these validators proposed with a build string since early 2025, 10,904 carry a build that Coinbase's own retail validators were running at the time, and none names an operator. Week by week the mix of builds matches Coinbase's retail fleet (median similarity 0.97). For comparison, Binance's validators score 0.07 and ether.fi's 0.01; MetaMask's validator staking shows the same mix (decision 0135). Coinbase's retail fleet is itself one fleet: 97% of its stake runs only builds the rest of it runs. A fleet of that size is Coinbase's own, not one of the partners to which Coinbase routes some stake.

Why Coinbase is the allocator. Coinbase holds the accounts as custodian and runs the validators, so it chose the operator: itself. [Coinbase reports](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/ethereum-validator-performance-report-q1-2026) running validators holding about 4.5M ETH in the first quarter of 2026, excluding stake routed to partner providers. Some of these addresses may use Coinbase's non-custodial [dedicated staking service](https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/staking/staking-api/protocols/dedicated-eth/overview), in which Coinbase creates and runs the validators while the customer's own address receives withdrawals ([usage](https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/staking/staking-api/protocols/dedicated-eth/usage)); Coinbase would be the allocator in that case too.

In October 2026, 59 addresses were removed, 57 of them Grayscale's custody addresses (decision 0165). Their validators form a separate fleet that is not shown to be Coinbase's: they changed relays on a date when no Coinbase fleet did, and never emit build strings. Explorer labels on the accounts involved are recorded as leads. The decision would change with an operator's name in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying that this stake is run by partners.

0135-consensys-metamask-validator-stakin.summary: MetaMask's validator staking contract, though deployed by Kiln, is administered by Consensys, whose Safes are its only operator's fee recipient and its treasury; validators deposited through it are allocated by Consensys, not Kiln.
0135-consensys-metamask-validator-stakin.decision: This contract, behind MetaMask's validator staking, is Consensys's; validators deposited through it are allocated by Consensys.

grounds.text: Its admin, which adds operators and sets fees, is the withdrawal address Consensys's Rocket Pool Oracle DAO node registered
Its only operator's fee recipient and its treasury were first funded by the account that also funded that Consensys Safe
MetaMask's launch coverage names Consensys Staking as the one running the validators

0135-consensys-metamask-validator-stakin.would_change: A Consensys or Kiln statement that Kiln chooses the operator, or an operator added that Consensys does not control.
0135-consensys-metamask-validator-stakin.explanation:
The contract 0xdc71…bebd runs MetaMask's validator staking. Although Kiln's deployment account created it, Consensys administers it, and validators first deposited through it are attributed to Consensys as allocator and operator, while each MetaMask user keeps their own withdrawal address. 8,016 validators were deposited through it between January 2024 and September 2026; about 1,090 were active in October 2026 with some 35k ETH.

What the contract records. It is Kiln's staking contract code, but reading it on chain shows who holds its roles. Its administrator, which adds operators and sets fees, is a Safe multisig. Only one operator has ever been registered, itself a Safe, whose fee recipient is another Safe. The contract takes a 10% commission, of which 90% goes to the operator's fee recipient and the rest to a treasury account. Nothing on chain gives Kiln any role or fee since the contract was created.

Why Consensys. The administrator Safe is the withdrawal address registered by Consensys's node in Rocket Pool's Oracle DAO, a node whose member ID ("consensyscodefi") and URL Consensys set itself, admitted by the other members' vote, as read from Rocket Pool's registry (decision 0071). The treasury and the operator's fee recipient were both first funded by an account that also sent ETH to that Consensys Safe, and the Safe's creator first funded three of the fee recipient's owners. So the commission goes to Consensys. Coverage of MetaMask's launch in January 2024 ([The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/273656/metamask-introduces-ethereum-validator-staking-feature-powered-by-consensys), [ForkLog](https://forklog.com/en/news/metamask-introduces-ethereum-validator-staking-feature)) says MetaMask partnered with Consensys Staking to run the validators, and does not mention Kiln. [MetaMask's bug bounty](https://hackenproof.com/programs/metamask-validator-staking-smart-contracts) describes the contract as Kiln's on-chain staking code.

Who runs the nodes. The validators' client builds follow the fleet that runs Coinbase's own retail validators, release by release. Coinbase Cloud [joined Kiln's on-chain platform in 2023](https://www.kiln.fi/post/coinbase-cloud-joins-the-kiln-on-chain-platform-to-offer-staking-for-coinbase-wallet-and-other-self-custodial-wallets) as an operator for self-custodial wallets, so Consensys may run these validators on Coinbase's infrastructure. No source names Coinbase for MetaMask, so Consensys remains the operator of record.

The decision would change with a Consensys or Kiln statement that Kiln chooses the operator, or an operator added that Consensys does not control.

0136-grayscale-figment.summary: Grayscale's ether funds split each custody deposit across operators in a fixed order; the validators in Figment's share are Figment's, which takes precedence over the custody-address decisions 0114 and 0134 for them.
0136-grayscale-figment.decision: These 363 validators, the share of Grayscale's ether funds' stake that Figment runs, are allocated by Figment; for them this takes precedence over decisions 0114 and 0134.

grounds.text: Grayscale's published staked ether matches 363 custody deposits of 3,200 ETH, each split across operators in a fixed order
In January 2026 this share's validators signed the same client string as Figment's own, starting and stopping that week
Like Figment's own, they voted against the 60M gas limit and never used the Aestus or Agnostic relays

0136-grayscale-figment.would_change: Grayscale naming another provider for this share, or these validators' behaviour diverging from Figment's fleet.
0136-grayscale-figment.explanation:
These 363 validators are the share of Grayscale's ether funds' stake that Figment runs, and are attributed to Figment as allocator. For them this takes precedence over the decisions covering the Coinbase Prime custody addresses they withdraw to (0134 and 0167). In October 2026 they held about 1.0M ETH, most in compounding validators.

Grayscale's deposits. Grayscale's two ether funds hold their ETH with Coinbase Custody, and their fund pages ([ETHE](https://etfs.grayscale.com/ethe), [ETH](https://etfs.grayscale.com/eth)) report the amount staked. On 14 October 2025 the pages gave 694,400 ETH staked for ETHE (217 lots of 3,200 ETH) and 467,200 ETH for the Mini Trust (146 lots). That matches exactly the 363 deposit transactions of 3,200 ETH sent between 6 and 8 October 2025 through Coinbase's batch deposit contract, each by the custody address its validators withdraw to. ETHE's later figure (204 lots on 2 January 2026) matches the 13 transactions whose validators fully exited in December 2025. Each transaction splits its 3,200 ETH across two or three operators in one of three fixed patterns, so the same position in each pattern belongs to the same operator.

Identifying Figment's share. [Grayscale chose Figment as a staking provider](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251009122610/en/Grayscale-Selects-Figment-as-a-Staking-Provider-for-U.S.-ETH-ETPs-and-SOL-Trust) for its ETH funds in October 2025. Two of the pattern positions behave as Figment's own validators do. In one week of January 2026 they signed the same bare client-version graffiti string as Figment's own validators, starting and stopping in the same week; a fleet-wide configuration change, also seen on other validators Figment runs. Independently, they voted against raising the gas limit to 60 million as Figment's validators did, and, like Figment's, never used the Aestus or Agnostic relays. A third position signs Galaxy's graffiti and is Galaxy's; the remaining one never signs and its operator is not identified.

The decision is made validator by validator because each custody address holds two or three operators' validators. Grayscale, the funds' manager, is recorded as principal in decision 0165. The decision would change if Grayscale named another provider for this share, or if these validators' behaviour diverged from Figment's fleet.

evidence.ref: 363 transactions through Coinbase's batch contract 0x8ebda19ddee719dab78def3e22c3d37970e35217 on 2025-10-06 to 2025-10-08, each sent by the custody address its validators withdraw to
evidence.note: Each is 3,200 ETH split into two or three validators in one of three fixed shapes (1,400/1,800; 600/800/1,800; 832/1,056/1,312), the shares in the same rotating order in every transaction. Figment's share is the 832 ETH validator of the third shape and the 800 ETH validator of the second.

evidence.ref: ETHE: 217 lots of 3,200 ETH staked on 14 Oct, 4 Nov, 6 Nov, 11 Nov and 14 Nov 2025, 204 on 2 and 6 Jan 2026; Mini Trust: 146 lots on 14 Oct, 3 Nov, 4 Nov and 11 Nov 2025
evidence.note: Total ether times the staked share on Grayscale's fund pages: 217 + 146 = 363 lots, the number of these transactions. ETHE's drop of 13 lots by 2 January matches the 13 transactions whose validators exited in December 2025, none having exited by 14 November.

evidence.ref: 353 validators from the October 2025 deposits, and 10 Figment-fingerprinted validators deposited on 2026-04-24 to the same custody addresses
evidence.note: 55 of the 353 have since exited, with the rest of their transactions' validators.

evidence.note: Figment's own validators (1,312 of them) and the Lido validators Figment operates (236) signed exactly this string, starting and stopping in the same week; outside that week they propose blank blocks.
Like Figment's own validators, they voted to keep the 45M gas limit until the network moved to 60M; most of Coinbase's validators voted for 60M throughout.

evidence.note: None of their blocks, nor any of Figment's own, was delivered by the Aestus or Agnostic relays, which Coinbase's validators used for about a fifth of their blocks.

0137-coinbase-prime-custody-figment.summary: Validators of Coinbase Prime custody clients that carry Figment's fleet fingerprint are run by Figment, which takes precedence over the custody-address decisions 0114 and 0134 for them.
0137-coinbase-prime-custody-figment.decision: These 179 validators, Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake that Figment runs, are allocated by Figment; for them this takes precedence over decisions 0114 and 0134.

grounds.text: Each was deposited through Coinbase's batch contract by the custody address it withdraws to
In January 2026 each signed the same client string as Figment's own validators, starting and stopping that week
Like Figment's own, they voted against the 60M gas limit and never used the Aestus or Agnostic relays

0137-coinbase-prime-custody-figment.would_change: The custody clients or Coinbase naming another operator for these validators, or their behaviour diverging from Figment's fleet.
0137-coinbase-prime-custody-figment.explanation:
These 179 validators, the stake of Coinbase Prime custody clients, carry the fingerprint of Figment's validator fleet and are attributed to Figment as allocator. For them this takes precedence over the decisions covering the custody addresses they withdraw to (decisions 0134 and 0167). In October 2026 they were active with about 100k ETH.

The deposits. Each was deposited through Coinbase's batch deposit contract by the custody address it withdraws to, as Coinbase Prime custody clients' validators are.

Figment's fingerprint. In one week of January 2026 these validators signed the same bare client-version graffiti string as Figment's own validators, starting and stopping in the same week: a fleet-wide configuration change, also seen on Grayscale's Figment validators (decision 0136). Independently, they voted against raising the gas limit to 60 million as Figment's validators did, and, like Figment's, never used the Aestus or Agnostic relays.

Why Figment is the allocator. Coinbase Prime clients choose their staking providers, and these validators are run by Figment's fleet; Figment is therefore the provider the clients chose. Only validators that proposed a block in that week carry the fingerprint, so other Figment-run custody validators may remain under the custody decisions. Other validators with the same fingerprint but nothing showing whose stake they are have not been attributed. The decision would change with the custody clients or Coinbase naming another operator for these validators, or their behaviour diverging from Figment's fleet.

evidence.note: 130 withdraw to custody addresses attributed to Coinbase Prime by 0114 or 0134; 49, deposited from December 2025 to April 2026, withdraw to custody addresses not yet attributed.

Like Figment's own validators, they voted to keep the 45M gas limit until the network moved to 60M; most of Coinbase's validators voted for 60M throughout.

evidence.note: None of their blocks, nor any of Figment's own, was delivered by the Aestus or Agnostic relays, which Coinbase's validators used for about a fifth of their blocks.

0138-bitmine-staking-control-check.summary: Two addresses that proved common control together with BitMine's wallets, and stake the same way, are BitMine's treasury staking.
0138-bitmine-staking-control-check.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 2 addresses are BitMine's treasury staking.

grounds.text: Both sent 0.001 ETH in the same 73 minutes as all of BitMine's wallets in decision 0087, to the same two new accounts
Like BitMine's, each deposits compounding validators to itself; one runs on the same SSV operators, one on the same client build
Their 45k ETH, staked from October 2025, brings BitMine's January 2026 total within 1% of the figure it reported

0138-bitmine-staking-control-check.would_change: Evidence that either address is held by someone other than BitMine, or a provider identified for these validators.
0138-bitmine-staking-control-check.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xcc31…df43 and 0xdd6a…b30a are BitMine Immersion Technologies' treasury staking, with BitMine as allocator. In October 2026 the two addresses held 36 compounding validators with about 47k ETH, deposited from October 2025.

Common control. Both addresses took part in the control transfers of 31 August 2026 described under decision 0087, sending 0.001 ETH to the same two new accounts within the same 73 minutes as all 111 of BitMine's wallets in that decision.

The same way of staking. Each deposits compounding validators to itself, through the same two batch contracts BitMine's other wallets used. The first address's validators run on the same SSV operators as part of decision 0087's validators, registered by an owner account funded by the same account as those of 0087. The second's validators run on two of the fleets that also run validators of decisions 0087 and 0115: Nimbus with its default graffiti, and the Nethermind build seen only on BitMine's validators.

The match with BitMine's figures. [BitMine's first weekly figure](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-4-144-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-14-2-billion-302652341.html), 659,219 ETH staked as of 4 January 2026, is 6% above the deposits of decisions 0087 and 0115 by then; with these two addresses the deposits are 1% above it. Their figures as of 30 August 2026 are also part of the match described under decision 0087 ([release](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-5-90-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash-holdings-of-15-6-billion-302864579.html)).

Limits. As for decision 0087, the control transfers show one holder, or parties acting together, and the identification with BitMine rests on the match with its reported figures. These two addresses began staking about twelve weeks before BitMine's other wallets; that they fill the gap in its first weekly figure is the only evidence for the timing, and an outside client of the same providers would look the same. The decision would change with evidence that either address is held by someone other than BitMine, or with a provider identified for these validators.

0139-okx-por-staking.summary: Validators at five more withdrawal addresses, three accounts and two EigenLayer pods that OKX's signed proof of reserves lists as its staked ETH, are OKX's staking.
0139-okx-por-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 5 addresses are OKX's staking.

grounds.text: OKX's signed proof-of-reserves file lists every validator at these addresses as its staked ETH, signed with each address's key
The two EigenLayer pods are owned on chain by accounts whose signatures on the same file name them OKX's

0139-okx-por-staking.would_change: OKX dropping these validators from its proof of reserves while they stay active, or a statement that they are a client's.
0139-okx-por-staking.explanation:
Validators at five more withdrawal addresses, three accounts and two EigenLayer pods that OKX's signed proof of reserves lists as its staked ETH, are OKX's staking, with OKX as allocator. In October 2026 they held about 330 active validators with some 31k ETH, all of them previously unattributed. They add to the stake of OKX's main deposit account (decision 0025).

OKX's own proof of reserves. OKX publishes [a wallet file with each proof of reserves](https://static.okx.com/cdn/okx/por/chain/por_csv_2026100300_V4.zip); the snapshot of 3 October 2026 was used. Among its native ETH staking rows are validators withdrawing to the three accounts, each row signed over the message "I am an OKX address", with a signature that recovers to the withdrawal address the row names: whoever made the file holds those keys. Among its EigenLayer staking rows are validators listed under two owner accounts, signed by those owners. On chain, those validators withdraw to two EigenLayer pods whose owners are those two accounts, and the file also lists both pods as OKX addresses.

What this establishes. A signed row shows that OKX holds the withdrawal key and counts the validator in its reserves as staked customer ETH, which makes OKX the allocator. Restaking through EigenLayer delegates the pods' stake to an operator without changing who chose to stake. Every validator now withdrawing to these addresses is taken to be OKX's, including any deposited after the snapshot. The file does not say who operates the validators, so no operator is recorded.

The decision would change if OKX dropped these validators from its proof of reserves while they stayed active, or with a statement that they are a client's.

0141-coinbase-cloud-vpool.summary: The validators of the vPool 0x8eea…75f4, which names itself and its operator Coinbase Cloud, are allocated by Coinbase Cloud, not Kiln.
0141-coinbase-cloud-vpool.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x116b…5e9f, the withdrawal contract of the Coinbase Cloud vPool, are allocated by Coinbase Cloud.

grounds.text: It names itself "Coinbase Cloud vPool Shares", and its factory recorded "Coinbase Cloud" as its operator's name
Its factory's keys are registered by an account first funded by one that withdrew ETH from Coinbase's custody
None of its validators' blocks name Kiln, unlike every block of Kiln's own vPool

0141-coinbase-cloud-vpool.would_change: A Coinbase or Kiln statement that the pool's validators are allocated by Kiln or by another party.
0141-coinbase-cloud-vpool.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x116b…5e9f, the withdrawal contract of a vPool that names itself and its operator Coinbase Cloud, are attributed to Coinbase Cloud as allocator. The vPool, a pooled-staking contract built from Kiln's code, deposited 5,064 validators; about 3,550 were active in October 2026 with some 0.11M ETH. The decision replaces an earlier one (0040) that had given the pool to Kiln.

What the pool records about itself. The pool's name() returns "Coinbase Cloud vPool Shares", and when its factory was created it recorded "Coinbase Cloud" as its operator's name; the record has never changed. Kiln's own vPool, built from the same code and the same factory system, names itself "Kiln vPool Shares" and records "Kiln" (decision 0039). Both factories were created through the same deployment contract, so Kiln's tooling set up both.

Keys and graffiti. Every key added to the Coinbase Cloud factory came from its administrator account, which was first funded by an account that had received ETH from one of Coinbase's custody wallets. No transfer links the Coinbase Cloud factory's accounts to Kiln's. Of the 14,065 blocks its validators have proposed, 13,846 are blank and the rest carry client version strings; none names Kiln, whereas every block of Kiln's own vPool is signed "Kiln.fi". Every deposit crediting the withdrawal contract came from this pool.

Why Coinbase Cloud is the allocator. The names a contract records for itself are set by whoever sets the pool up for its owner, so they say whose product it is. Whether Coinbase Cloud runs the validators itself or Kiln runs them as a white-label provider, the pool is Coinbase Cloud's offering, which makes Coinbase Cloud the allocator. No operator is recorded. The single funding link to Coinbase's custody wallet fits this but would not on its own identify the pool.

The decision would change with a Coinbase or Kiln statement that this pool's validators are allocated by Kiln or another party.

evidence.ref: eth_call 0x8eea6cc08d824b20efb3bf7c248de694cb1f75f4 name() = "Coinbase Cloud vPool Shares"; factory() = 0x2d5e65ff87d986d18ac224e725dc654bec3a04cd

evidence.note: Creation of the vFactory, emitting SetMetadata("Coinbase Cloud", "", ""), block 18,114,639
0x84e1…3b46 first funds the factory admin 0xe9d7…7469 (0.5 ETH)

0142-consensys-staking-depositor-224fc4.summary: Validators this account deposited are Consensys Staking's: it batched them as Consensys's platform does, they paid the client's own fee recipient, and their software changed in step with Consensys's other validators.
0142-consensys-staking-depositor-224fc4.decision: Validators whose first deposit this account sent are run and allocated by Consensys (Consensys Staking).

grounds.text: Consensys's staking guide sends clients' batch deposits through the contract this account used, up to 100 validators a time
This account never sent more than 100 in a transaction, and its validators paid a fee recipient of the client's own
Their client software changed release by release at the same slots as Consensys's other validators

0142-consensys-staking-depositor-224fc4.would_change: A Consensys or Staked statement contradicting it, or evidence that another operator ran these validators.
0142-consensys-staking-depositor-224fc4.explanation:
The account 0x224f…9495 is the deposit account of a Consensys Staking client. Validators whose first deposit it sent are attributed to Consensys as allocator and operator, while the client keeps its own withdrawal address. It sent the first deposits of 625 validators on 28 December 2020, through the batch deposit contract 0x39dc…da29. All have since exited.

The route. [Consensys's staking guide](https://docs.staking.consensys.io/staking-help/create-stake) sends clients' batch deposits through this contract, up to 100 validators (3,200 ETH) a transaction, and lets the client choose the fee recipient. The contract was written and deployed by Staked ([its repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract)), whose own deposit accounts use it too; they batch up to 185 validators at once and pay Staked's fee recipient. This account never sent more than 100 validators in one transaction. Their blocks paid 0xed33…85bf, a fee recipient of the client's own.

The operator. The validators' graffiti carries client version strings only. Across the client releases from early 2024, these and Consensys's other validators first used each version within hours to a day or two of one another, while the network as a whole had first used it days or weeks earlier. Coinbase's validator fleet adopts releases at almost the same times, so the timing alone does not separate the two; the route does, since this is the contract Consensys's guide names, not Coinbase's.

Why Consensys is the allocator. A client staking through a provider's platform has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address (the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts, decision 0005). Consensys's validator staking for MetaMask is recorded in decision 0135. Explorer labels naming the account as one of Staked's depositors are recorded as leads; they had earlier led to these validators being attributed to Staked. The decision would change with a Consensys or Staked statement contradicting it, or evidence that another operator ran these validators.

0150-whale-eth-depositor.decision: This account's validators, and those withdrawing to the address they moved to, were whale.eth's own staking.

grounds.text: The account's ENS primary name is whale.eth, and the name resolves back to it
It deposited 710 validators from its own ETH and traded on DeFi from 2020, as a private holder does

0150-whale-eth-depositor.would_change: A PieDAO or Auxo statement that the account deposited for it, or evidence the stake belonged to someone else.
0150-whale-eth-depositor.explanation:
The account 0x6682…6ba8, whose ENS name is whale.eth, deposited 710 validators from its own ETH between November and December 2020: its validators, and those withdrawing to the address they moved to, are attributed to whale.eth's own staking, with the account as allocator. They made up 1.8% of all stake at the beacon chain's launch, and all exited in April 2023.

Identification. The account's ENS primary name is whale.eth, and whale.eth resolves back to the account. The ENS name is used as the account's own public label; no person is named.

On chain. The account was first funded in January 2020 and has traded actively since, wrapping and swapping ETH on decentralised exchanges, as a private holder does. It deposited the 710 validators, 22,720 ETH, with BLS credentials, all later changed to a single address, which paid out the ETH after the validators exited.

Why not PieDAO. An explorer label once named the account as a depositor for PieDAO, and these validators had been attributed to PieDAO on that basis alone. PieDAO's published documentation and code mention neither the account nor its withdrawal address. The label is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with a PieDAO or Auxo statement that the account deposited for it, or evidence that the stake belonged to someone else.

0151-stader-ethx.summary: Stader's own contract list names the two contracts that send every ETHx validator's first deposit; validators deposited through them, withdrawing to their own Stader vaults, are Stader ETHx's.
0151-stader-ethx.decision: Validators whose first deposit Stader's Stake Pool Manager sent, and those withdrawing to the vaults those deposits name, are Stader ETHx's.

grounds.text: Stader's ETHx repository names this contract its Stake Pool Manager
It sent the first 1 ETH deposit of 5,074 validators, each to its own withdrawal vault

0151-stader-ethx.would_change: A Stader statement contradicting it, or evidence the contract deposited for others.
0151-stader-ethx.explanation:
The contract 0xcf5e…d299 is the Stake Pool Manager of Stader's liquid staking token ETHx. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and those withdrawing to the vaults those deposits name, are attributed to Stader ETHx as allocator.

Identification. [Stader's ETHx repository](https://github.com/stader-labs/ethx/blob/9d4a9211431d6c0cdf014bd64d3718cba4ce96ab/README.md) lists its mainnet contracts, naming this one as its Stake Pool Manager. Every ETHx validator's first deposit, of 1 ETH, is sent by one of two contracts on that list: the Stake Pool Manager (decision 0151) or the Permissionless Node Registry (decision 0152). Each deposit names the validator's own withdrawal vault.

On chain. 5,074 validators' first deposits came through this contract between June 2023 and April 2026, each to a different withdrawal address, Stader's per-validator vaults. Together the two contracts deposited 8,457 validators from June 2023; about 2,270 were active in October 2026, with some 73k ETH.

Why Stader is the allocator. ETHx assigns stakers' ETH to its node operators by its own rules, so Stader chooses the operators. Some operators sign their own names in graffiti; before this decision 65 validators had been attributed to those operators on that basis, and this claim now takes precedence. The decision would change with a Stader statement contradicting it, or evidence that the contract deposited for others.

evidence.note: A first deposit sent through the Stake Pool Manager

0153-staked-fee-recipient.decision: This address is Staked's fee recipient; otherwise unattributed validators paying it are run and allocated by Staked.

grounds.text: Validators deposited through Staked's accounts pay their fees and MEV to it, as Staked says it collects them
It was first funded by, and pays commission to, a wallet the creator of Staked's batch contract funded
2,858 other validators paid it in 98.6% of their blocks, as the fee recipient their operator set

0153-staked-fee-recipient.would_change: Evidence that clients of other providers also use this address as their fee recipient.
0153-staked-fee-recipient.explanation:
The address 0xe94f…6ca0c is Staked's execution-reward pool: Staked's validators pay their transaction fees and MEV to it, and it pays them on to stakers after Staked's commission. Validators otherwise unattributed that paid it are attributed to Staked as allocator for as long as they did. Staked has been part of Kraken since 2021. 3,946 validators have paid it since the Merge; in October 2026 about 2,800 relied on this decision, with some 0.11M ETH.

Identification. [Staked's FAQ on withdrawals](https://staked.us/faq/ethereum-withdrawals/) explains that it collects its validators' execution-layer rewards and pays them on, keeping its commission. The validators deposited by the accounts that used Staked's own batch deposit contract ([its repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract); decisions 0047 to 0066) pay this address. Its first incoming transfer came from a wallet funded by the creator of Staked's batch contract, which has since received 800 ETH from it in commission, and it has made 9,066 payments on to stakers.

The other validators. 2,858 validators not otherwise attributed paid it in 98.6% of their blocks, as the fee recipient their operator set. Most are registered on SSV under one owner account, which also owns validators deposited through Staked's accounts. This matches Staked's move of its fleet to SSV in early 2025, visible in its validators' graffiti. 19 validators otherwise attributed to Bitfinex paid it in 41% of their blocks; they keep their Bitfinex attribution, since a fee recipient yields to every other allocator claim.

Staked is the allocator for its clients, who keep their own withdrawal addresses. The decision would change with evidence that clients of other providers also use this address as their fee recipient.

evidence.note: 0x87bc makes the first transfer to this address
This address pays 0x87bc (first of 4 transfers, 800 ETH)

0156-bitflyer-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are attributed to bitFlyer's staking (strongly suggestive, not conclusive).
