All deposits go through the 3-of-3 multisig they withdraw to, which got 256,246 ETH from one wallet

0156-bitflyer-staking.would_change: An address list or statement from bitFlyer that excludes this multisig, or evidence that the multisig or the wallet funding it belongs to someone else.
0156-bitflyer-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to the multisig wallet 0x51b4…b913 are attributed to the ETH staking of bitFlyer, the Japanese exchange. The evidence is strongly suggestive but not conclusive: bitFlyer names no address, and the link rests on timing and size. 11,922 validators have been deposited since May 2025; about 8,080 were active in October 2026 with some 0.26M ETH. Most were deposited through Kiln's and Blockdaemon's contracts, so those providers are their allocators; this decision applies only to validators no provider claims, and decision 0188 records bitFlyer as principal of all of them.

The multisig. It is a multisig wallet with three owners, all of whom must sign. Every deposit was sent through it by its owners. One wallet sent it 256,246 ETH in 30 transfers from May 2025 to February 2026, and it is its validators' own fee recipient.

The timing. bitFlyer's [staking page](https://bitflyer.com/ja-jp/s/staking) launched ETH staking for customers who opt in, with the amount staked to be increased in stages; [its business report for 2025](https://bitflyer.com/pub/business-report-12th.pdf) confirms the launch in August 2025, and [CoinPost dates it to 12 August](https://coinpost.jp/?p=641425). After two test deposits in May, this multisig began its large deposits at 17:21 Japan time on 12 August 2025.

The size. [bitFlyer's audited accounts for 2025](https://bitflyer.com/pub/financial-statement-12th.pdf) give 272,751 ETH held, its own and its customers', at 31 December 2025. The validators then held 245,666 ETH and the multisig 2,792 ETH, about 90% of the total; a larger fleet could not have been bitFlyer's. bitFlyer also publishes the rate it earned each month; the fleet's rates are close but not distinctive enough to count either way.

Limits. Nothing bitFlyer signed or sent ties it to the multisig. bitFlyer's FAQ says it uses a staking service provider, unnamed, which fits the providers found. Explorer labels on the funding wallet are recorded as leads. The decision would change with an address list or statement from bitFlyer that excludes this multisig, or evidence that the multisig or the wallet funding it belongs to someone else.

evidence.note: First deposit of the main fleet, 12 August 2025 08:21 UTC (17:21 JST), the day bitFlyer launched ETH staking
Test deposit through the multisig, 22 May 2025
0x8350…bd96's first transfer to the multisig (0.01 ETH test)
0x8350…bd96's last transfer to the multisig (6,720 ETH, February 2026)

0157-swell-deposit-manager.summary: The swETH token's own on-chain registry names this contract its Deposit Manager; validators deposited through it, all withdrawing to it, are Swell swETH's.
0157-swell-deposit-manager.decision: Validators whose first deposit Swell's Deposit Manager sent, and those withdrawing to it, are Swell swETH's.

grounds.text: The swETH token's AccessControlManager names this contract its DepositManager, and it points back to that manager
Swell's published code uses the Deposit Manager's own address as its validators' withdrawal credentials
It sent the deposits of 7,784 validators from 19 April 2023, all withdrawing to it; 350 are active now

0157-swell-deposit-manager.would_change: A Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the swETH contracts are not Swell's.
0157-swell-deposit-manager.explanation:
The contract 0xb3d9…8f39 is the Deposit Manager of Swell's liquid staking token swETH. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and validators withdrawing to it, are attributed to Swell swETH as allocator. It deposited 7,784 validators between April 2023 and October 2025, holding as much as 249k ETH; 350 were active in October 2026, with 11,200 ETH.

Identification on chain. The swETH token contract (name and symbol "swETH") names an access-control manager, and that manager names this contract as its DepositManager and the token as its swETH; the Deposit Manager in turn names the same access-control manager. [Swell's published code](https://github.com/SwellNetwork/v3-core-public/blob/5827c4f1294b00f2939e582b1d3ac448f87fa218/contracts/lst/contracts/implementations/DepositManager.sol) sets the Deposit Manager's own address as its validators' withdrawal credentials, and every one of the 7,784 validators withdraws to it. All the deposits were sent by one operating account.

Consistency with public information. The active validators' 11,200 ETH, together with the 301 ETH the Deposit Manager holds, is close to the ETH behind swETH's supply (about 12,160 ETH at its exchange rate). [DefiLlama has measured Swell's staked value](https://github.com/DefiLlama/DefiLlama-Adapters/blob/f9f37f8d82936bdc63bbc93ac0262fa29a2c8988/projects/swell/index.js) from the same swETH contract since a week after the first deposit. No Swell web page naming the address could be retrieved.

Not covered: Swell's restaking token, rswETH, has its own Deposit Manager, which deposited 4,018 validators in 2024; none is active. The decision would change with a Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the swETH contracts are not Swell's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through Swell's Deposit Manager, 19 April 2023

0158-swell-rsweth-deposit-manager.summary: The rswETH token's own on-chain registry names this contract its Deposit Manager; validators it deposited in 2024, withdrawing to its own EigenPod, are Swell rswETH's.
0158-swell-rsweth-deposit-manager.decision: Validators whose first deposit Swell's rswETH Deposit Manager sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenPod those deposits name, are Swell rswETH's.

grounds.text: The rswETH token's AccessControlManager names this contract its DepositManager, and it points back to that manager
It sent the deposits of 4,018 validators in 2024, all withdrawing to an EigenPod it owns; none is active now

0158-swell-rsweth-deposit-manager.would_change: A Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the rswETH contracts are not Swell's.
0158-swell-rsweth-deposit-manager.explanation:
The contract 0x5e63…4889 is the Deposit Manager of Swell's restaking token rswETH. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and validators withdrawing to the EigenLayer pod those deposits name, are attributed to Swell rswETH as allocator. Between January and May 2024 it deposited 4,018 validators, holding as much as 129k ETH; none is active now. Swell's later restaking deposits, made through its EigenLayer manager, are attributed in decision 0159.

Identification on chain. The rswETH token contract names an access-control manager; that manager names this contract as its DepositManager, and the Deposit Manager names the same access-control manager and an EigenLayer manager that in turn points back to it. The 4,018 validators all withdraw to an EigenLayer pod owned by the Deposit Manager; [Swell's published code](https://github.com/SwellNetwork/v3-core-public/blob/5827c4f1294b00f2939e582b1d3ac448f87fa218/contracts/lrt/contracts/implementations/EigenLayerManager.sol) now refers to that pod as deprecated, its restaking having moved to the EigenLayer manager's staker proxies.

Consistency with public information. [DefiLlama has measured Swell's restaking value](https://github.com/DefiLlama/DefiLlama-Adapters/blob/9791503c846c7970bd4c6900a933d18aa5f85c17/projects/swell-restaking/index.js) from the rswETH contract since 30 January 2024, the day after the first deposit. This is the same self-identification on chain by which Swell's swETH is recorded (decision 0157). The decision would change with a Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the rswETH contracts are not Swell's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through Swell's rswETH Deposit Manager, 29 January 2024

0159-swell-rsweth-eigenlayer-manager.summary: rswETH's Deposit Manager names this contract its EigenLayerManager; validators it deposited, withdrawing to the EigenPods of its staker proxies, are Swell rswETH's.
0159-swell-rsweth-eigenlayer-manager.decision: Validators whose first deposit Swell's rswETH EigenLayerManager sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenPods those deposits name, are Swell rswETH's.

grounds.text: rswETH's Deposit Manager names this contract its EigenLayerManager, which shares the rswETH token's AccessControlManager
Swell's published code has it stake validators through staker proxies, each with its own EigenPod
It sent the deposits of 3,856 validators from August 2024, all withdrawing to its proxies' pods; 168 are active now

0159-swell-rsweth-eigenlayer-manager.would_change: A Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the rswETH contracts are not Swell's.
0159-swell-rsweth-eigenlayer-manager.explanation:
The contract 0xc94c…0936 is the EigenLayer manager of Swell's restaking token rswETH. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenLayer pods of its staker proxies, are attributed to Swell rswETH as allocator. It deposited 3,856 validators from August 2024, holding as much as 26k ETH.

Identification on chain. rswETH's Deposit Manager (decision 0158) names this contract as its EigenLayer manager, and the manager shares the rswETH token's access-control manager. [Swell's published code](https://github.com/SwellNetwork/v3-core-public/blob/5827c4f1294b00f2939e582b1d3ac448f87fa218/contracts/lrt/contracts/implementations/EigenLayerManager.sol) has the manager stake validators through staker proxies, each with its own EigenLayer pod; on chain it has 40 such proxies, each owning a pod, and each proxy names the Deposit Manager as its own. Every validator it deposited withdraws to one of those pods.

Consistency with public information. [DefiLlama has measured Swell's restaking value](https://github.com/DefiLlama/DefiLlama-Adapters/blob/9791503c846c7970bd4c6900a933d18aa5f85c17/projects/swell-restaking/index.js) from the rswETH contract since the day after its first deposit. rswETH's supply exceeds the ETH staked by these validators; rswETH also accepts other liquid staking tokens, restaked in EigenLayer directly, which would account for the difference.

The decision would change with a Swell statement contradicting it, or evidence that the rswETH contracts are not Swell's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through Swell's rswETH EigenLayerManager, 26 August 2024

0160-nodedao-liquid-staking.summary: NodeDAO's own list of its contracts names this its LiquidStaking contract; validators deposited through it are NodeDAO nETH's.
0160-nodedao-liquid-staking.decision: Validators whose first deposit NodeDAO's LiquidStaking contract sent, and those withdrawing to the addresses those deposits name, are NodeDAO nETH's.

grounds.text: NodeDAO's published list of its Ethereum contracts names this its LiquidStaking proxy
It sent the deposits of 508 validators from March 2023 to March 2024; 506 withdraw to NodeDAO's ConsensusVault
None of these validators is active now

0160-nodedao-liquid-staking.would_change: A NodeDAO statement contradicting it, or evidence that the listed contracts are not NodeDAO's.
0160-nodedao-liquid-staking.explanation:
The contract 0x8103…3096 is the LiquidStaking contract of NodeDAO's liquid staking token nETH. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and those withdrawing to the addresses those deposits name, are attributed to NodeDAO nETH as allocator. It sent 508 deposits between March 2023 and March 2024, holding as much as 15k ETH; none is active now.

Identification. [NodeDAO's repository](https://github.com/NodeDAO/NodeDAO-Protocol/blob/aad124c73ff66eb1bc1a7c05f9a963d48a4eaec7/README.md) lists its Ethereum contracts: a timelock controller, this LiquidStaking proxy and a ConsensusVault proxy. On chain, the timelock owns both proxies. 506 of the 508 deposits name the ConsensusVault as withdrawal address; the other two each name an ordinary account, for reasons not established, but NodeDAO's contract sent them.

NodeDAO chooses the operators of its pool, so it is the allocator. No operator is recorded. The decision would change with a NodeDAO statement contradicting it, or evidence that the listed contracts are not NodeDAO's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through NodeDAO's LiquidStaking contract, 3 March 2023

0161-nodedao-restaking-pool.summary: This contract and its pool token, Restaking Node ETH, are owned by the timelock NodeDAO lists as its own; validators it deposited, withdrawing to an EigenPod NodeDAO also controls, are NodeDAO rnETH's.
0161-nodedao-restaking-pool.decision: Validators whose first deposit NodeDAO's restaking pool sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenPod those deposits name, are NodeDAO rnETH's.

grounds.text: Its owner, and the owner of its pool token Restaking Node ETH (rnETH), is the timelock NodeDAO lists as its own
It sent the deposits of 368 validators from April 2024, all withdrawing to an EigenPod whose owner the same timelock owns
Its validator manager, which sent every deposit, has the verified ENS name nodedao.eth; 298 validators are active now

0161-nodedao-restaking-pool.would_change: A NodeDAO statement contradicting it, or evidence that the timelock or these contracts are not NodeDAO's.
0161-nodedao-restaking-pool.explanation:
The contract 0x0d6f…25bc is NodeDAO's restaking pool, whose token is rnETH (Restaking Node ETH). Validators whose first deposit it sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenLayer pod those deposits name, are attributed to NodeDAO rnETH as allocator. It sent 368 deposits between April 2024 and May 2025; 298 validators were active in October 2026 with about 9,500 ETH.

Identification. [NodeDAO's repository](https://github.com/NodeDAO/NodeDAO-Protocol/blob/aad124c73ff66eb1bc1a7c05f9a963d48a4eaec7/README.md) lists its timelock controller but predates this contract. On chain, the pool's owner is that timelock, as is the owner of its pool token, "Restaking Node ETH" (rnETH). Every deposit was sent by the pool's validator manager, whose verified ENS name is nodedao.eth, and every deposit withdraws to one EigenLayer pod, whose owner is itself owned by the same timelock.

NodeDAO chooses the operators of its pool, so it is the allocator. No operator is recorded. The decision would change with a NodeDAO statement contradicting it, or evidence that the timelock or these contracts are not NodeDAO's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through NodeDAO's restaking pool, 23 April 2024

0162-celsius-staking-2021.summary: This address was Celsius's staking (2021-2024): its funding and its exits run through the wallets that hold and pay for the CEL token cited in the examiner's report on Celsius.
0162-celsius-staking-2021.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address were Celsius's staking, from 2021 until they exited in 2023-2024.

grounds.text: The court examiner's report on Celsius cites the CEL token and lists Direct Staking among Celsius's deployments
CEL's deployer made one account its owner and sent it all 700M CEL; the wallets around it moved most of the supply
A wallet that paid that owner's gas and sent it CEL received this address's ETH after its validators exited
The address's first 32 ETH, and nearly all its later funding, came from wallets in that same CEL-handling network

0162-celsius-staking-2021.would_change: Evidence that this address staked for someone other than Celsius, that the CEL owner's wallets are not Celsius's, or that a provider chose the operators.
0162-celsius-staking-2021.explanation:
The address 0xeee2…e4c8 held Celsius's staking from 2021 until its validators exited in 2023 and early 2024: validators withdrawing to it are attributed to Celsius as allocator. 4,943 validators deposited directly by it from August 2021 to April 2022 remain attributed here, peaking at 158k ETH in May 2022. The 6,294 it deposited later through Blockdaemon's batch contract are attributed to Blockdaemon as allocator (decision 0041).

The court record. The examiner's report in Celsius's bankruptcy ([Doc. 1956](https://cases.stretto.com/public/x191/11749/PLEADINGS/1174901312380000000039.pdf)) cites Celsius's token CEL by its contract address and lists direct staking among Celsius's deployments. It names no wallet.

The link through CEL. CEL's first transaction makes one account its owner, and the deployer then sent that account the whole supply of 700 million CEL; only the issuer would hold that. A wallet that paid the owner's gas in 2021 and sent it CEL trades both ETH and CEL with a hub that, together with a custody wallet, moved most of CEL's supply, as only Celsius would. That hub supplies a trading wallet which sent 0xeee2…e4c8 its first 32 ETH on the day of its first deposit in August 2021. Every material payment into the address came from this same network, and after its validators exited it sent its ETH back into it: 161k ETH to the custody wallet and 205k ETH to the wallet that had paid the owner's gas.

The address was the sender and the withdrawal address of all its deposits. Explorer labels on the wallets involved are recorded as leads, not relied on. Celsius's other staking account, which deposited only through Figment's contracts, is attributed to Figment under decisions 0029 and 0031. The decision would change with evidence that this address staked for someone other than Celsius, that the CEL owner's wallets are not Celsius's, or that a provider chose the operators.

evidence.note: CEL's deployer sets 0x9173 as the token's owner (April 2018)
CEL's deployer sends the owner the whole 700M CEL supply
0xdb31 pays the CEL owner's gas (0.5 ETH, 30 September 2021)
0xeee2 sends 1,926 ETH to 0x4131 after the exits

0163-celsius-principal.summary: Celsius's two staking accounts: Celsius chose the providers (Blockdaemon, Figment) or staked directly, and received the withdrawals.
0163-celsius-principal.decision: Celsius was the principal of the validators withdrawing to these two addresses: it hired their allocators, or staked itself.

grounds.text: Each address sent its own deposits and withdraws to itself, so whoever holds it chose the staking route and got the ETH back
Both were first funded by the same wallet, and after the exits sent their ETH to the same two wallets
Decision 0162 ties those wallets to the CEL token cited in the court examiner's report on Celsius

0163-celsius-principal.would_change: Evidence that either address held stake for someone other than Celsius, or that the CEL-handling wallets are not Celsius's.
0163-celsius-principal.explanation:
Celsius, the crypto lender, was the principal of the validators withdrawing to its two staking accounts, 0xeee2…e4c8 and 0x1ced…9074: the ETH was Celsius's, and Celsius chose how it was staked. Where it staked through a provider, the provider is the allocator: Blockdaemon for the validators 0xeee2…e4c8 deposited through Blockdaemon's contract (decision 0041), and Figment for all the validators of 0x1ced…9074, deposited through Figment's contracts (decisions 0029 and 0031). The validators 0xeee2…e4c8 deposited directly are Celsius's own (decision 0162). This decision records Celsius as principal of all 25,344 validators, so Celsius's stake can be shown without counting it twice. All exited by January 2024.

Common control. Each account sent its own deposits and is its own withdrawal address, so whoever holds it chose the staking route and received the ETH back. 0x1ced…9074 was first funded by the same trading wallet that first funded 0xeee2…e4c8, and received most of its ETH from that wallet and others in the same network; the two accounts also sent each other ETH. After the exits, both sent their ETH to the same two wallets, each making its last large transfer on 23 January 2024.

The link to Celsius. Decision 0162 traces those wallets to the owner of Celsius's CEL token, which the [examiner's report in Celsius's bankruptcy](https://cases.stretto.com/public/x191/11749/PLEADINGS/1174901312380000000039.pdf) cites, and which only the issuer would control. Explorer labels on the wallets are recorded as leads, not relied on.

The decision would change with evidence that either account held stake for someone other than Celsius, or that the wallets handling CEL are not Celsius's.

evidence.note: 0x1ced's first deposit, through Figment's depositor contract
0xeee2's first deposit through Blockdaemon's batch contract
0x1ced sends its last 354,991 ETH to 0xdb31 (23 January 2024)
0xeee2 sends its last 202,090 ETH to 0xdb31 (23 January 2024)

0165-grayscale-principal.summary: Grayscale's ether funds hold these custody addresses' stake and chose its staking providers (Figment, Galaxy and one not yet identified).
0165-grayscale-principal.decision: Grayscale's ether funds (ETHE and the Mini Trust) are the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 363 custody addresses.

grounds.text: Grayscale's published staked ether matches 363 custody deposits of 3,200 ETH, one from each of these addresses
Each address sent its own deposit and is its validators' withdrawal address
Figment says Grayscale selected it as a staking provider, and Coinbase that its custody clients select their providers

0165-grayscale-principal.would_change: Grayscale's staked ether diverging from these deposits, or evidence that the addresses hold another client's ether.
0165-grayscale-principal.explanation:
Grayscale's two ether funds, the Grayscale Ethereum Trust (ETHE) and the Ethereum Mini Trust, are the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 363 addresses: the ETH is the funds', held in custody by Coinbase. In October 2026 the addresses held about 916 active validators with some 1.0M ETH.

The match with Grayscale's figures. The funds' pages ([ETHE](https://etfs.grayscale.com/ethe), [ETH](https://etfs.grayscale.com/eth)) report the amount staked: on 14 October 2025, 694,400 ETH for ETHE and 467,200 ETH for the Mini Trust, 217 and 146 lots of 3,200 ETH. Between 6 and 8 October 2025 exactly 363 deposits of 3,200 ETH were sent through Coinbase's batch deposit contract, one by each of these addresses to validators withdrawing to the same address. Each deposit was split across two or three operators in a fixed pattern (decision 0136 describes the patterns). The addresses later deposited 57 more validators in the same way. Which address belongs to which fund is not known.

Who chose the operators. [Figment announced that Grayscale selected it](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251009122610/en/Grayscale-Selects-Figment-as-a-Staking-Provider-for-U.S.-ETH-ETPs-and-SOL-Trust) as a staking provider for the funds, and in [a later release with Figment](https://www.figment.io/insights/coinbase-figment-expand-divisified-institutional-staking/) Coinbase said that Coinbase Prime lets institutions choose their providers while it keeps custody. Coinbase is therefore the custodian of this stake, not its allocator. Each provider Grayscale hired allocates its share: Figment (decision 0136), Galaxy (identified by its graffiti), and a third operator whose validators never sign graffiti and which has not been identified.

For that third share, where no provider is identified, Grayscale itself is taken as the allocator. The decision would change if Grayscale's reported staked ether diverged from these deposits, or with evidence that the addresses hold another client's ether.

evidence.ref: 363 transactions through Coinbase's batch contract 0x8ebda19ddee719dab78def3e22c3d37970e35217 on 2025-10-06 to 2025-10-08, each 3,200 ETH sent by the address its validators withdraw to
evidence.note: One per address; the funds' pages show 217 (ETHE) and 146 (Mini Trust) lots of 3,200 ETH staked on 14 October 2025.

0166-coinbase-prime-custody-figment-addr.summary: Validators at 15 Coinbase Prime custody addresses that also deposit through Figment's batch contract, and behave like Figment's fleet, are run and allocated by Figment.
0166-coinbase-prime-custody-figment-addr.decision: These 1,614 validators, at 15 custody addresses whose other validators Figment runs, are allocated by Figment; for them this takes precedence over decisions 0114 and 0134.

grounds.text: 11 of the 15 addresses also deposited validators through Figment's documented batch contract (973 in all), or hold ones 0137 names
Like Figment's own fleet, their blocks voted only against raising the gas limit to 60M (232 of 232); Coinbase's fleet voted for it
Like Figment's, none of their 2,640 relay blocks came through Aestus or Agnostic; most of Coinbase's fleet used them for about a fifth
None of their blocks carries a client build string of Coinbase's fleet

0166-coinbase-prime-custody-figment-addr.would_change: Coinbase or the custody clients naming another operator for these validators, or their behaviour diverging from Figment's fleet.
0166-coinbase-prime-custody-figment-addr.explanation:
These 1,614 validators, at fifteen Coinbase Prime custody addresses whose other validators Figment runs, are attributed to Figment as allocator. For them this takes precedence over the custody decisions covering those addresses (0134 and 0167). In October 2026, 1,220 of them were active with about 47k ETH.

The link to Figment. Eleven of the fifteen addresses also hold validators deposited through [Figment's documented batch contract](https://docs.figment.io/docs/our-eth-batch-smart-contract), 973 in all, or validators decision 0137 identifies as Figment's. [Coinbase Prime clients choose their staking provider](https://www.figment.io/insights/coinbase-figment-expand-divisified-institutional-staking/), and these clients chose Figment for those validators.

Figment's fleet behaviour. Every recorded gas-limit vote from these validators, 232 of 232, was against raising the limit to 60 million, as Figment's own fleet voted, whereas Coinbase's fleet voted for it. None of their 2,640 blocks delivered through relays came through the Aestus or Agnostic relays, as with Figment's fleet; most of Coinbase's fleet used those relays for about a fifth of its blocks. None of their blocks carries one of the client build strings Coinbase's fleet signs.

Limits. The relay test alone would not separate them from Coinbase, since a few of Coinbase's retail addresses also never used those relays; but those sign Coinbase's build strings and split their gas votes. Four of the fifteen addresses have no validators deposited through Figment's contract and rest on behaviour alone. The decision would change with Coinbase or the custody clients naming another operator for these validators, or their behaviour diverging from Figment's fleet.

evidence.ref: 973 validators withdrawing to 11 of these addresses first deposited through Figment's batch contract 0xf0075b3cf8953d3e23b0ef65960913fd97eb5227
evidence.note: The 1,614 named here were deposited through Coinbase's batch contract 0xefe9a82d56cd965d7b332c7ac1feb15c53cd4340 (1,200) or straight to the deposit contract (414), by the same addresses.
232 of their blocks voted the gas limit down and none up; Figment's own validators voted down in 95% of blocks, Coinbase's retail validators up in 97%.

evidence.ref: MEV-Boost payloads delivered from October 2025 to October 2026 (ethPandaOps Xatu relay data)
evidence.note: None of their 2,640 relay blocks came through Aestus or Agnostic; Coinbase's retail and Prime validators used them for 19% to 24% of blocks before 5 March 2026 and more after.

0167-coinbase-prime-custodian.summary: Coinbase holds these 1,313 withdrawal addresses in custody for Coinbase Prime clients; who chose and runs their staking is decided elsewhere.
0167-coinbase-prime-custodian.decision: Coinbase is the custodian of the validators withdrawing to these 1,313 addresses, held for Coinbase Prime custody clients.

grounds.text: Each address's deposits came from accounts funded, or given gas, by Coinbase custody or staking wallets (decisions 0114, 0134)
The account giving gas paid for 361 of the 363 deposits of Grayscale's ether funds, whose custodian is Coinbase Custody
Coinbase says Prime custody clients select their staking providers, so custody is recorded apart from allocation

0167-coinbase-prime-custodian.would_change: Evidence that an address is held by its owner or another custodian, not by Coinbase for a Prime client.
0167-coinbase-prime-custodian.explanation:
Coinbase holds these 1,313 withdrawal addresses in custody for clients of Coinbase Prime, its institutional service. The decision records custody only. Who chose the staking provider for each address is settled by other decisions: where one names a provider (Coinbase's own fleet under 0134, Figment under 0136, 0137 and 0166, or a provider named in graffiti or by a fee pool), that provider is the allocator; where a principal is known (Grayscale's ether funds, 0165), the principal follows. Only where nothing else shows an allocator is Coinbase, as custodian, assumed to be it.

The custody evidence. Each address's validators were deposited by accounts that Coinbase's custody systems funded or paid gas for. The key account is 0xa863…6c0f, which pays small amounts of gas to accounts shortly before they deposit. It paid for 361 of the 363 deposit transactions of Grayscale's two ether funds, whose fund pages ([ETHE](https://etfs.grayscale.com/ethe), [ETH](https://etfs.grayscale.com/eth)) name Coinbase Custody Trust Company as custodian. An account whose gas Coinbase pays is one whose keys Coinbase holds. Of the 541 addresses carried over from decision 0114, 539 have a depositing account that 0xa863…6c0f paid gas to, and 475 of those accounts were also first funded by one of two Coinbase custody wallets. The addresses from decision 0134 rest on the evidence set out there.

Why custody is recorded apart from allocation. Coinbase Prime clients choose among staking providers; [Figment's announcement with Coinbase Prime](https://www.figment.io/insights/coinbase-figment-expand-divisified-institutional-staking/) describes one such option. Custody alone does not show who runs the validators.

Wallets into which Coinbase's retail staking pays out are not treated as evidence of custody: they also fund ordinary customers' withdrawals, including home stakers. Two addresses that rested on them alone were removed. Explorer labels on the custody wallets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that an address is held by its owner, or by another custodian, rather than by Coinbase for a Prime client.

The same funder gives Grayscale's custody address 0x251b… gas, block 23,534,308
0x3cd7…9699 first funds the custody deposit funder (106 ETH), block 13,805,672

0170-gate-staking.summary: A self-run fleet, compounding its own rewards, whose deposits Gate's hot wallet funded; Gate named the cold wallet behind it as its own.
0170-gate-staking.decision: Validators sharing the fee recipient 0xcda9…7062, withdrawing to these seven addresses, are Gate's staking.

grounds.text: Gate named 0xc882…f071 as one of its cold wallets in November 2022; it then held 140,860 ETH, as Gate said
0xc882 and 0x0d07…92fe have sent each other 1.6M ETH each way; 0x0d07 funded three of the five depositors
All these validators pay block fees to one address, which pays every depositor ETH to restake
Each withdrawal address sends its ETH only back to its depositor, to be restaked

0170-gate-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0xc882 or 0x0d07 is not Gate's, or that Gate holds this stake for a single client.
0170-gate-staking.explanation:
Validators that pay their block fees to 0xcda9…7062 and withdraw to these addresses are Gate's ETH staking, with Gate, the exchange, as allocator. In October 2026 there were about 5,700 active validators with some 0.18M ETH. Gate offers ETH staking to its customers, whose stake this is.

The fleet. Since 2025 every block these validators proposed through a relay names the same fee recipient, 0xcda9…7062, and their graffiti is blank or a client version string. That fee recipient pays ETH to each of the five deposit accounts and to the withdrawal addresses. Each withdrawal address sends its ETH only back to its own deposit account, which deposits it again: one operator compounding its rewards by hand. Each deposit account has its own withdrawal address, and they deposited between May 2023 and July 2025. A further 1,000 validators deposited in November 2020 and since exited belong to the same staker (decision 0075): their principal was sent to one of these deposit accounts and restaked.

The link to Gate. In November 2022 Gate published one of its cold wallets, 0xc882…f071, as holding 140,000 ETH ([as reported by TokenInsight](https://tokeninsight.com/en/news/gate.io-says-assets-analyzed-on-web-only-portion-of-its-assets)); on chain it then held 140,860 ETH. That wallet and 0x0d07…92fe have sent each other about 1.5M ETH in each direction since 2022, and 0x0d07…92fe, which has sent ten million transactions to 1.45 million addresses, is an exchange's hot wallet. It funded three of the five deposit accounts, directly or through one intermediary. The other two were funded mostly from another exchange's hot wallets, as an exchange moving funds between venues would be; they are tied to the fleet by the shared fee recipient and its payments.

Limits. Gate's statement survives only as reported by a third party, and it names the cold wallet rather than the staking addresses. A community-maintained tracker lists five of the withdrawal addresses as Gate's staked ETH; that and explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that 0xc882…f071 or 0x0d07…92fe is not Gate's, or that Gate holds this stake for a single client.

evidence.note: Fee recipient 0xcda9 pays depositor 0x9f1d 73 ETH, block 21,321,824

0174-thedao-security-fund-dappnode.summary: TheDAO Security Fund's staked endowment: Dappnode runs it, and the validators say so in their blocks.
0174-thedao-security-fund-dappnode.decision: Dappnode is the allocator of the validators withdrawing to 0x5201…b756, TheDAO Security Fund's staked endowment.

grounds.text: The fund says roughly 69,000 ETH of its endowment is staked on infrastructure run by Dappnode
Most of their blocks are signed validating_from_dappnode_TDSF
The address deposited 69,420 ETH in February 2026, the amount the fund said it would stake
Its owner, thedaofund.eth, is a 4-of-7 Safe, as the fund describes its curators' multisig

0174-thedao-security-fund-dappnode.would_change: The fund naming another operator, or blocks of these validators signed by another one.
0174-thedao-security-fund-dappnode.explanation:
Dappnode is the allocator of the validators withdrawing to the Safe multisig 0x5201…b756, the staked endowment of TheDAO Security Fund. There are 34 compounding validators, holding about 69k ETH in October 2026. The fund itself is recorded as principal (decision 0175).

What the fund and the press say. [The fund's site](https://thedao.fund/) says roughly 69,000 ETH of its endowment is staked on decentralised infrastructure run by Dappnode, and that its seven curators sign a 4-of-7 multisig. [Decrypt reported at the fund's launch](https://decrypt.co/356404/ethereum-crisis-reborn-220-million-security-fund), on 29 January 2026, that about 69,420 ETH would be staked.

On chain. The Safe's owners are another Safe with seven owners and a threshold of four, whose verified ENS name is thedaofund.eth, and a second Safe sharing an owner with it. The Safe made all its deposits itself on 1 and 2 February 2026: 69,420 ETH to the 34 validators. Of the validators' blocks, 2,060 of 2,389 are signed "validating_from_dappnode_TDSF", the rest blank.

The fund hired Dappnode to run the stake, so Dappnode is the allocator and operator; the fund is the principal. The decision would change with the fund naming another operator, or blocks of these validators signed by another one.

evidence.note: 0x5201 tops the 34 validators up with 69,386 ETH, block 24,365,072

0175-thedao-security-fund-principal.summary: TheDAO Security Fund owns the stake at 0x5201…b756 and chose Dappnode to run it.
0175-thedao-security-fund-principal.decision: TheDAO Security Fund is the principal of the validators withdrawing to 0x5201…b756.

grounds.text: The fund says it staked its endowment, roughly 69,000 ETH, with Dappnode
The address is a Safe owned by thedaofund.eth, which made the deposits and receives the withdrawals

0175-thedao-security-fund-principal.would_change: Evidence that 0x5201 or thedaofund.eth is not the fund's.
0175-thedao-security-fund-principal.explanation:
TheDAO Security Fund is the principal of the validators withdrawing to the Safe multisig 0x5201…b756: the 69,420 ETH staked there is the fund's endowment, and the fund chose Dappnode to run it (decision 0174, which gives the evidence).

[The fund's site](https://thedao.fund/) says roughly 69,000 ETH of its endowment is staked with Dappnode. On chain, the Safe is owned by the fund's multisig, thedaofund.eth (a 4-of-7 Safe, as the fund describes its curators' multisig), together with a second Safe; it made the deposits itself and receives the withdrawals.

The decision would change with evidence that the Safe or thedaofund.eth is not the fund's.

0180-gemini-staking.summary: Gemini's ETH staking: the key that administers Gemini's own GUSD token operates these withdrawal wallets, and Gemini's printer funds them.
0180-gemini-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to these nine addresses are Gemini's staking.

grounds.text: Gemini publishes its GUSD token; GUSD's contracts name 0xd244 their printer, and 0x4c2f acted as their custodian
0x4c2f operates the contract withdrawal wallets; 0xd244, or the hub 0xf517 it funds, funded every depositor
Gemini says it stakes customers' Ether on validators it controls
A tracing expert's declaration filed in a 2022 court case lists 0xd244 as a Gemini address

0180-gemini-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0xd244 or 0x4c2f is not Gemini's, or that this stake is a single client's held outside Gemini's staking.
0180-gemini-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these nine addresses are Gemini's ETH staking, with Gemini as allocator. In October 2026 about 3,260 of them were active, with some 0.22M ETH; four of the addresses held validators from 2021 to 2025 that have all exited.

The link through Gemini's own token. Gemini issues the GUSD stablecoin, whose contract [Gemini's GUSD page](https://www.gemini.com/dollar) gives; Gemini's [annual report on Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2055592/000205559226000026/gemi-20251231.htm) calls GUSD a stablecoin issued by Gemini. Reading GUSD's contracts on chain gives the account allowed to mint it, 0xd244…6853, and shows another, 0x4c2f…5346, acting as the contracts' custodian, an action only the custodian can take. Separately, a tracing expert's declaration [filed in a 2022 court case](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.wied.100405/gov.uscourts.wied.100405.4.0_2.pdf) lists 0xd244…6853 as a Gemini address.

Control and funding. 0x4c2f…5346 is the account that operates six of the withdrawal addresses, which are wallet contracts built from two shared implementations; it also made the deposits for four of them, and 0xd244…6853 has paid its gas since 2017. Every depositor of the other addresses was funded by 0xd244…6853 or by 0xf517…, a high-volume hot wallet that 0xd244…6853 funds. The two largest groups, deposited from 2023 to 2026, went through Staked's batch deposit contract ([Staked's repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract)); the newer compounding validators, from November 2025, were deposited directly.

What Gemini says. Its annual report says it provides ETH staking using staking validators it controls, and its quarterly report for mid-2026 describes building out in-house validator capabilities, matching the new compounding fleets from November 2025. Staked may have run the earlier validators, but no operator is recorded.

Other accounts that Gemini's wallets funded look like customers' withdrawals, spread across many providers, and are not attributed. Explorer labels on Gemini's wallets are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that 0xd244…6853 or 0x4c2f…5346 is not Gemini's, or that this stake is a single client's held outside Gemini's staking.

evidence.note: 0xd244 mints GUSD through the print limiter (block 26,236,897)
0x4c2f confirms a custodian change on GUSD's implementation (block 26,156,774)

0183-crypto-com-staking.summary: Crypto.com's ETH staking: the wallet that pays for the keys of Crypto.com's CDCETH token is the only source of this staking wallet's ETH.
0183-crypto-com-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x93db…bc8b are Crypto.com's staking.

grounds.text: Crypto.com's bug bounty names 0xfe18 its CDCETH contract; it publishes the audit of the token's code
0xcffa sent CDCETH's admin key 0xfdaa and its rate oracle 0x59b0 the only ETH either has received
0xcffa sent 0x93db 149,383 ETH, nearly all its ETH, and 0x93db returned 77,203 ETH to it
0x93db made all its deposits itself, each to its own address, through Figment, Kiln and P2P contracts and directly

0183-crypto-com-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0xcffa is not Crypto.com's, or that 0x93db stakes for a single client rather than for Crypto.com's staking.
0183-crypto-com-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x93db…bc8b are Crypto.com's ETH staking. The wallet deposited 5,619 validators between March 2023 and October 2026, all crediting itself; about 2,230 were active in October 2026 with some 78k ETH. Most were deposited through providers' contracts (Figment, Kiln and P2P.org), and those providers are their allocators; this decision covers the rest, chiefly the compounding validators it has deposited directly since 2026. Decision 0184 records Crypto.com as principal of all of them.

The anchor: Crypto.com's CDCETH token. Crypto.com's [bug bounty programme](https://hackerone.com/crypto/policy_scopes) lists 0xfe18…c38e as its CDCETH smart contract, and Crypto.com publishes [the audit of the token's code](https://crypto.com/document/blocksec_securityaudit2024); [a proposal co-authored by Crypto.com to list CDCETH on Aave](https://governance.aave.com/t/temp-check-onboard-cdceth-to-aave-v3-on-ethereum/18259) gives the same contract. On chain, every privileged role of the token is held by one key, which minted its whole Ethereum supply, and a separate oracle account has made all its exchange-rate updates.

The link to the staking wallet. A high-volume exchange wallet, 0xcffa…0703, sent the token's admin key and its oracle the only ETH either has ever received; Crypto.com's keys are therefore funded from it. The same wallet gave the staking wallet its first ETH, and sent it 149,383 ETH in all, nearly all it holds; the staking wallet has returned 77,203 ETH to it. The staking wallet is also its validators' own fee recipient.

Limits. The link from the token to the stake is the shared funding wallet, not a role the staking wallet exercises on the token. Other accounts that the same wallet funded look like customers' withdrawals and are not attributed. The decision would change with evidence that 0xcffa…0703 is not Crypto.com's, or that the staking wallet stakes for a single client rather than for Crypto.com's staking.

evidence.note: CDCETH's admin key 0xfdaa mints 2,000 CDCETH to itself (block 19,025,952)
0x59b0 updates CDCETH's exchange rate as its oracle (block 19,907,723)
0xcffa sends CDCETH's admin key 0xfdaa its only ETH (block 19,016,637)
0xcffa pays the gas of CDCETH's oracle 0x59b0 (block 19,881,760)

0184-crypto-com-principal.summary: Crypto.com's staking wallet chose its providers (Figment, Kiln, P2P) or staked directly, and receives the withdrawals.
0184-crypto-com-principal.decision: Crypto.com is the principal of the validators withdrawing to 0x93db…bc8b: it hired their allocators, or staked itself.

grounds.text: 0x93db sent all its own deposits and withdraws to itself, so whoever holds it chose the staking route
Decision 0183 ties 0x93db to the wallet that funds the keys of Crypto.com's CDCETH token

0184-crypto-com-principal.would_change: Evidence that 0x93db holds stake for someone other than Crypto.com, or that 0xcffa is not Crypto.com's.
0184-crypto-com-principal.explanation:
Crypto.com is the principal of the validators withdrawing to its staking wallet 0x93db…bc8b: the ETH is Crypto.com's, staked for its customers, and Crypto.com chose how it is staked. In October 2026 about 2,230 such validators were active, with some 78k ETH.

The wallet sent all its own deposits and is its validators' withdrawal address, so whoever holds it chose each staking route. Some deposits went through providers' contracts, of Figment, Kiln and P2P.org; those validators keep the provider as their allocator, and this decision names the client that hired it. The others it staked directly.

Why the wallet is Crypto.com's. Decision 0183 sets out the link: the wallet is tied to the account that funds the keys of Crypto.com's staked-ETH token, CDCETH. That token's contract appears in [Crypto.com's audit of its wrapped tokens](https://crypto.com/document/blocksec_securityaudit2024) and in [a proposal co-authored by Crypto.com to list CDCETH on Aave](https://governance.aave.com/t/temp-check-onboard-cdceth-to-aave-v3-on-ethereum/18259), and Crypto.com's own bug bounty programme lists it.

Crypto.com's customers are the ultimate owners of the stake; the principal recorded here is the account holder that chose the providers. The decision would change with evidence that the wallet holds stake for someone other than Crypto.com, or that the account it is tied to is not Crypto.com's.

0187-bitstamp-staking.summary: Bitstamp's ETH staking: two BitGo multisig wallets whose deposits were made, and whose gas was paid, by keys that Bitstamp's own wallet operator funded.
0187-bitstamp-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x88a4…c20b or 0xf666…48ae are Bitstamp's staking.

grounds.text: Bitstamp's records, filed in a U.S. court case, name 0x1522 as its ETH wallet; 0x00bd deployed and operates it
0x538d's ETH came from 0x1522, 0x00bd and a wallet it co-signs, which also sent 0x3a1e its only ETH
0x538d made every deposit to 0x88a4 (2023 to 2025), and 0x3a1e every deposit to 0xf666 (since February 2025)
0x88a4's withdrawals reach Bitstamp's hot wallet 0x7f60, into which the contracts 0x3a1e operates also empty

0187-bitstamp-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0x538d or 0x3a1e acts for a client of Bitstamp, or for BitGo, rather than for Bitstamp's own staking.
0187-bitstamp-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x88a4…c20b or 0xf666…48ae are the staking of Bitstamp, the exchange, with Bitstamp as allocator. In October 2026 they held about 1,540 active validators with some 49k ETH. Both addresses are BitGo multisig wallets, each with three signers. Bitstamp says it delegates its customers' stake to a staking node operator. Since 30 October 2026 that operator is recorded as Staked: the validators run on SSV operators funded from the same source as those of Staked's own validators, and their early blocks paid Staked's fee recipient. Bitstamp was acquired by Robinhood in 2025; the stake is recorded under Bitstamp, the service that holds it.

The anchor. An expert report filed in a U.S. court case ([CFPB v. Consumer Advocacy Center, Doc. 364-3](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.762326/gov.uscourts.cacd.762326.364.3.pdf)) cites Bitstamp's records giving 0x1522…e428 as the address that sent a customer's ETH withdrawals. The account 0x00bd…74ed deployed that contract in 2017 and has called it about two million times: Bitstamp's wallet operator.

The deposit keys. The signer that deployed 0x88a4…c20b got its ETH only from Bitstamp's wallet contract, from its operator, and from a BitGo wallet it co-signs; it made every deposit to 0x88a4…c20b, from 2021 (with BLS credentials, later changed to the address) to February 2025. The signer that deployed 0xf666…48ae got its only ETH from that same co-signed wallet, in transactions sent by the first signer, and has made every deposit to 0xf666…48ae since February 2025.

Where the ETH goes. Withdrawals from 0x88a4…c20b pass through further wallets to 0x7f60…b752, a hot wallet into which Bitstamp's wallet contract empties, and the second signer operates thousands of contracts that also empty into it. The hot wallet's identification as Bitstamp's is itself inferred.

Limits. No Bitstamp document names the signers or the staking wallets. Bitstamp Europe's accounts for 2021 to 2023 list staked ether, consistent with the 2021 deposits. The decision would change with evidence that the signers act for a client of Bitstamp, or for BitGo, rather than for Bitstamp's own staking.

evidence.note: 0x00bd has Bitstamp's wallet 0x1522 send 0x538d its first ETH, 2 ETH (block 8,398,598)
0x538d moves 18,374 ETH of withdrawals from 0x88a4 to 0x4c76 (block 24,196,202)
0x538d has wallet 0x48ec send 0x3a1e its first ETH (block 21,229,264)
0x3a1e moves 9,284 ETH from 0x2e6b to Bitstamp's hot wallet 0x7f60 (block 24,568,641)

0188-bitflyer-principal.summary: bitFlyer's staking multisig chose its providers (Kiln, then Blockdaemon) and receives the withdrawals.
0188-bitflyer-principal.decision: bitFlyer is the principal of the validators withdrawing to 0x51b4…b913: it hired their allocators (strongly suggestive, not conclusive).

grounds.text: 0x51b4 made all its validators' deposits, through Kiln's and Blockdaemon's batch contracts, and they withdraw to it
Decision 0156 ties 0x51b4 to bitFlyer's ETH staking, launched on 12 August 2025, and to the ETH in its accounts

0188-bitflyer-principal.would_change: An address list or statement from bitFlyer that excludes this multisig, or evidence that it stakes for someone other than bitFlyer.
0188-bitflyer-principal.explanation:
bitFlyer, the Japanese exchange, is the principal of the validators withdrawing to the multisig wallet 0x51b4…b913: the ETH is bitFlyer's, staked for its customers, and bitFlyer hired the providers that run it. In October 2026 about 8,080 of these validators were active, with some 0.26M ETH.

The deposits. Tracing the multisig's deposit transactions shows that it called providers' batch deposit contracts rather than the deposit contract itself: Kiln's (decision 0034) for 3,838 validators between May and August 2025, all since exited, and Blockdaemon's (decision 0041) for 8,084 between May 2025 and February 2026. Those providers are the validators' allocators; this decision names the client that hired them.

The link to bitFlyer. Decision 0156 sets out why the multisig is taken to be bitFlyer's: its staking began alongside the launch of [bitFlyer's ETH staking service](https://bitflyer.com/ja-jp/s/staking) in August 2025, and its holdings are consistent with the ETH reported in [bitFlyer's financial statements for 2025](https://bitflyer.com/pub/financial-statement-12th.pdf). The link is strongly suggestive but not conclusive.

The decision would change with an address list or statement from bitFlyer that excludes this multisig, or evidence that it stakes for someone other than bitFlyer.

0189-infstones-imtoken-batch-deposit.summary: The batch-deposit contract behind imToken's in-wallet ETH staking, whose validators InfStones runs; its stake to 31 May 2021 matches imToken's own figure exactly.
0189-infstones-imtoken-batch-deposit.decision: This contract is InfStones' depositor contract for imToken's in-wallet staking; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by InfStones.

grounds.text: InfStones and imToken say InfStones runs a validator for every 32 ETH staked in imToken's wallet from May 2021
imToken reported 5,216 ETH staked by 31 May 2021; this contract had then taken exactly 5,216 ETH
Its owner 0xc8a6 collects a per-node fee, funds SSV operator account 0x52ec, and trades ETH with InfStones' 0xe2f8

0189-infstones-imtoken-batch-deposit.would_change: An InfStones or imToken statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys InfStones does not run are deposited through it.
0189-infstones-imtoken-batch-deposit.explanation:
The contract 0xbf15…c178 is the batch deposit contract behind the in-wallet ETH staking of the imToken wallet, whose validators InfStones runs. Validators first deposited through it are attributed to InfStones as allocator and operator; the stakers keep their own withdrawal addresses, and imToken, as the wallet through which they stake, never holds the stake. 4,493 deposits, about 144k ETH, went through it between April 2021 and October 2026, from 550 sending accounts; about 1,700 validators were active in October 2026 with some 55k ETH.

What InfStones and imToken say. [InfStones announced in May 2021](https://infstones.com/news/clients/imtoken-selects-infstones-as-staking-infrastructure-provider-for-in-wallet-eth20-staking), and [imToken likewise](https://support.token.im/hc/en-us/articles/900007069303-imToken-now-with-native-Eth2-integration-and-staking-as-a-service), that InfStones establishes a validator for every 32 ETH staked through imToken's wallet. [imToken's guide](https://www.campaign.token.im/infstones) says users buy 32 ETH nodes from their own address and pay a service fee to InfStones. [imToken's progress update of 31 May 2021](https://support.token.im/hc/en-us/articles/900007676643-Progress-Update-2021-05-31) reported 164 validators with 5,216 ETH staked; this contract had by then taken exactly 5,216 ETH.

On chain. The contract is stakefish's open batch deposit code with a fee per node, and its owner, 0xc8a6…53b8, created it and withdraws the fees. That owner funded the owner account of 20 private SSV operators, under which almost all of this contract's validators were registered. It also traded ETH with, and delegated to, the owner of InfStones' validator on Polygon. 176 of the 550 senders have traded through Tokenlon, imToken's in-wallet exchange.

Why InfStones is the allocator. Stakers choose InfStones' service through the wallet, and InfStones' key owns the contract and takes the fees; this is the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005), as for Kiln's Ledger Live contract (decision 0035). Neither company names the contract or its owner, and the contract can be called by anyone, though its fee makes that unlikely. The decision would change with an InfStones or imToken statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys InfStones does not run are deposited through it.

evidence.note: 0xc8a6 sends 6.78 ETH to InfStones' Polygon validator owner 0xe2f8
0xc8a6 sends 895 ETH to 0x07af, paid out to the contract's stakers (April 2025)

0192-maicoin-staking.summary: MaiCoin's ETH staking: 23 Safes with the same six owners, whose deposits were made by a key that MaiCoin's hot wallet funded, and by a second key depositing to the same Safes.
0192-maicoin-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 23 Safes are MaiCoin's staking.

grounds.text: A tracing report filed in a U.S. court case names 0xf803 a MaiCoin deposit address; it sweeps to 0x477b
0x477b sent deposit key 0x5a43 27,018 ETH in 263 transfers; it and 0x8e69 made every deposit to these Safes
All 23 are 3-of-6 Safes with the same six owners, who also own the Safe receiving their block rewards

0192-maicoin-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0x477b is not MaiCoin's, or that 0x5a43, 0x8e69 or the Safes' owners act for a MaiCoin client rather than MaiCoin.
0192-maicoin-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 23 Safe multisigs are the staking of MaiCoin, the Taiwanese exchange operator, with MaiCoin as allocator. In October 2026 they held 843 active validators with about 27k ETH, all previously unattributed. MaiCoin offers its customers ETH staking; who runs the validators is not established.

The anchor. A tracing report filed in a U.S. court case ([2:24-cv-06769, exhibit 1-1](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cacd.936897/gov.uscourts.cacd.936897.1.1_1.pdf)) names 0xf803…6975 as a MaiCoin deposit address in March 2023. That address was given gas by, and swept everything it received to, 0x477b…6b6f, a hot wallet.

The deposits. The hot wallet funded the deposit key 0x5a43…f212 with 27,018 ETH in 263 transfers from September 2023, and the key's first deposit followed within minutes of its first funding. That key and a second, 0x8e69…b1c4, which deposited to some of the same Safes, made every deposit to these 23 Safes, mostly in groups of 40 or 10 validators per Safe. Rewards withdrawn from the Safes flow back to the first key.

The Safes. Each is a 3-of-6 Safe with the same six owners, who also own the Safes receiving the validators' block rewards. The hot wallet also funded the creator and owner of MAX, MaiCoin's exchange token.

Limits. The court record names a customer deposit address, not the staking; the link from the hot wallet rests on funding, as for Bitstamp (decision 0187). MaiCoin's own pages describe its staking product but name no address. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the hot wallet is not MaiCoin's, or that the deposit keys or the Safes' owners act for a MaiCoin client rather than MaiCoin.

evidence.note: The deposit to MaiCoin address 0xf803 named in the court report (block 16,830,758)
0x477b sends deposit key 0x5a43 its first 32 ETH (block 18,219,510)
0x5a43's first deposit crediting one of the 23 Safes, 0x77ac (block 20,891,170)

0195-ethereum-foundation-staking.summary: The Ethereum Foundation's treasury staking: the validator it links as its first withdraws to Safe 0xc061, and so do 33 more of about 2,048 ETH each, about 70,000 ETH as it announced.
0195-ethereum-foundation-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to the Safe 0xc061…0b6d are the Ethereum Foundation's treasury staking.

grounds.text: The EF's announcement links its first staking validator, which withdraws to this Safe and took 2,016 ETH that day
The EF said about 70,000 ETH on 0x02 credentials, roughly 35 keys; this Safe has 34 validators holding 69,632 ETH
One of the Safe's seven owners created the Safe that made the first deposits; the Safe itself made the top-ups

0195-ethereum-foundation-staking.would_change: An Ethereum Foundation statement naming other validators, or evidence that the Safe is not the EF's.
0195-ethereum-foundation-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to the Safe multisig 0xc061…0b6d are the Ethereum Foundation's treasury staking, with the Foundation as allocator. There are 34 compounding validators, holding 69,632 ETH in October 2026, all previously unattributed. The Foundation stakes its own treasury and says it runs the validators itself; operators are left to graffiti.

What the Foundation published. [The Foundation's announcement of 24 February 2026](https://blog.ethereum.org/2026/02/24/staking) describes staking about 70,000 ETH with compounding (0x02) credentials across roughly 35 keys, and links the first of these validators. That validator withdraws to this Safe, and received 2,016 ETH on the day of the announcement. The Safe now has 34 validators holding 69,632 ETH.

On chain. The first validators' initial deposits were sent through other Safes, one of which was created by an owner of this Safe; the Safe itself then topped each validator up to about 2,048 ETH between 30 March and 3 April 2026. The Safe has seven owners and a threshold of four. It also received 160,000 ETH in one transfer from the Foundation's long-standing wallet, which is widely known but not relied on here.

Explorer labels naming the Safes as the Foundation's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Foundation statement naming other validators, or evidence that the Safe is not the Foundation's.

evidence.note: 2,016 ETH to the validator the EF links, 24 February 2026 (block 24,525,550)
That validator's first deposit, 1 ETH, 23 January 2026 (block 24,299,640)
33 further validators, 1 ETH each, through Safe 0x9fc3 (block 24,628,967)
First 2,047 ETH top-up made by the Safe itself (block 24,768,379)

0196-coinbase-prime-custodian-2026.summary: Coinbase holds 167 more withdrawal addresses in custody for Coinbase Prime clients, found by 0134's gas test; who chose and runs their staking is decided elsewhere.
0196-coinbase-prime-custodian-2026.decision: Coinbase is the custodian of the validators withdrawing to these 167 addresses, held for Coinbase Prime custody clients.

grounds.text: Each address sent its own deposits, and Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863 paid its gas in the 50 blocks before the first
The account giving gas paid for 361 of the 363 deposits of Grayscale's ether funds, whose custodian is Coinbase Custody
Coinbase says Prime custody clients select their staking providers, so custody is recorded apart from allocation

0196-coinbase-prime-custodian-2026.would_change: Evidence that an address is held by its owner or another custodian, not by Coinbase for a Prime client.
0196-coinbase-prime-custodian-2026.explanation:
Coinbase holds these 167 withdrawal addresses in custody for Coinbase Prime clients. The decision records custody only: who chose and runs the staking is settled elsewhere, and where nothing else shows an allocator Coinbase is assumed to be it. In October 2026 the addresses held about 545 active validators with some 0.62M ETH, mostly compounding validators.

The custody test. Each address sent its own deposits through Coinbase's batch deposit contract, and in the 50 blocks before its first deposit Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863…6c0f sent it a small amount of gas. That account paid for 361 of the 363 deposit transactions of Grayscale's ether funds, whose fund pages ([ETHE](https://etfs.grayscale.com/ethe), [ETH](https://etfs.grayscale.com/eth)) name Coinbase Custody as custodian; an account whose gas Coinbase pays is one whose keys Coinbase holds. Many of the accounts were also funded by Coinbase's custody wallets.

Why custody is recorded apart from allocation. Coinbase Prime clients choose their staking providers, as [Figment's announcement with Coinbase Prime](https://www.figment.io/insights/coinbase-figment-expand-divisified-institutional-staking/) describes. 140 of these addresses also hold validators that sign Galaxy's graffiti, and Galaxy runs custody stake for Prime clients; the remaining validators propose blank blocks or carry client version strings only. Validators that graffiti or another claim gives to Galaxy or Figment keep it.

Not included: 38 accounts depositing through the same contracts without the gas payment, holding about 42k ETH. The absence of the payment proves nothing, but nothing else here shows custody. The decision would change with evidence that an address is held by its owner, or by another custodian, rather than by Coinbase for a Prime client.

evidence.note: 0xa863…6c0f gives 0x9312…7840 gas, block 24,649,866, seven blocks before its first deposit
Earliest of the 167: gas to 0x98f1…51ec, block 22,673,260

0199-etoro-staking.summary: Validators withdrawing to an address whose staking took off in the days eToro relaunched ETH staking, and whose rewards are swept out monthly, are attributed to eToro's staking; the evidence is suggestive but not conclusive, as eToro names no address.
0199-etoro-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to this address are attributed to eToro's staking (suggestive, not conclusive).

grounds.text: eToro launched ETH staking on 31 July 2024; 298 of these validators were deposited on 29-31 July, their first large deposits
eToro says it runs its own validators and passes users part of the rewards; these validators' rewards are swept out monthly
One account made every deposit since July 2024, funded only by two wallets that a third wallet supplied

0199-etoro-staking.would_change: A statement or address list from eToro that includes or excludes this address, or evidence that the wallets funding it belong to someone else.
0199-etoro-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x1135…de29 are attributed to the ETH staking of eToro, the trading platform, with eToro as allocator. The evidence is suggestive but not conclusive: eToro names no address, and there is no check of the stake's size against eToro's accounts. 2,482 validators were deposited from July 2024; 2,322 were active in October 2026 with about 74k ETH.

What eToro says. eToro's [annual report on Form 20-F for 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1493318/000121390026022034/ea0278371-20f_etoro.htm) says it stakes ETH using staking validators that it controls, keeping a portion of the rewards and passing the rest to users. Press reports of eToro's announcement of 31 July 2024 ([FX News Group](https://fxnewsgroup.com/forex-news/cryptocurrency/etoro-launches-staking-for-solana-and-ethereum/), [Finance Magnates](https://www.financemagnates.com/fintech/etoro-launches-staking-for-solana-and-ethereum-intro-days-and-eligibility/)) date the launch of ETH staking to that day, say it requires users to opt in, and describe monthly reward updates.

The timing. One account made every deposit since July 2024, all directly to the deposit contract. After four isolated deposits earlier in July, 46 validators were deposited on 29 July 2024, 135 on 30 July and 117 on 31 July, the day of the launch. Later bursts match no announcement found; since staking is opt-in they may be waves of users opting in.

The pattern. The depositing account's ETH came only from two wallets in turn, both supplied by a third. About once a month, nearly always between the 2nd and the 13th, the withdrawal address sends most of the month's rewards back to the current funding wallet, consistent with monthly reward updates. Graffiti is blank or carries client versions, and fee recipients are block builders, so no operator identifies itself; eToro's report says it controls the validators.

Searches of court records, SEC filings and eToro's own former token contracts found no eToro address that would anchor the attribution more firmly. Explorer labels naming the funding wallets as eToro's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a statement or address list from eToro that includes or excludes this address, or evidence that the wallets funding it belong to someone else.

evidence.note: First of 298 deposits on 29-31 July 2024, around eToro's relaunch of ETH staking on 31 July
0x3f08 funds 0x1435 for the first time (0.1 ETH test), 3 July 2024
A monthly sweep: 0x1135 sends 90 ETH of rewards to 0x3f08, 4 February 2025

0200-htx-eth2-depositor-3.summary: Reserve wallets whose ownership HTX (formerly Huobi) proved by signature funded the multisig wallets that supplied this account's ETH and the key that created its withdrawal wallets; it is HTX's third deposit account.
0200-htx-eth2-depositor-3.decision: This account made HTX's (formerly Huobi) staking deposits from May 2023; validators withdrawing to the addresses it used are HTX's.

grounds.text: Three wallets HTX's proof of reserves signs for sent 66,082 ETH to two multisig wallets that later sent this account most of its ETH
Two signed HTX reserve wallets first funded the key that created its withdrawal wallets; that key also paid gas for this account
One withdrawal wallet's ETH was moved to a Safe and deposited again through this account, with the Safe as withdrawal address

0200-htx-eth2-depositor-3.would_change: An HTX statement contradicting it, or evidence that the funding multisigs or the creating key belong to someone else.
0200-htx-eth2-depositor-3.explanation:
The account 0xd57d…194e made HTX's staking deposits from May 2023: validators withdrawing to the addresses it used are attributed to HTX (formerly Huobi) as allocator. It sent 9,388 deposits, about 300k ETH, between May 2023 and April 2025; in October 2026 about 2,650 of its validators were active with some 85k ETH. HTX's customers own the stake.

HTX's reserve wallets. HTX's proof-of-reserves snapshots of [December 2022](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/9c076d8b56423de666100a481566e0a30a8db0fc/snapshot/huobi_por_20221201_part.csv) and [May 2023](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/a3b042159258e58f6b10198788367a3ebf6d0dfa/snapshot/huobi_por_20230501.csv) list reserve addresses, each with a signature from the address's own key over a fixed message, which proves that HTX controls it.

The funding. The account received about 270k ETH, most of it from four multisig wallets. Three of the signed reserve wallets sent 66,082 ETH to two of those multisigs. The key that created the withdrawal wallets through a multisig wallet factory was itself first funded by two signed reserve wallets, and it also paid gas to the signers of two of the funding multisigs and sent the deposit account 3 ETH. The signers of the funding multisigs overlap with those of the withdrawal wallets. In December 2024 one withdrawal wallet's ETH, 56,839 ETH, passed through a Safe multisig back to this account, which deposited it again with the Safe as withdrawal address.

The deposits went through a public batch deposit contract that anyone can use, which is not itself evidence. Some 2024 funding came from other exchanges' hot wallets, as exchanges move funds between venues. Several operators sign some of these validators' blocks, mostly in SSV clusters; they remain operators only, with HTX as allocator. An explorer label is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with an HTX statement contradicting it, or evidence that the funding multisigs or the creating key belong to someone else.

evidence.note: Signed HTX reserve wallet 0x28ff sends 20,000 ETH to multisig 0x3dd2, which later funds this account
Signed HTX reserve wallet 0xcac7 sends 20,000 ETH to 0x3dd2
Signed HTX reserve wallet 0xa5d7 funds 0x6720, which creates the withdrawal wallets
Withdrawal wallet 0x7832 moves 56,839 ETH to Safe 0xd19d, 20 December 2024

0201-htx-principal-ebunker.summary: HTX's withdrawal wallet 0xc15c handed 380 of its validators to Ebunker, whose own accounts registered them on SSV; HTX is their principal.
0201-htx-principal-ebunker.decision: HTX is the principal of the validators withdrawing to 0xc15c…8b8b; Ebunker is the allocator of those it registered on SSV (0205).

grounds.text: HTX's deposit account 0xd57d (0200) made all of 0xc15c's deposits, and they withdraw to it
Ebunker's own accounts registered 380 of them on SSV with Ebunker's operators (0205)

0201-htx-principal-ebunker.would_change: Evidence that Ebunker ran these validators for someone other than HTX, or that 0xc15c isn't HTX's.
0201-htx-principal-ebunker.explanation:
HTX (formerly Huobi) is the principal of the validators withdrawing to the multisig wallet 0xc15c…8b8b: the ETH was HTX's customers', and HTX chose how it was staked. All 470 of these validators were deposited on 21 August 2023 by HTX's deposit account (decision 0200), and all have since exited.

Who allocated them. Ebunker's own accounts registered 380 of the validators on the SSV network, on clusters of operators Ebunker had registered under its own name (decision 0205), so HTX handed those validators to Ebunker, which is their allocator. The other 90 remain HTX's as allocator.

The wallet. 0xc15c…8b8b is a multisig wallet created through the same wallet factory, by the same key, as HTX's other withdrawal wallets, and that key was first funded by reserve wallets that HTX's proof of reserves signs for ([December 2022](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/9c076d8b56423de666100a481566e0a30a8db0fc/snapshot/huobi_por_20221201_part.csv), [May 2023](https://github.com/huobiapi/Tool-Node.js-VerifyAddress/blob/a3b042159258e58f6b10198788367a3ebf6d0dfa/snapshot/huobi_por_20230501.csv)).

The decision would change with evidence that Ebunker ran these validators for someone other than HTX, or that the wallet is not HTX's.

0202-puffer-protocol.summary: Puffer's deployment scripts name this contract PufferProtocol; validators it funded, withdrawing to its modules' EigenPods, are Puffer pufETH's.
0202-puffer-protocol.decision: Validators whose first deposit PufferProtocol sent, and those withdrawing to the EigenPods those deposits name, are Puffer pufETH's.

grounds.text: Puffer's deployment scripts give 0xf7b6…238B as PufferProtocol on Ethereum mainnet
Its validators withdraw to EigenPods whose owners are Puffer modules, each naming this contract as its PufferProtocol
It sent the deposits of 11,532 validators from May 2024 to October 2025, peaking at 290,176 ETH in October 2024; 300 are active now

0202-puffer-protocol.would_change: A Puffer statement naming another contract, or evidence that validators deposited through it are not funded from the pufETH vault.
0202-puffer-protocol.explanation:
The contract 0xf7b6…238b is PufferProtocol, the core contract of Puffer's liquid staking token pufETH. Validators whose first deposit it sent, and validators withdrawing to the EigenLayer pods those deposits name, are attributed to Puffer pufETH as allocator. It deposited 11,532 validators between May 2024 and October 2025, holding as much as 290k ETH in October 2024; about 300 were active in October 2026.

Identification. [Puffer's deployment scripts](https://github.com/PufferFinance/puffer-contracts/blob/e3845041981862fb68b9277c38530f22ed54b18a/mainnet-contracts/script/DeployerHelper.s.sol#L409-L412) give this address as PufferProtocol on Ethereum mainnet. Puffer's documentation describes PufferProtocol as the contract with which node operators register validators, after posting a pufETH bond and buying validator tickets, and which funds each validator with 32 ETH from the pufETH vault. On chain, the validators withdraw to EigenLayer pods whose owners are Puffer modules, and each module names this contract as its PufferProtocol.

Why Puffer is the allocator. Puffer's node operators join without permission by posting a bond; Puffer is the service to which stakers handed their ETH, and the protocol assigns it to operators by its own rules. Puffer is therefore shown as the allocator, as for Stader's permissionless pool. The operators are not recorded. Before this decision most of these validators were unattributed; a few had been attributed to operators by earlier decisions or by graffiti.

The decision would change with a Puffer statement naming another contract, or evidence that validators deposited through it are not funded from the pufETH vault.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent through PufferProtocol, 8 May 2024

0203-bedrock-unieth-staking.summary: Bedrock's README and documentation name this contract uniETH's staking contract; validators it deposited, withdrawing to it or to Bedrock's EigenPods, are Bedrock uniETH's.
0203-bedrock-unieth-staking.decision: Validators whose first deposit was sent to Bedrock's uniETH staking contract, and those withdrawing to the addresses those deposits name, are Bedrock uniETH's.

grounds.text: Bedrock's README lists 0x4beF…9E9d as uniETH's mainnet staking contract, with its restaking contract 0x3F4e…9850 and EigenPod 0x9267…1cCE
Bedrock's documentation gives the same contract as the place to read the total ETH staked for uniETH
Its deposits withdrew to itself from October 2022, then to the EigenPod 0x9267 and to pods owned by proxies the restaking contract created

0203-bedrock-unieth-staking.would_change: A Bedrock statement naming another contract, or evidence that deposits sent to it are not uniETH's.
0203-bedrock-unieth-staking.explanation:
The contract 0x4bef…9e9d is the staking contract of uniETH, the liquid staking token of Bedrock. Validators whose first deposit was sent to it, and those withdrawing to the addresses those deposits name, are attributed to Bedrock uniETH as allocator. 2,380 validators were deposited from October 2022, holding as much as 49k ETH in June 2024; 316 were active in October 2026, all previously unattributed.

Identification. [Bedrock's repository](https://github.com/Bedrock-Technology/stake/blob/549a4ec1e450b6e20e70a835884ef783312f4971/README.md#5-official-deployment) lists this contract as uniETH's mainnet staking contract, together with its restaking contract and an EigenLayer pod. [Bedrock's documentation](https://docs.bedrock.technology/security/smart-contracts/unieth) gives the same contract as the place to read the total ETH staked for uniETH. Its code stakes pending ETH whenever users' minting brings the balance to 32 ETH.

On chain. The validators first withdrew to the staking contract itself (369 of them, from October 2022 to January 2024), then to the EigenLayer pod named in the repository, owned by the restaking contract (1,506 from January 2024), and then to nine more pods owned by proxies the restaking contract created. Most blocks carry plain client version graffiti, and the fee recipient is the staking contract itself.

Bedrock chooses the operators of its pool, so it is the allocator; no operator is recorded. RockX is also one of Lido's node operators, a separate role not merged here. The decision would change with a Bedrock statement naming another contract, or evidence that deposits sent to it are not uniETH's.

evidence.note: The first deposit sent to Bedrock's uniETH staking contract, 13 October 2022

0204-bedrock-direct-staking.summary: A direct-staking contract created by the deployer of Bedrock's uniETH staking contract; its validators pay their block rewards to a Bedrock reward pool from the same deployer.
0204-bedrock-direct-staking.decision: This contract is Bedrock's direct-staking contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Bedrock.

grounds.text: It was created by 0x899c…c94f, the account that created Bedrock's uniETH staking contract, which Bedrock's README names
Its validators pay their block rewards to a reward pool contract created by the same account
It deposited 1,164 validators for 15 clients from March 2023, each client keeping its withdrawal address; peak 32,960 ETH

0204-bedrock-direct-staking.would_change: A Bedrock statement that the contract is not its own, or evidence that its validators are run by another operator.
0204-bedrock-direct-staking.explanation:
The contract 0xe823…4572 is taken to be Bedrock's direct-staking contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Bedrock as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. It deposited 1,164 validators between March 2023 and April 2026 for fifteen clients, to twenty withdrawal addresses; they held as much as 33k ETH in March 2024, and 256 were active in October 2026, all previously unattributed.

Identification. No published source names this contract. It was created by the same account that created Bedrock's uniETH staking contract, which [Bedrock's repository](https://github.com/Bedrock-Technology/stake/blob/549a4ec1e450b6e20e70a835884ef783312f4971/README.md#5-official-deployment) names (decision 0203). The same account created the reward-pool contract to which most of these validators' blocks pay their fees. The validators' graffiti follows the same client-release timeline as the uniETH validators, and a few blocks of both groups paid an address that Bedrock's repository gives for its testnet staking contract, a configuration shared with Bedrock's own setup.

Why Bedrock is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address (decision 0005). This is weaker than decision 0203, since no document names the contract. The decision would change with a Bedrock statement that the contract is not its own, or evidence that its validators are run by another operator.
