evidence.note: The first deposit sent through Bedrock's direct-staking contract, 7 March 2023

0205-ebunker-ssv.summary: Validators Ebunker's own accounts registered on SSV, on clusters of operators Ebunker registered under its name.
0205-ebunker-ssv.decision: Ebunker is the allocator of these 1,096 validators, registered on SSV by its accounts 0x0881…5b7a and 0x5e4f…74e3.

grounds.text: Ebunker registered SSV operators 5, 55 and 67-70 under its name from 0x7d4f…9609; every one of these validators runs on them
0x7d4f first funded 0x0881, which registered these validators and funded 0x5e4f, the other account that did
Both accounts set one fee recipient on SSV, 0x3484…a1ce3, so their validators' block fees go to Ebunker

0205-ebunker-ssv.would_change: Evidence that 0x0881 or 0x5e4f registers validators on SSV for a party that chose its own operators.
0205-ebunker-ssv.explanation:
Ebunker is the allocator of these 1,096 validators, which its own accounts registered on the SSV network, a distributed validator network, on clusters of operators Ebunker registered under its name. 250 were active in October 2026, with about 8,300 ETH; nearly all had previously been unattributed.

Ebunker's operators. Ebunker registered SSV operators 5, 55 and 67 to 70 under its name ([operator 5](https://api.ssv.network/api/v4/mainnet/operators/5)), from the account 0x7d4f…9609, and operators 143 to 146 from another account under the name "Ebunker EtherFi". Every one of these validators runs on a cluster that includes Ebunker's operators. The other operators in some clusters, belonging to P2P.org, XHash and others, are co-operators that Ebunker's accounts chose.

Ebunker's accounts. The validators were registered on SSV by two accounts. The account behind Ebunker's operators first funded the first of them, which in turn first funded the second. Both set the same fee recipient on SSV, so their validators' block fees go to Ebunker, and some of the blocks are signed ebunker.io.

Why Ebunker is the allocator. Ebunker describes itself as a non-custodial staking pool: the withdrawal addresses are its clients', and Ebunker is the service to which the stake was handed. No operator is recorded, since each validator is run by a cluster of operators. 218 validators that Ebunker registered as a node operator for Puffer are left to Puffer (decision 0202), the service those stakers chose; HTX is recorded as principal of 380 of these validators (decision 0201). The decision would change with evidence that Ebunker's accounts register validators on SSV for a party that chose its own operators.

evidence.note: Ebunker's operator owner 0x7d4f first funds 0x0881, block 18,519,151
0x0881 adds its first validator on SSV (operators 5, 25, 26, 55), block 18,520,062
0x0881 sets fee recipient 0x3484 on SSV, block 18,768,659

0206-xhash-batch-deposit.summary: XHash's batch deposit contract, which XHash's staking documentation names and its web application sends deposits to.
0206-xhash-batch-deposit.decision: This contract is XHash's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by XHash.

grounds.text: XHash's documentation names it as the 'XHash batch deposit contract' for its non-custodial staking
The script xhash.com serves for staking sends each deposit (pubkey, signature, deposit data root) to it
It deposited 3,923 validators for 32 senders from March 2023, each keeping its withdrawal address; peak 65,056 ETH

0206-xhash-batch-deposit.would_change: An XHash statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys XHash does not run are deposited through it.
0206-xhash-batch-deposit.explanation:
The contract 0xa863…9cba6 is XHash's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to XHash as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. It deposited 3,923 validators between March 2023 and August 2025, for 32 sending accounts, holding as much as 65k ETH in May 2024; 117 were active in October 2026, all previously unattributed.

Identification. [XHash's documentation](https://docs.xhash.com/staking/non-custodial-staking/no-mnemonic-staking) for its non-custodial staking, in which XHash generates the keys and the staker connects a wallet and stakes multiples of 32 ETH, names this address as the XHash batch deposit contract. [The script xhash.com serves for staking](https://xhash.com/assets/index-BsyCGbML.js) builds each deposit transaction to the same address. The contract's creator remains its owner.

The operators. Most of the validators' blocks carry SSV's default graffiti, with "XHash.com" and other operators' names on the rest: XHash runs most of these validators as SSV clusters with itself among the operators, which is its own choice of operators, so it remains the allocator.

Why XHash is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address (decision 0005). XHash's "Quick Mode" deposits go directly to the beacon deposit contract and are not covered here; they are identified by XHash's fee recipient (decision 0228). The contract is open to anyone, though in practice it is used only through XHash's application. The decision would change with an XHash statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys XHash does not run are deposited through it.

evidence.note: The first deposit through it, 26 March 2023

0207-paralinker-batch-deposit.summary: Paralinker's deployment of Staked's batch deposit contract, which its own repository names and its staking guide links; its validators sign 'Staking via Paralinker'.
0207-paralinker-batch-deposit.decision: This contract is Paralinker's batch deposit contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Paralinker.

grounds.text: Paralinker's eth2-batch-contract repository gives this address as its mainnet deployment
Paralinker's staking guide says it uses batch mode for staking deposits and links that repository
1,069 of the 1,069 blocks its validators proposed carry the graffiti 'Staking via Paralinker'

0207-paralinker-batch-deposit.would_change: A Paralinker statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys Paralinker does not run are deposited through it.
0207-paralinker-batch-deposit.explanation:
The contract 0xfc3e…c81f is Paralinker's batch deposit contract: validators first deposited through it are attributed to Paralinker as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. It deposited 1,073 validators between December 2022 and July 2025, for seventeen sending accounts, holding as much as 30k ETH in February 2024; 112 were active in October 2026, all previously unattributed.

Identification. [Paralinker's repository](https://github.com/paralinker/eth2-batch-contract/blob/224ca2161cf929d8f88369fd9ca516120762f965/README.md), a copy of Staked's open batch deposit contract, gives this address as its mainnet deployment. [Paralinker's staking guide](https://paralinker.gitbook.io/paralinker-docs/stake/ethereum/how-to) says it uses batch mode for staking deposits and links that repository; Paralinker's staking is non-custodial, with stakers keeping their withdrawal addresses.

The graffiti. Every one of the 1,069 blocks its validators have proposed is signed "Staking via Paralinker", and nearly all paid the same fee recipient. The contract has no owner and is open to anyone, but the uniform graffiti shows that Paralinker ran all of its validators.

A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider (decision 0005). The decision would change with a Paralinker statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys Paralinker does not run are deposited through it.

evidence.note: The first deposit through it, 30 December 2022

0208-infstones-batch-deposit-proxy.summary: The batch deposit proxy InfStones' key created in June 2026, three days after the last deposit through its imToken contract (0189), used by the same stakers.
0208-infstones-batch-deposit-proxy.decision: This contract is InfStones' successor depositor contract; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by InfStones.

grounds.text: InfStones' key 0xc8a6, owner of 0189's imToken contract, created it and is its owner and proxy admin
The older contract's last deposit was on 24 June 2026, this one's first on 27 June; 6 of its 21 senders used both
Some of its validators pay fee Safe 0x3928, which replaced the fee recipient of InfStones' SGP-SSV operators

0208-infstones-batch-deposit-proxy.would_change: An InfStones or imToken statement that the contract is not theirs, or evidence that keys InfStones does not run are deposited through it.
0208-infstones-batch-deposit-proxy.explanation:
The contract 0x85a5…42c9 is InfStones' successor to its batch deposit contract for the imToken wallet (decision 0189): validators first deposited through it are attributed to InfStones as allocator and operator, while the stakers keep their own withdrawal addresses. It deposited 152 validators between June and October 2026; 128 were active in October 2026 with about 5,900 ETH.

Identification. No document names this contract; it rests on its ownership. InfStones' key, the owner of the imToken contract identified in decision 0189 (which [InfStones](https://infstones.com/news/clients/imtoken-selects-infstones-as-staking-infrastructure-provider-for-in-wallet-eth20-staking) and [imToken](https://support.token.im/hc/en-us/articles/900007069303-imToken-now-with-native-Eth2-integration-and-staking-as-a-service) announced), created this contract and its implementation, and is its owner and proxy administrator.

The handover. The older contract's last deposit was on 24 June 2026, and this one's first on 27 June. Six of its 21 senders used both, and four of its withdrawal addresses already held validators deposited through the older contract. Some of its validators' blocks pay the Safe that replaced the fee recipient of InfStones' SSV operators.

This is weaker than decision 0189's match with imToken's published figures, but the ownership is direct. The decision would change with an InfStones or imToken statement that the contract is not theirs, or evidence that keys InfStones does not run are deposited through it.

evidence.note: The first deposit through it, 27 June 2026

0209-blockdaemon-batch-deposit-2.summary: Blockdaemon's BatchDeposit2 for compounding validators, whose mainnet address Blockdaemon's own repository lists.
0209-blockdaemon-batch-deposit-2.decision: This contract is Blockdaemon's BatchDeposit2; validators deposited through it are run and allocated by Blockdaemon.

grounds.text: The README of Blockdaemon's batch deposit repository (v2 branch) lists this address as its mainnet deployment
Its verified source is BatchDeposit2 from that repository, with the deadline check of Blockdaemon's staking API
Five withdrawal addresses it deposited for also have validators deposited through Blockdaemon's first contract (0041)

0209-blockdaemon-batch-deposit-2.would_change: A Blockdaemon statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys Blockdaemon does not run are deposited through it.
0209-blockdaemon-batch-deposit-2.explanation:
The contract 0xdc8d…9ae0 is Blockdaemon's second batch deposit contract, BatchDeposit2, built for compounding (0x02) validators of up to 2,048 ETH. Validators first deposited through it are attributed to Blockdaemon as allocator and operator, while each client keeps its own withdrawal address. 324 validators were deposited through it between July 2025 and September 2026, from 14 sending accounts; 258 were active in October 2026 with about 130k ETH.

Identification. [The README of Blockdaemon's batch deposit repository](https://gitlab.com/Blockdaemon/open-source/eth2-batch-deposit-contract/-/blob/9145fa7274a690cb320a19c86ee8e9c5f37237e2/README.md) lists this address as BatchDeposit2's mainnet deployment. The contract's verified source is BatchDeposit2 from that repository, including the deadline check that [Blockdaemon's staking API](https://docs.blockdaemon.com/reference/postethereumstakeintent) relies on when it reserves validators for a client. Five of the withdrawal addresses it deposited for also hold validators deposited through Blockdaemon's first batch contract (decision 0041).

Why Blockdaemon is the allocator. A client depositing through a provider's contract has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address. This is the rule applied to all providers' depositor contracts (decision 0005). Most of the validators' blocks carry client version strings only.

The decision would change with a Blockdaemon statement naming another contract, or evidence that keys Blockdaemon does not run are deposited through it.

evidence.note: The first deposit through it, 24 July 2025

0212-bitbank-staking.summary: bitbank's ETH staking: compounding validators deposited by the cold wallet that bitbank's customer deposit contract forwards every deposit to.
0212-bitbank-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x3727…6be8 are bitbank's staking.

grounds.text: bitbank says its ETH deposit addresses are contracts since 9 March 2021, and a deposit needs 45,672 gas
Deposits to the 0xbb… proxies forwarding through 0x265c use exactly 45,672 gas; 0x265c runs bitbank's ExchangeDeposit code
0x265c's coldAddress() is 0x3727, which deposited these validators and receives their rewards
bitbank stakes its customers' ETH itself; first validators July 2026, service launched 25 August 2026

0212-bitbank-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0x265c is another exchange's deployment of bitbank's code, or that 0x3727 stakes for a client of bitbank.
0212-bitbank-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x3727…6be8 are the staking of bitbank, the Japanese exchange, with bitbank as allocator. They are compounding validators deposited from July 2026; 77 were active in October 2026, with about 72k ETH. The address is the cold wallet to which bitbank's customer deposit contract forwards every deposit.

bitbank's deposit system. [bitbank's support article](https://support.bitbank.cc/hc/en-us/articles/900005800363-Some-deposit-addresses-including-ETH-are-contract-addresses) says its ETH deposit addresses are contracts, changed on 9 March 2021 ([its notice that day](https://blog.bitbank.cc/202103_05/)), and that a deposit from an ordinary account needs a gas limit of at least 45,672. bitbank publishes [the code of its deposit contract](https://github.com/bitbankinc/exchangeDepositContract/blob/7b32b873bad1a459e28178ee25949719dee02f3a/contracts/ExchangeDeposit.sol): one small proxy per customer, forwarding each deposit to the main contract's cold address. On chain, 0x265c…84aa is a verified deployment of that code, created in February 2021 with its proxy factory. Deposits to its customer proxies forward through it to 0x3727…6be8 and cost exactly 45,672 gas. It has forwarded over 89,000 deposits there since early 2025, the pattern of an exchange's cold wallet.

bitbank's staking. bitbank [launched an ETH staking service on 25 August 2026](https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000259.000024344.html), in which staking that bitbank itself carries out earns rewards for customers' ETH held in their accounts; [its rules](https://bitbank.cc/guide/staking-rule) say it stakes a quantity of its choosing and compensates any slashing. The cold wallet itself made every deposit: one 32 ETH validator in February 2026, then the compounding validators from July 2026, shortly before the launch. Every block with a known fee recipient paid the cold wallet, and the graffiti is blank. No operator is recorded.

Limits. bitbank does not publish the main contract's or the cold wallet's address, and its code is open source, so the match rests on the gas figure, the deployment date and the staking timeline. Community labels on the addresses are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that the main contract is another exchange's deployment of bitbank's code, or that the cold wallet stakes for a client of bitbank.

evidence.note: A customer deposit to proxy 0xbb47…bde1, forwarded to 0x3727; gas used 45,672
0x3727 deposits a 1,024 ETH compounding validator, 14 July 2026

0215-bitvavo-staking.summary: Bitvavo's ETH staking: validators of two addresses funded by the cold wallet that refills Bitvavo's hot wallet, which Bitvavo named to a customer.
0215-bitvavo-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0xedc6…87c9 or 0xfc57…d030 are Bitvavo's staking.

grounds.text: Bitvavo told a customer (ENS forum) that 0x95b5 is its hot wallet; a refund sent there reached the customer's account
The customer's Bitvavo withdrawal came from 0x95b5, and their Bitvavo deposit address swept tokens to it
0xedc6 refills 0x95b5 and funded 0xfc57, which deposited validators itself, as did 0xedc6
Bitvavo stakes customers' ETH itself, under keys it controls

0215-bitvavo-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0xedc6 or 0xfc57 hold a client's ETH rather than Bitvavo's, or a Bitvavo statement that 0x95b5 is not its wallet.
0215-bitvavo-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xedc6…87c9 or 0xfc57…d030 are the staking of Bitvavo, the Dutch exchange, with Bitvavo as allocator. In October 2026 they held 522 active validators with about 64k ETH: twenty compounding validators at the first address and 502 at the second.

The anchor: Bitvavo's hot wallet. In a [discussion on the ENS governance forum](https://discuss.ens.domains/t/accidentally-sending-ens-tokens-to-ens-contract-address/15696) in December 2022, a customer who had withdrawn ENS tokens from Bitvavo to the wrong address relayed Bitvavo's answer: 0x95b5…cc8a is its hot wallet, and a refund sent there would be credited. The refund was sent there, and the customer confirmed that the tokens were back. On chain, the customer's withdrawal came from that wallet, and the customer's Bitvavo deposit address swept tokens into it: the wallet both pays Bitvavo's withdrawals and collects its deposits.

From the hot wallet to the staking. 0xedc6…87c9 refills that hot wallet and a second one, 0x079a…dc63, which pays the first one's gas: a cold wallet refilling the exchange's hot wallets. 0xedc6…87c9 deposited validators itself, and funded 0xfc57…d030, which deposited its own validators, partly through Kiln's and Coinbase's batch deposit contracts and partly directly. Another wallet in the same circle of transfers is 0xfc57…d030's main funder.

What Bitvavo says. [Bitvavo says it stakes customers' assets itself](https://support.bitvavo.com/hc/en-us/articles/4405243949841-Staking-at-Bitvavo). [Its proof of reserves at 30 June 2026](https://widget.app.ledgerlens.io/bitvavo?tab=summary&datasetId=N-2XtKQu_A9or4XdsWlDU) counts 267,278 ETH, including staked ETH under keys Bitvavo controls. One address's validators sign P2P.org's graffiti, as their operator; no operator is recorded here.

Limits. Bitvavo's statement reaches this record through its customer, and the staking addresses are tied to the hot wallet by ETH flows rather than by a Bitvavo statement. Community trackers and explorer labels listing the wallets as Bitvavo's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that either address holds a client's ETH rather than Bitvavo's, or a Bitvavo statement that 0x95b5…cc8a is not its wallet.

evidence.note: A Bitvavo customer's ENS withdrawal, sent by 0x95b5, 17 December 2022
The ENS Meta-governance Safe refunds the 10 ENS to 0x95b5, 25 December 2022
The customer's Bitvavo deposit address sweeps DIA to 0x95b5
0xfc57's first validator deposit, through Kiln's batch deposit contract, 5 February 2025

leads.title: add bitvavo (PR #18526, commit d19d35e, merged 25 March 2026)

0216-bitvavo-principal-coinbase-prime.summary: Bitvavo's stake held at Coinbase Prime: the validators paying fee recipient 0x13f2, which forwards to Bitvavo's wallets, as several of their withdrawal addresses do.
0216-bitvavo-principal-coinbase-prime.decision: Bitvavo is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 39 addresses; Coinbase Prime stays their allocator (0134) and Coinbase their custodian.

grounds.text: Nearly all their blocks pay fee recipient 0x13f2, whose outgoing payments went to Bitvavo's hot and cold wallets
12 of the 39 addresses sent ETH straight to Bitvavo's cold wallet 0xedc6, 0xb0a3 or hot wallet 0x079a, often in one batch
Bitvavo holds assets at Coinbase Prime (its proof of reserves); 0xedc6 is tied to Bitvavo's named hot wallet (0215)

0216-bitvavo-principal-coinbase-prime.would_change: Evidence that 0x13f2 or these addresses serve another Coinbase Prime client, or that Bitvavo's transfers to them were customer payments.
0216-bitvavo-principal-coinbase-prime.explanation:
Bitvavo, the Dutch exchange, is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 39 addresses: its stake held at Coinbase Prime. Coinbase Prime remains their allocator (decision 0134) and Coinbase their custodian; this decision names the client. In October 2026 the addresses held 2,415 active validators with about 96k ETH.

Bitvavo's wallets. In a [discussion on the ENS governance forum](https://discuss.ens.domains/t/accidentally-sending-ens-tokens-to-ens-contract-address/15696), Bitvavo identified 0x95b5… as its hot wallet to a customer, and a refund sent there reached the customer's account. The cold wallet 0xedc6…87c9 refills that hot wallet (decision 0215).

The fee recipient. Of the blocks these validators proposed, 99.7% paid the same fee recipient, 0x13f2…f334. Its outgoing payments went to the cold wallet 0xedc6…87c9 (500 ETH) and to 0x079a…dc63 (800 ETH), a second hot wallet, which pays the named hot wallet's gas and returns ETH to the cold wallet.

Direct payments. Twelve of the 39 addresses have sent ETH straight to these wallets, often several in one block: five addresses paid the cold wallet 8,576 ETH in a single block on 14 August 2025, and ten paid 0x079a…dc63 within a few days in May 2024. The other 27 are tied to Bitvavo only through the shared fee recipient.

Bitvavo and Coinbase Prime. [Bitvavo's proof of reserves at 30 June 2026](https://widget.app.ledgerlens.io/bitvavo?tab=summary&datasetId=N-2XtKQu_A9or4XdsWlDU) states that some of its assets are held at Coinbase Prime. Coinbase runs these validators, by the client-build test of decision 0134.

Limits. Bitvavo has not named the fee recipient or the custody addresses. The decision would change with evidence that the fee recipient or these addresses serve another Coinbase Prime client, or that Bitvavo's transfers to them were payments to customers.

evidence.note: Fee recipient 0x13f2 sends Bitvavo's cold wallet 0xedc6 500 ETH
Fee recipient 0x13f2 sends Bitvavo's hot wallet 0x079a 800 ETH
One of five withdrawal addresses sending 0xedc6 ETH in block 23,140,441

0218-bitpanda-principal.summary: Bitpanda's staking wallets, tied to Bitpanda by its BEST token: they hold the issuer's supply and make the monthly burns Bitpanda announces; Kiln and Figment run the validators.
0218-bitpanda-principal.decision: Bitpanda is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 19 addresses: it chose Kiln and Figment as their allocators.

grounds.text: Bitpanda names BEST's contract; 31% of its supply passed from the mint to 0xf197, which funded the other addresses
Bitpanda's monthly BEST burns, as tabulated, were made by 0xb8cb and later by 0x0529, with the exact amounts and dates
0xf197, 0xb10e and 0x0529 funded each address, which then deposited through Kiln's or Figment's contract
Bitpanda and Kiln announced Kiln as Bitpanda's staking provider in May 2023

0218-bitpanda-principal.would_change: Evidence that these addresses hold a Bitpanda client's ETH, or that BEST's treasury is held by a party other than Bitpanda.
0218-bitpanda-principal.explanation:
Bitpanda, the European exchange, is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 19 addresses: the ETH is Bitpanda's, held for its customers, and Bitpanda chose the providers that run it. Validators deposited through Kiln's or Figment's contracts keep those providers as allocators. In October 2026 the addresses held 274 active validators with about 0.28M ETH, many of them compounding; the earliest three held about 200k ETH in early 2024.

The link through Bitpanda's token. Bitpanda [gives the contract address of BEST](https://blog.bitpanda.com/en/how-to-withdraw-and-add-best-to-an-erc20-compatible-wallet-2), its exchange token. On chain, the whole supply of one billion BEST passed at creation to one account, and in 2023 313 million BEST, nearly a third of the supply, passed from there to 0xf197…, which in turn sent large amounts to 0xb10e… and 0xb8cb…. Only the issuer holds a third of its own token's supply. Bitpanda announced a burn of BEST each month until BEST was merged into its Vision token in 2025 ([Vision token page](https://www.bitpanda.com/en/web3/vision-token)). Bitpanda's own table of burns is no longer published, so the amounts were checked against [an independent copy of the table](https://cryptocalc.cc/en/best-burn/). From October 2022 to June 2024, 21 burns came from 0xb8cb…, and from July 2024 nine came from 0x0529…, each matching the published amount and date.

The stake. 0xb8cb…, 0xf197… and 0xb10e… deposited 6,269 validators between March 2023 and February 2024 through Kiln's first batch deposit contract. This matches [Bitpanda's launch of ETH staking in May 2023](https://blog.bitpanda.com/en/ethereum-eth-now-available-stake-bitpanda), which [Kiln announced it was powering](https://www.kiln.fi/post/staking-is-now-available-on-bitpanda-powered-by-kiln) and describes in [a customer story](https://www.kiln.fi/customers-story/bitpanda). Most of those validators exited in mid-2025. Since 2025 these accounts and 0x0529…, which also pays out to many customers as an exchange hot wallet does, have funded fresh addresses with 15,000 to 40,000 ETH each; each then deposited its own validators through Kiln's or Figment's contract.

Limits. Bitpanda does not name these addresses; the link runs through its token's treasury and burns. Community label sets naming the accounts as Bitpanda's are recorded as leads. The decision would change with evidence that these addresses hold a Bitpanda client's ETH, or that BEST's treasury is held by a party other than Bitpanda.

evidence.note: BEST's creator sends 998,999,999 BEST to 0x06fe at launch

0219-sharedstake-minter.summary: SharedStake's own contract list and docs name this its vETH2 Minter, which staked the pool's ETH; validators deposited through it are SharedStake's.
0219-sharedstake-minter.decision: Validators whose first deposit SharedStake's Minter relayed, and those withdrawing to the address they later set, are SharedStake vETH2's.

grounds.text: SharedStake's contract list and docs name 0xbca3 its Minter, which stakes the pool's ETH to the deposit contract
It relayed the deposits of 500 validators (16,000 ETH) in February-April 2021, all with BLS credentials
490 later set withdrawal address 0xa1fe, the node operator in SharedStake's deploy script and its fee recipient
Their blocks carry the graffiti set in SharedStake's own validator config (SharedStake.org)

0219-sharedstake-minter.would_change: A SharedStake statement contradicting it, or evidence that validators deposited through the Minter were not SharedStake's.
0219-sharedstake-minter.explanation:
The contract 0xbca3…da4d is the vETH2 Minter of SharedStake, a liquid staking pool. Validators whose first deposit it relayed, and those withdrawing to the address they later set, are attributed to SharedStake vETH2 as allocator. It relayed the deposits of 500 validators, 16,000 ETH, between February and April 2021; 40 remained active in October 2026, with 1,280 ETH.

Identification. [SharedStake's list of its contracts](https://github.com/SharedStake/Contracts/blob/a1abdb5064839d42a23ca275d192e5ca13c76d5d/Readme.md) names this contract as its Minter, responsible for minting and burning vETH2 and for staking ether to the beacon chain, and [its documentation](https://github.com/SharedStake/Docs/blob/2ec9c3ecf6c9472da2a8c437ec3f48856620a32c/untitled/staking-to-eth2.md) explains that the Minter is paused while SharedStake deploys validators to the deposit contract. [Its validator configuration](https://github.com/SharedStake/infra/blob/ad1314e15f166775a7b044463eb23c68b0f213d9/config.yaml) sets the graffiti "SharedStake.org Prysm Validators".

On chain. All 500 deposits were sent through the Minter by 0xa1fe…409e (sharedstake.eth), with BLS credentials. 490 of the validators later changed to that address as their withdrawal address; the other ten still have BLS credentials. The address is the fee recipient of nearly all their blocks, and most blocks carry SharedStake's graffiti. SharedStake's later deployment script names the same address as its node operator.

The withdrawal address is an account SharedStake's developer also uses for deployments, so the withdrawals may go to SharedStake's operator rather than to vETH2 holders; the validators were funded by the pool either way. The decision would change with a SharedStake statement contradicting it, or evidence that validators deposited through the Minter were not SharedStake's.

evidence.note: The first deposit relayed by SharedStake's Minter, 3 February 2021

0222-hashkey-exchange-staking.summary: HashKey Exchange's staking: validators deposited by the cold wallet HashKey named, withdrawing to an address that sweeps its rewards back to it.
0222-hashkey-exchange-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x7317…89e9 are HashKey Exchange's staking.

grounds.text: HashKey staff named 0xee1b HashKey Exchange's second ETH cold wallet (DefiLlama PR 13793)
0xee1b sent all 140 deposits of the validators withdrawing to 0x7317 (March-October 2026)
0x7317 is their fee recipient, sweeps their rewards back to 0xee1b and requests their exits itself

0222-hashkey-exchange-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0x7317 holds a client's ETH under another allocator, or a HashKey statement that 0xee1b is not its wallet.
0222-hashkey-exchange-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x7317…89e9 are the staking of HashKey Exchange, the Hong Kong exchange, with HashKey Exchange as allocator. 140 compounding validators were deposited between March and October 2026; 88 were active in October 2026 with about 7,000 ETH.

The anchor. In [a change to DefiLlama's adapter for HashKey Exchange](https://github.com/DefiLlama/DefiLlama-Adapters/pull/13793), merged in March 2025, a HashKey employee, whose public profile shows a hashkey.com email address, added 0xee1b…7ad9 as HashKey Exchange's second ETH cold wallet, citing the transfer of 65,340 ETH to it from the first.

On chain. That cold wallet sent all 140 deposits of the validators withdrawing to 0x7317…89e9, and no other deposits came from it, from the first cold wallet or from the withdrawal address. The withdrawal address is the fee recipient of all their blocks, has swept 4,732 ETH of rewards back to the cold wallet, and has itself sent 35 exit and partial-withdrawal requests: whoever holds it runs the stake and returns its rewards to HashKey's cold wallet.

The operator. The blocks carry only client tags, so no operator is recorded. HashKey Cloud, HashKey Group's staking business, [says it runs staking for an Ethereum ETF](https://www.hashkey.cloud/newsroom/hashkey-cloud-launches-etf-staking-pro-supporting-asias-first-ethereum-spot-etfs-to-pioneer-a-new-era-of-on-chain-finance) with HashKey Exchange as custodian; some of this stake may be the ETF's, held by HashKey Exchange, which chose how to stake it either way. The decision would change with evidence that the withdrawal address holds a client's ETH under another allocator, or a HashKey statement that the cold wallet is not its own.

evidence.note: HashKey's cold wallet 1 sends 65,340 ETH to cold wallet 2 (0xee1b), cited in DefiLlama PR 13793
0xee1b's first validator deposit, withdrawing to 0x7317, 25 March 2026

0225-ssv-labs-staking.summary: SSV Labs' staking: validators of the one account SSV Labs' private operator admits, which it spreads across SSV operators of its choice.
0225-ssv-labs-staking.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x5e33…a9cb are SSV Labs' staking.

grounds.text: SSV operator 1, named SSV Labs, is private and admits only 0x5e33, as SSV Labs' own docs also show
0x5e33 owns 140 SSV clusters (126 active), each on four operators it chose from 24 (P2P.org, Nansen, Ankr, ...)
Its validators withdraw to 0x5e33, which is the fee recipient of most of their blocks

0225-ssv-labs-staking.would_change: Evidence that 0x5e33 registers validators for a client that chose its own operators, or an SSV Labs statement that it is not its account.
0225-ssv-labs-staking.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x5e33…a9cb are the staking of SSV Labs, the developer of the SSV distributed validator network, with SSV Labs as allocator. In October 2026, 91 validators were active, with 2,880 ETH.

The anchor. [SSV operator 1](https://api.ssv.network/api/v4/mainnet/operators/1) is named "SSV Labs" by its owner. It is private, and the only address it admits is 0x5e33…a9cb, a setting its owner made on chain. [SSV Labs' developer documentation](https://github.com/ssvlabs/gitbook-docs/blob/ffc3b79261e4b2ac0ab7e847f74fc3ebf300fc86/docs/developers/README.md) uses the same operator, owner and admitted address as its worked example on a test network.

On chain. The address owns 140 SSV clusters, 126 of them active, each on four operators it chose from 24, including P2P.org, Nansen, Ankr and others. Choosing the operators makes it the allocator; the operators run the validators. Its validators were deposited in 2020 and 2023, by two accounts, and all withdraw to the address, which is also the fee recipient of most of their blocks. Their graffiti is SSV's default (earlier that of Blox, SSV Labs' former name).

Limits. The tie is SSV Labs' operator naming and admitting this address, not a statement that SSV Labs holds it; a partner admitted to SSV Labs' private operator would look the same. A community label is recorded as a lead. The decision would change with evidence that the address registers validators for a client that chose its own operators, or an SSV Labs statement that it is not its account.

0226-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-exited.summary: Institutional stake deposited through Coinbase's batch contract from 2022 to 2025 and run on Coinbase's own validator fleet, nearly all of it since exited: Coinbase Prime clients' stake run by Coinbase, as in 0134.
0226-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-exited.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 1,433 addresses are Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake, run by Coinbase.

grounds.text: 947 addresses' validators signed only the client builds Coinbase's retail validators were signing in the same week; none names an operator
The other 486 never signed graffiti and pay fee recipients that only those addresses, or 0134's, also pay
Every address has a sender that Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863 paid gas to, or that its custody wallets first funded
Coinbase reports running validators for its institutional clients, excluding stake it routes to partner providers

0226-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-exited.would_change: A named operator in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying this stake was run by partners.
0226-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-exited.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 1,433 addresses were the stake of Coinbase Prime custody clients, run by Coinbase on its own validator fleet, as in decision 0134; Coinbase is the allocator. The decision extends 0134 to stake it left out because 0134 considered only validators still active. The validators, 45,671 in all, were deposited through Coinbase's batch deposit contract from May 2022; they held as much as 815k ETH in January 2024, and nearly all have since exited.

Selection. The starting point was validators deposited through Coinbase's two batch deposit contracts and attributed to no one. Since the contracts are open to anyone, the route alone is no evidence.

Operator. Until early 2025 most clients wrote a default version string into block graffiti (for example "Lighthouse/v4.4.1-2841f60"); which versions a fleet runs, and when, is characteristic of the fleet. Coinbase's retail validators (decisions 0016, 0017 and 0020) provide the reference: the strings they signed in each week. Between May 2022 and February 2025 the weekly mix of non-blank graffiti on these validators matches Coinbase's retail fleet with a median similarity of 0.99. Validators of other operators score far lower on the same measure: Binance 0.38, Lido 0.22, ether.fi 0.05, Kiln 0.01. For 947 of the addresses, at least 95% of their non-blank blocks carry a string that Coinbase's retail validators signed in the same week, and none ever names an operator. Another 486 addresses never signed graffiti but pay fee recipients that only those addresses, or 0134's, also pay; recipients shared with builders or unrelated validators are not counted.

Custody. Every one of the 1,433 addresses has a depositing account that Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863…6c0f paid gas to, or that one of Coinbase's custody wallets first funded (the tests of decision 0227).

Why Coinbase is the allocator. As in 0134, the validators ran on Coinbase's fleet and nothing names another operator. [Coinbase reports](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/ethereum-validator-performance-report-q1-2026) running validators for its institutional clients, excluding stake it routes to partner providers. Some of this stake may have been Coinbase's non-custodial [dedicated staking](https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/staking/staking-api/protocols/dedicated-eth/overview) rather than Prime custody ([usage](https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/staking/staking-api/protocols/dedicated-eth/usage)); Coinbase would be the allocator either way.

Limits. No published source names these addresses. 0227-coinbase-prime-custodian-exited.summary: Coinbase held 930 more withdrawal addresses in custody for Coinbase Prime clients, their validators deposited through its batch contract from 2022 and nearly all since exited; who chose and ran their staking is decided elsewhere.
0227-coinbase-prime-custodian-exited.decision: Coinbase is the custodian of the validators withdrawing to these 930 addresses, held for Coinbase Prime custody clients.

grounds.text: Each was deposited via Coinbase's batch contract by an account that Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863 paid gas to
That gas account paid for 361 of the 363 deposits of Grayscale's ether funds, whose custodian is Coinbase Custody
Coinbase says Prime custody clients select their staking providers, so custody is recorded apart from allocation

0227-coinbase-prime-custodian-exited.would_change: Evidence that an address is held by its owner or another custodian, not by Coinbase for a Prime client.
0227-coinbase-prime-custodian-exited.explanation:
Coinbase held these 930 withdrawal addresses in custody for Coinbase Prime clients. The decision records custody only: who chose and ran the staking is settled elsewhere, and where nothing else shows an allocator Coinbase is assumed to be it. The validators, 34,747 in all, were deposited through Coinbase's batch deposit contract from January 2022; they held as much as 735k ETH in January 2025, and nearly all have since exited.

The custody test. Every one of the 930 addresses has a depositing account to which Coinbase's custody gas account 0xa863…6c0f sent a transaction. That account pays small amounts of gas to accounts whose keys Coinbase holds: it paid for 361 of the 363 deposit transactions of Grayscale's ether funds, whose fund pages ([ETHE](https://etfs.grayscale.com/ethe), [ETH](https://etfs.grayscale.com/eth)) name Coinbase Custody as custodian. Before 2025 the gas often arrived just after an account was funded rather than just before it deposited, so the test looks at any time rather than a short window before the first deposit. For 542 of the addresses the depositing account was also first funded by one of Coinbase's two custody wallets. Custody accounts also pass ETH along among themselves: one received 72,592 ETH, was given gas by 0xa863…6c0f nineteen blocks later, and then funded seventeen of the depositing accounts.

Why custody is recorded apart from allocation. Coinbase Prime clients choose their staking providers, as [Figment's announcement with Coinbase Prime](https://www.figment.io/insights/coinbase-figment-expand-divisified-institutional-staking/) describes. Most of these validators never signed graffiti and share no fee recipient with Coinbase's fleet, so decision 0226 does not cover them. Validators on these addresses that another claim gives to a provider keep it (for example those paying Coinbase's own fee recipient, or signing Galaxy's graffiti).

Wallets into which Coinbase's retail staking pays out are not used as a test: they also fund ordinary customers' withdrawals. The decision would change with evidence that an address is held by its owner, or by another custodian, rather than by Coinbase for a Prime client.

Gas account 0xa863…6c0f gives 0x4fad…1e63 gas, block 17,161,144; it deposited 225 validators through 0xefe9 from block 17,161,872

0228-xhash-fee-recipient.summary: The fee recipient of validators deposited through XHash's own batch contract and of validators signing XHash.com; otherwise unattributed validators paying it are taken to be run by XHash.
0228-xhash-fee-recipient.decision: This address is XHash's fee recipient; otherwise unattributed validators paying their fees to it are run and allocated by XHash.

grounds.text: 845 validators deposited through XHash's batch contract, which XHash's docs name, pay it
Of the 3,216 validators that ever paid it, all but 3 blocks signed XHash.com or SSV's default graffiti
Validators of several unrelated stakers pay it (HTX, Puffer, XHash's own clients), so it is the operator's, not a client's

0228-xhash-fee-recipient.would_change: Evidence that validators XHash does not run also pay this address, or that it belongs to one of XHash's clients.
0228-xhash-fee-recipient.explanation:
The address 0xaecd…0983 is XHash's fee recipient: validators XHash runs pay their transaction fees and MEV to it. Validators otherwise unattributed whose blocks paid it are attributed to XHash as allocator for as long as they did. They held as much as 45k ETH, mostly in 2023 and 2024; 89 were active in October 2026.

Who pays it. 3,216 validators have paid it since September 2022. 845 of them were deposited through XHash's own batch deposit contract, which [XHash's documentation names](https://docs.xhash.com/staking/non-custodial-staking/no-mnemonic-staking) (decision 0206). 848 belong to HTX's staking, for which XHash is among the operators, and 36 to Puffer; those keep their own allocators, since a fee recipient claim yields to every other allocator claim. The remaining 1,432 were unattributed. Validators of several unrelated stakers pay it, so it is the operator's address, not a client's. The address itself also deposited 45 validators in 2022.

The graffiti. Of the 13,301 blocks paying it, 7,715 were signed "XHash.com" and 5,751 carry SSV's default graffiti; only seven carry anything else.

Why these validators needed this decision. XHash's "Quick Mode" deposits go directly to the beacon deposit contract, so its batch contract does not cover them. Their "XHash.com" graffiti was not enough on its own, because the same validators, or their withdrawal addresses, also propose blocks with SSV's default graffiti, and a name in one block of a distributed validator identifies only the member that proposed it.

No document names the address, and its outgoing payments go mostly to two accounts not identified. The decision would change with evidence that validators XHash does not run also pay this address, or that it belongs to one of XHash's clients.

evidence.note: 7,715 signed XHash.com and 5,751 SSV's default graffiti; 7 signed anything else

0229-consensys-staking-depositor-f8c1c8.summary: Validators this account deposited are Consensys Staking's: it batched them as Consensys's platform does, they paid the client's own fee recipient, and their software changed in step with Consensys's other validators.
0229-consensys-staking-depositor-f8c1c8.decision: Validators whose first deposit this account sent are run and allocated by Consensys (Consensys Staking).

grounds.text: Consensys's staking guide sends clients' batch deposits through the contract this account used, up to 100 validators a time
This account never sent more than 100 in a transaction, and its validators paid a fee recipient of the client's own
Their client software changed release by release within days of Consensys's other validators, weeks before most of the network

0229-consensys-staking-depositor-f8c1c8.would_change: A Consensys or Staked statement contradicting it, or evidence that another operator ran these validators.
0229-consensys-staking-depositor-f8c1c8.explanation:
The account 0xf8c1…83b1 is the deposit account of a Consensys Staking client. Validators whose first deposit it sent are attributed to Consensys as allocator and operator, while the client keeps its own withdrawal address. It sent the first deposits of 2,278 validators between 7 March 2022 and 4 May 2023, through the batch deposit contract 0x39dc…da29. All have since exited.

The route. [Consensys's staking guide](https://docs.staking.consensys.io/staking-help/create-stake) sends clients' batch deposits through this contract, up to 100 validators (3,200 ETH) a transaction, and lets the client choose the fee recipient. The contract was written and deployed by Staked ([its repository](https://github.com/Stakedllc/eth2-batch-contract)), whose own deposit accounts use it too; they batch up to 185 validators at once and pay Staked's fee recipient. This account never sent more than 100 validators in one transaction. Their blocks paid 0xf17d…358f, a fee recipient of the client's own. The same client also deposited through two other accounts recorded in their own decisions: the three were given their first gas by one account within a few blocks of one another, and their validators share a Safe multisig.

The operator. The validators' graffiti carries client version strings only. Across the 36 client releases they signed, their first block with each version came a median 0.21 days from the first by Consensys's other validators, while the network as a whole had first used the same version a median 12.4 days earlier. Coinbase's validator fleet adopts releases at almost the same times, so the timing alone does not separate the two; the route does, since this is the contract Consensys's guide names, not Coinbase's.

Why Consensys is the allocator. A client staking through a provider's platform has chosen that provider, who generates the keys and runs the validators; the client keeps the withdrawal address (the rule applied to providers' depositor contracts, decision 0005). Consensys's validator staking for MetaMask is recorded in decision 0135. Explorer labels are recorded as leads. The decision would change with a Consensys or Staked statement contradicting it, or evidence that another operator ran these validators.

0238-bitmine-staking-october-2026.summary: Six addresses that proved common control together with BitMine's wallets deposited exactly the 159,728 ETH by which BitMine's reported staked ETH rose in the week of 20 October 2026.
0238-bitmine-staking-october-2026.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 6 addresses are BitMine's treasury staking.

grounds.text: All six sent 0.001 ETH in the same window on 31 August 2026 as all of BitMine's wallets in decision 0087, to the same new account
On 20 October 2026 they deposited 159,728 ETH; no other BitMine address deposited in October
BitMine's reported staked ETH rose from 5,067,309 (18 October) to 5,227,037 (25 October): by exactly 159,728
Like BitMine's other wallets, each deposits compounding validators to itself, through the same batch contracts

0238-bitmine-staking-october-2026.would_change: A later BitMine figure these deposits do not fit, or evidence that an address is held by someone other than BitMine.
0238-bitmine-staking-october-2026.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these six addresses are BitMine Immersion Technologies' treasury staking, with BitMine as allocator. On 20 October 2026 the six deposited 159,728 ETH in 84 compounding (0x02) validators of about 1,900 ETH, each address depositing to itself. In late October 2026 the deposits were still waiting to be processed by the beacon chain, so the validators are attributed as they appear.

Common control. All six took part in the control transfers of 31 August 2026 described under decision 0087: each sent 0.001 ETH to the same newly created account as BitMine's other wallets, within the same 73 minutes. Until 20 October none of them had staked; they were among the senders that held unstaked ETH.

The match with BitMine's figures. BitMine reported 5,067,309 ETH staked as of [11 October](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-6-03-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash--marketable-securities-holdings-of-16-2-billion-302905339.html) and again as of [18 October 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/es/comunicados-de-prensa/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-anuncia-que-sus-tenencias-de-eth-alcanzan-los-6-04-millones-de-tokens-302912524.html), and 5,227,037 ETH as of [25 October 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/in/news-releases/bitmine-immersion-technologies-bmnr-announces-eth-holdings-reach-6-05-million-tokens-and-total-crypto-and-total-cash--marketable-securities-holdings-of-15-billion-302919315.html). The rise, 159,728 ETH, equals these six addresses' deposits to the ETH, and no address of decisions 0087, 0115 or 0138 deposited during October. BitMine therefore counts ETH as staked from the time it is deposited, before the validators are active.

The same way of staking. Each address deposits compounding validators to itself, as BitMine's other wallets do: five of them through the two batch contracts that BitMine's other wallets also used, and one directly to the deposit contract.

Limits. As for decision 0087, the control transfers show one holder, or parties acting together, and the identification with BitMine rests on its reported figures; an exact match to the ETH makes coincidence unlikely. No operator has been identified for these validators. The decision would change with a later BitMine figure these deposits do not fit, or with evidence that an address is held by someone other than BitMine.

0240-sharplink-principal.summary: Wallets that received the 10,000 ETH Sharplink bought from the Ethereum Foundation, and whose LsETH tracks Sharplink's reported LsETH, stake through Figment and Coinbase: they are Sharplink's.
0240-sharplink-principal.decision: Sharplink is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 21 addresses: the ETH is Sharplink's, staked through Figment and Coinbase.

grounds.text: The Ethereum Foundation sent exactly 10,000 ETH into the group the day after Sharplink's purchase of 10,000 ETH from it closed
The group minted 256k ETH of LsETH in mid-2025; less its redemptions it matches Sharplink's reported LsETH on four dates
Its LsETH redemptions went into ether.fi in January and March 2026, as Sharplink's weETH grew by the same amount
The 21 addresses were all funded from within the group, from 31 May 2025, and each stakes through Figment or Coinbase

0240-sharplink-principal.would_change: A Sharplink disclosure these balances do not fit, or evidence that a wallet in the group holds ETH for someone else.
0240-sharplink-principal.explanation:
Sharplink, Inc. is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 21 addresses: the ETH is Sharplink's, and Sharplink chose its providers. In October 2026 the addresses held about 9,400 active validators with some 301k ETH: about 179k in validators run by Figment, about 100k in validators deposited through Figment's batch contract whose blocks are all signed by Galaxy, and 22k in Coinbase's custody staking, in vaults of 3,200 ETH. Figment, Galaxy and Coinbase remain the allocators of these validators; this decision records whose stake it is.

The Ethereum Foundation's sale. Sharplink [bought 10,000 ETH from the Ethereum Foundation](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1981535/000164117225018680/ex99-1.htm) in a transaction that closed on 10 July 2025. On 11 July 2025 the Foundation's address (decision 0195) sent exactly 10,000 ETH to 0x3536…4feb, a wallet of this group that otherwise received ETH only from 0x0b26…3e57 and passed it on to the group's LsETH wallet.

The wallets. One account, 0xcd9e…5f75, itself funded by a single account, 0x3356…6836, began passing ETH to the group on 31 May 2025, after Sharplink's private placement of 26 May; Sharplink's [first treasury release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001981535/000164117225014970/ex99-1.htm) reported 176,271 ETH on 13 June 2025, over 95% of it in staking and liquid staking. From there ETH was passed from wallet to wallet within the group, and each of the 21 addresses deposits validators through Figment's batch deposit contract or Coinbase's. Three of the addresses, 0x2560…5136 and the two it funded, received their ETH through single-use relay addresses from a trading account rather than from the group, but 0x2560…5136 also passed ETH to the group's wallet 0x24eb…b391.

The match with Sharplink's LsETH. Sharplink reports its holdings split into native ETH, LsETH and weETH. The group minted 256,474 ETH of LsETH between 30 May and 23 July 2025 and was paid redemptions of 35,627 ETH on 26 December 2025 and 16,740 ETH on 2 March 2026. With LsETH's growth from rewards, about 2.2% a year, that leaves about 224k ETH on 15 February and 208k on 31 March 2026. Sharplink reported [225,429 ETH on 15 February](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1981535/000149315226007427/form8-k.htm), and [209,361 on 31 March and 209,789 on 4 May 2026](https://s3.amazonaws.com/b2icontent.irpass.cc/2597/rl165636.pdf), with no redemption in between, as on chain. Both redemptions passed through 0x0323…91b1 into ether.fi, on 7 January and 6 March 2026; between 15 February and 31 March Sharplink's weETH rose by 17,018 ETH, against 16,740 deposited. Redemptions of 29,152 ETH paid on 3 to 5 July 2026 match Sharplink's [LsETH falling to 181,299 ETH by 28 June](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001981535/000149315226031202/form8-k.htm); they went to a different address, which passed them to 0x3356…6836, the account that first funded the group.

Limits. No document names these addresses. Apart from the Ethereum Foundation's transfer, the identification rests on the timing and on the match with Sharplink's figures. LsETH redemptions reach their owners through a forwarding contract shared by other holders, so the link to the July 2026 redemptions is weaker than to the earlier ones. The account that funded the group had been used once before, in 2022. The 21 addresses hold about half of the 589k native ETH Sharplink reported in March 2026; the rest has not been found. The decision would change with a Sharplink disclosure these balances do not fit, or with evidence that a wallet in the group holds ETH for someone else.

0241-sharplink-coinbase-vaults.summary: 86 Coinbase custody vaults share one fee recipient and one reward sweep with seven vaults that Sharplink's own wallet funded; with decision 0240 they account for Sharplink's reported native ETH.
0241-sharplink-coinbase-vaults.decision: Sharplink is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 88 addresses: 86 Coinbase custody vaults and the two wallets that collect and restake their rewards.

grounds.text: All 93 vaults, including seven funded by Sharplink's wallet in decision 0240, sweep their rewards to the same two wallets
Their validators share a fee recipient that no other validator has used, in 316 blocks from August 2025
They were deposited from August to October 2025, mostly in the four weeks when Sharplink bought most of its ETH
With decision 0240, deposits by 19 October 2025 total 600,114 ETH; Sharplink reported 601,143 native ETH that day

0241-sharplink-coinbase-vaults.would_change: A Sharplink disclosure these deposits do not fit, or evidence that the fee recipient or the reward wallets serve another client.
0241-sharplink-coinbase-vaults.explanation:
Sharplink, Inc. is the principal of the validators withdrawing to these 88 addresses. 86 of them are vaults in Coinbase's custody staking, most staking 3,200 ETH in 100 validators; the other two collect the vaults' rewards and stake them again. In October 2026 the addresses held about 9,000 active validators with some 296k ETH. Coinbase remains the custodian of the vaults and, by decisions 0134 and 0242, their allocator; this decision records whose stake it is.

The link to Sharplink. Decision 0240 identifies a group of Sharplink's wallets, one of which funded seven Coinbase vaults of 3,200 ETH in August 2025. Those seven vaults pay their consensus rewards to the same two wallets, 0xf036…51e2 until October 2025 and 0x42c5…02bb since, as 86 further vaults do. The two wallets stake what they collect in validators of their own, through Coinbase's batch deposit contract. The vaults' validators also name one fee recipient, 0xd6a7…4a61, for their execution-layer rewards: it appears in 316 blocks from August 2025 to October 2026, every one proposed by a validator of these vaults, and it too passes its balance to the reward wallets. A custodian's settings of this kind are per client, so the 93 vaults are taken to belong to one client, Sharplink.

The match with Sharplink's figures. The vaults received 308k ETH of deposits between 4 August and 7 September 2025, the weeks in which Sharplink bought most of its ETH: its holdings reached [740,760 ETH on 17 August](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001981535/000164117225024734/ex99-1.htm) and [797,704 on 24 August](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001981535/000164117225025469/ex99-1.htm). Sharplink reports its native ETH, the part not held as LsETH or weETH. By 19 October 2025 these vaults and the wallets of decision 0240 had deposited 600,114 ETH to validators; Sharplink reported [601,143 native ETH and 258,710 ETH in LsETH that day](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1981535/000149315225018731/ex99-1.htm). By 31 March 2026 the deposits were 607,615 ETH against [589,305 native ETH](https://s3.amazonaws.com/b2icontent.irpass.cc/2597/rl165636.pdf); some validators of decision 0240 had exited by then.

Limits. No document names these addresses. The identification rests on the shared reward and fee settings, which tie these vaults to the seven funded by Sharplink's wallet, and on the match with Sharplink's figures; it would fail if Coinbase used one fee recipient and one reward wallet for several clients. The decision would change with a Sharplink disclosure these deposits do not fit, or with evidence that the fee recipient or the reward wallets serve another client.

0242-coinbase-prime-sharplink-custody-va.summary: 64 Coinbase custody vaults of Sharplink's run Coinbase's retail fleet's client builds week by week and share their fee recipient with 29 vaults already in decision 0134: Coinbase runs them, as it runs those.
0242-coinbase-prime-sharplink-custody-va.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 64 addresses are Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake, run by Coinbase, as in decision 0134.

grounds.text: 216 of their 217 blocks with a build string carry a build Coinbase's retail validators ran that week; none names an operator
They share one fee recipient, used by no other validator, with 29 Sharplink vaults that decision 0134 attributes to Coinbase
Coinbase holds them in custody (decision 0167) and they were deposited through Coinbase's batch deposit contract
Coinbase reports running validators holding about 4.5M ETH for itself and its clients, excluding stake routed to partners

0242-coinbase-prime-sharplink-custody-va.would_change: A named operator in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying this stake is run by partners.
0242-coinbase-prime-sharplink-custody-va.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 64 addresses are the stake of a Coinbase Prime custody client, Sharplink (decision 0241), run by Coinbase on its own validator fleet; Coinbase is the allocator, as decision 0134 finds for other custody clients. In October 2026 the addresses held about 6,400 active validators with some 205k ETH.

Why these were not in decision 0134. Decision 0134 tested custody addresses for Coinbase's fleet only among those not attributed at the time. These 64 were then attributed by an earlier decision, 0114, later replaced by a record of custody alone (decision 0167), so they were never tested and fell back to "Coinbase custody clients, provider not identified". 29 further vaults of the same client were tested, and are in decision 0134.

Operator. Clients write their version into block graffiti as a short build string. These validators mostly leave the graffiti blank, as Coinbase's own retail validators do; of the 217 blocks they proposed with a build string, 216 carry a build that Coinbase's retail validators were running in the same week, and none names an operator. They also name the same fee recipient, 0xd6a7…4a61, as Sharplink's 29 vaults in decision 0134, and no other validator has used it.

Custody and source. Coinbase holds the vaults in custody (decision 0167), and they were deposited through Coinbase's batch deposit contract. [Coinbase reports](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/ethereum-validator-performance-report-q1-2026) running validators holding about 4.5M ETH in the first quarter of 2026, excluding stake routed to partner providers.

Limits. Build strings appear in about 1% of these validators' blocks, so the operator evidence rests on few blocks, though all but one match; the shared fee recipient ties them to vaults that decision 0134 attributes on the same evidence. The decision would change with an operator's name in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying that this stake is run by partners.

0243-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-retest.summary: 171 Coinbase custody addresses that decision 0134's operator test never reached pass it: their validators run Coinbase's retail fleet's builds, or pay the same client fee recipients as validators that do.
0243-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-retest.decision: Validators withdrawing to these 171 addresses are Coinbase Prime custody clients' stake, run by Coinbase, as in decision 0134.

grounds.text: All 473 of their blocks with a build string since February 2025 carry builds Coinbase's retail validators were running then
Each is in a client group, linked by fee recipients that pay almost only Coinbase's validators, that runs Coinbase's builds
Since February 2025 none of their validators, nor any other at the same address, signed an operator's name
Coinbase holds them in custody (decision 0167) and reports running validators for its institutional clients

0243-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-retest.would_change: A named operator in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying this stake is run by partners.
0243-coinbase-prime-custody-fleet-retest.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to these 171 addresses are the stake of Coinbase Prime custody clients, run by Coinbase on its own validator fleet; Coinbase is the allocator, as decision 0134 finds for other custody addresses. In October 2026 the addresses held about 3,230 active validators with some 128k ETH.

Why these were not in decision 0134. Coinbase holds all of these addresses in custody (decision 0167). Decision 0134 tested custody addresses for Coinbase's fleet only among those not attributed at the time; these were then attributed by an earlier decision, 0114, later replaced by the record of custody alone, so they were left in "Coinbase custody clients, provider not identified" without the test.

The test. It is decision 0134's. Clients write their version into block graffiti as a short build string. Since February 2025 these addresses' validators proposed 473 blocks with a build string, and every one carries a build that Coinbase's own retail validators were running at the time; none carries a build only Galaxy's validators run, and none names an operator. 106 of the addresses have validators with such blocks. The rest mostly leave graffiti blank, as Coinbase's retail validators do, and are tied to the others by their fee recipients: resolving the builder's payment in each block, 150 of the addresses pay a recipient that receives at least 90% of its block payments from validators in Coinbase's custody and staking, and that addresses of decisions 0134, 0226 or 0242 also pay. Every one of the 116 client groups formed this way includes validators running Coinbase's builds or addresses already found to be on its fleet.

What was left out. Of the 675 custody addresses tested, 504 remain as they were: those whose validators never emit a build string and share no client fee recipient with Coinbase's fleet (about 456k ETH), those whose client group also runs another operator's builds (about 194k ETH), and those where other validators at the same address sign Galaxy's name, even when linked to Coinbase's fleet (about 95k ETH). For these, custody alone does not show who runs the validators.

Limits. Build strings appear in a small share of blocks, and for 65 addresses the evidence is the shared fee recipient alone, which shows the same client rather than the same operator; a client using Coinbase for some validators and another provider for others would look the same where the other provider leaves graffiti blank. [Coinbase reports](https://www.coinbase.com/blog/ethereum-validator-performance-report-q1-2026) running validators holding about 4.5M ETH in the first quarter of 2026, excluding stake routed to partner providers. The decision would change with an operator's name in these validators' graffiti, a build mix diverging from Coinbase's fleet, or Coinbase saying that this stake is run by partners.

0255-attestant-lido-operators.summary: Lido operators 1/29 and 4/0, and Lido's operator group 4.1, are Attestant's.
0255-attestant-lido-operators.decision: Lido's node operators 1/29 (Attestant (BVI) Limited) and 4/0 (Attestant - PGO), and Lido's operator group 4.1, are run by Attestant.

grounds.text: Lido's registry added operator 1/29 as "Attestant (BVI) Limited" on 16 December 2022
Operator 4/0 named itself "Attestant" in July 2026, then "Attestant - PGO"
Lido's metadata registry names operator group 4.1 "Attestant (BVI) Limited"

0255-attestant-lido-operators.would_change: A Lido or Attestant statement that these operators belong to another company.
0255-attestant-lido-operators.explanation: Lido's node operator registry, read on chain, added operator 29 of the curated module as "Attestant (BVI) Limited" on 16 December 2022. In the second curated module, operator 0 set its name to "Attestant" on 24 July 2026 and to "Attestant - PGO" on 4 August 2026, and Lido's operator metadata registry groups Attestant's operators as group 4.1, "Attestant (BVI) Limited". These operators are recorded as run by Attestant from the first registration. Who owns Attestant is a separate decision (0259).

evidence.note: Operator 4/0 sets its name to "Attestant - PGO"

The name has not changed since

0256-chorus-one-lido-operator.would_change: A Lido or Chorus One statement that the operator belongs to another company.

The operator is recorded as run by Chorus One from then. Who owns Chorus One is a separate decision (0260).

0257-pier-two-lido-operator.summary: Lido operator 1/36 is Pier Two's, since renamed MAVAN.
0257-pier-two-lido-operator.decision: Lido's node operator 1/36 is run by Pier Two, from its renaming to Pier Two on 24 August 2024.

grounds.text: Lido's registry added operator 1/36 as "Numic" in October 2023 and renamed it "Pier Two" on 24 August 2024
It was renamed "MAVAN" on 26 June 2026, after MAVAN bought Pier Two

0257-pier-two-lido-operator.would_change: Evidence that operator 1/36 was handed to a company other than Pier Two or its owners.
0257-pier-two-lido-operator.explanation: Lido's node operator registry, read on chain, added operator 36 of the curated module as "Numic" on 6 October 2023, renamed it "Pier Two" on 24 August 2024 and "MAVAN" on 26 June 2026, three months after MAVAN Holdings bought Pier Two (decision 0261). The operator is recorded as run by Pier Two from its renaming to Pier Two; before then, which company ran it is not recorded.

0258-mavan-lido-operator.decision: Lido's node operator 4/26 (MAVAN - PTO) is run by MAVAN.

grounds.text: Operator 4/26 named itself "MAVAN" on 28 July 2026, then "MAVAN - PTO"
MAVAN is BitMine's staking subsidiary, which owns Pier Two

0258-mavan-lido-operator.would_change: A Lido or MAVAN statement that the operator belongs to another company.

MAVAN Holdings is BitMine's staking subsidiary, which owns Pier Two (decisions 0261 and 0262). The operator is recorded as run by MAVAN from its first name.

0259-attestant-owned-by-bitwise.decision: Attestant is owned by Bitwise from 13 November 2024.

grounds.text: Bitwise announced its acquisition of Attestant Limited on 13 November 2024
Attestant's business continues as Bitwise Onchain Solutions

0259-attestant-owned-by-bitwise.would_change: A later sale of Attestant, or a Bitwise statement that the acquisition did not complete.
0259-attestant-owned-by-bitwise.explanation: Bitwise Asset Management [announced on 13 November 2024](https://bitwiseinvestments.com/newsroom/bitwise-acquires-ethereum-staking-provider-attestant) that it had acquired Attestant Limited, an Ethereum staking provider, and that Attestant's business would continue as Bitwise Onchain Solutions. 0260-chorus-one-owned-by-bitwise.summary: Bitwise owns Chorus One from 24 February 2026.
0260-chorus-one-owned-by-bitwise.decision: Chorus One is owned by Bitwise from 24 February 2026.

Chorus One joins Bitwise Onchain Solutions, Bitwise's staking business

0260-chorus-one-owned-by-bitwise.would_change: A later sale of Chorus One, or a Bitwise statement that the acquisition did not complete.
0260-chorus-one-owned-by-bitwise.explanation: Bitwise Asset Management [announced on 24 February 2026](https://bitwiseinvestments.com/newsroom/bitwise-acquires-staking-infrastructure-pioneer-chorus-one) that it had acquired Chorus One, a staking provider, which joins Bitwise Onchain Solutions, Bitwise's staking business. 0261-pier-two-owned-by-mavan.summary: MAVAN owns Pier Two from 24 March 2026.
0261-pier-two-owned-by-mavan.decision: Pier Two is owned by MAVAN Holdings from 24 March 2026.

Standard Validator LLC is now named MAVAN Holdings

0261-pier-two-owned-by-mavan.explanation: BitMine Immersion Technologies [reported on 24 March 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1829311/000149315226013609/form8-k.htm) that Standard Validator LLC, its majority-owned subsidiary, was the buyer of all outstanding shares of Pier Two Holdings Pty Ltd. 0262-mavan-owned-by-bitmine.summary: BitMine owns 98% of MAVAN, from at least 24 March 2026.
0262-mavan-owned-by-bitmine.decision: MAVAN Holdings is owned by BitMine from 24 March 2026 (98%).

0262-mavan-owned-by-bitmine.explanation: BitMine Immersion Technologies [reported on 24 March 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1829311/000149315226013609/form8-k.htm) that Standard Validator LLC, now MAVAN Holdings, was its majority-owned, consolidated subsidiary, and its [quarterly report to 31 May 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001829311/000162828026048157/bmnr-20260531.htm) gives its ownership interest as 98%; the remaining 2% is held by Ethereum Tower LLC. 0273-a41-lido-operators.decision: Lido's node operator 1/32 ("A41") is run by A41.

0322-merge-sweeps-to-0x2bc1.summary: Six withdrawal addresses whose rewards are swept together to 0x2bc1…8d56 belong to one staker.
0322-merge-sweeps-to-0x2bc1.decision: The validators withdrawing to these six addresses belong to one staker, as its rewards all go to one collecting account, 0x2bc1…8d56.

grounds.text: All six addresses send their ETH to 0x2bc1…8d56, which passes everything on to one account
They do so in the same four rounds (22 December 2024, 26 March 2025, 27 August 2025, 12 May 2026), each within about 150 blocks, and in the same order in the first three

0322-merge-sweeps-to-0x2bc1.would_change: Evidence that 0x2bc1…8d56 collects for several unrelated stakers, such as a service sweeping for its clients.
0322-merge-sweeps-to-0x2bc1.explanation: Six withdrawal addresses, holding 456 validators (15,000 ETH) in four clusters, send their withdrawn rewards to the same account, 0x2bc1…8d56, which passes all of it on to a single account. The sweeps come in four rounds (22 December 2024, 26 March 2025, 27 August 2025 and 12 May 2026), each finished within about 150 blocks, with the addresses sweeping in the same order in the first three. Such coordinated sweeps are run by whoever controls all six addresses, so the four clusters are joined as one staker, at the reward level. The staker is not identified.

evidence.note: Round 1 (block 21,459,718): 0x6acc…f39a sweeps to 0x2bc1…8d56; the other five follow within 136 blocks
Round 2 (block 22,133,281): the same six, in the same order, within 76 blocks
Round 3 (block 23,235,496): the same six, in the same order, within 231 blocks
Round 4 (block 25,082,053): the same six within 120 blocks, the larger three first

0323-binance-staking-withdrawal-address.summary: Binance's own reserve wallets staked to 0x8e60…8224, or funded the account that did: validators withdrawing to it are Binance's staking.
0323-binance-staking-withdrawal-address.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0x8e60…8224 are Binance's staking.

grounds.text: 0x32e1…1149, a wallet in Binance's reserve list of 1 October 2026, made 40 deposits naming this address in April 2026
0x2d59…b177 made 146 deposits (290,032 ETH) naming it from April to October 2026, funded only by five wallets in the same list
Binance's deposit account 0xbdd7…32a8 names it in every deposit; it sends its withdrawn stake to wBETH's staking address

0323-binance-staking-withdrawal-address.would_change: A later Binance reserve list or statement placing 0x8e60…8224 with a client, or evidence that its validators belong to someone other than Binance.
0323-binance-staking-withdrawal-address.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0x8e60…8224 are attributed to Binance's staking as allocator. In October 2026 about 76,900 active validators, some 3.54M ETH, withdraw there.

Binance's proof-of-reserves page lists the wallets behind its reserve report of 1 October 2026. One of its Ethereum hot and cold wallets, 0x32e1…1149 (80,000 ETH at the report), itself made 40 beacon deposits between 21 and 28 April 2026, every one naming 0x8e60…8224 as the withdrawal address. A second account, 0x2d59…b177, made 146 deposits naming the same address between 1 April and 22 October 2026, 290,032 ETH in all; every ETH it received came from five wallets on the same list, among them 0x28c6…1d60, and it has sent ETH nowhere but the deposit contract.

This confirms decision 0006, which identified the address through Binance's deposit account 0xbdd7…32a8 and the wBETH token: all of that account's execution-layer deposits name 0x8e60…8224, and the address has sent its withdrawn stake only to the staking address set in wBETH's contract. The address itself is not on Binance's list, which covers wallets holding liquid assets; a validator's stake sits on the beacon chain, not in its withdrawal address. Whether Binance runs these validators itself is not established, so no operator is recorded.

evidence.note: 0x32e1…1149 (listed Binance wallet) deposits with 0x8e60 credentials, block 24,927,241 (2026-04-21), the first of 40

0324-okx-staking-withdrawal-addresses.summary: OKX's signed proof-of-reserves file lists every validator withdrawing to 0xe839…506c and 0xd5f8…7634 as OKX's staked ETH: they are OKX's staking.
0324-okx-staking-withdrawal-addresses.decision: Validators withdrawing to 0xe839…506c or 0xd5f8…7634 are OKX's staking.

grounds.text: OKX's proof-of-reserves file of 3 October 2026 lists 7,678 validators at the two addresses as its native ETH staking
Each row is signed with the withdrawal address's key; every signature recovers to that address
Every validator active at the two addresses in October 2026 is in the file

0324-okx-staking-withdrawal-addresses.would_change: A later OKX reserve file leaving these addresses out, or an OKX statement that their validators belong to clients.
0324-okx-staking-withdrawal-addresses.explanation:
Validators withdrawing to 0xe839…506c or 0xd5f8…7634 are attributed to OKX's staking as allocator. In October 2026 about 5,960 active validators withdraw there, some 618,000 ETH (0xe839…506c: 5,572 validators, 178,000 ETH; 0xd5f8…7634: 388 compounding validators, 440,000 ETH).

OKX publishes a wallet file with each proof of reserves. The file for 3 October 2026 lists, under "Native ETH Staking", 7,290 validators withdrawing to 0xe839…506c and 388 withdrawing to 0xd5f8…7634, each row with the message "I am an OKX address" signed by the withdrawal address. The signer of every row recovers to the address the row names, so whoever compiled the file holds those keys. Every validator active at the two addresses in October 2026 is in the file.

Decision 0025 already identified OKX's deposit account from the same file. This decision attributes the two withdrawal addresses directly, so the validators rest on OKX's own listing rather than on the deposit route. Who operates them is not stated in the file, so no operator is recorded.
